| CMH-OFFLINE-04 | Offline export stripping is data-safe and egress-safe: it skips comment-data and layer-descriptor JSON scripts even when comment text mentions `import('https://...')` - an exemption those blocks now EARN by being inert data rather than CLAIM by id (below) -, strips runnable inline scripts with remote dynamic imports, bare remote imports, remote `from` imports, or network dynamic-import targets, strips a runnable inline script carrying a direct scripted navigation to a network URL literal (CMH-OFFLINE-05 - the one egress channel the CSP cannot close, where that row also records what the literal pattern misses and over-matches), ignores `data-id="commentableHtmlLayer"` descriptor decoys when retargeting mode, neutralizes every network-loading media path (`img`, `iframe`, `video`, `audio`, `source`, `track`, SVG `image`/`use`, `input[type=image]`, `object`, `embed`, and legacy `background`), clears an `iframe`'s `srcdoc` UNCONDITIONALLY - a nested document carried as an ATTRIBUTE VALUE, which no pass here can see into (every walk visits ELEMENTS, and that markup never becomes elements) and which the strict validator's tag index reads as attribute TEXT, so an inline handler, a meta refresh or a network loader parked inside one used to ride through an export and past `--strict` alike; the offline CSP does not close it either, since a `srcdoc` frame is content the policy is INHERITED into rather than a fetch `frame-src 'none'` blocks, and the inherited policy still allows inline script, which can navigate the top-level document. The direction chosen (issue #996, settled the way #926 settled the meta-refresh one) is that an offline document may not carry `srcdoc` at all: the strip clears the attribute on PRESENCE - an empty or inert one included, so nothing the gate blesses is a file an export still changes - and offline `--strict` rejects any that remains (CMH-OFFLINE-05), which is what makes the two sides agree BY CONSTRUCTION; recursively parsing the nested document on both sides is the alternative, and keeping two independent parsers in step is precisely the drift these rows exist to prevent. Issue #1080 re-opened that trade and CONFIRMED it rather than switching to sanitization, so the content cost is a DECISION and not an omission. Sanitizing - parsing each `srcdoc`, running the same network strip and handler scrub over the nested document, and writing it back - was prototyped on the abandoned `issue-991` branch (PR #1077, closed as superseded) rather than here, and weighing that prototype is what settled the question; it was rejected on four grounds: (1) it needs TWO independent recursive parsers, the exporter's browser DOM and this gate's pure-Python tokenizer, to agree at every depth on serialization, doctype reconstruction and rendering mode, fixed-point settling under serialize-then-reparse, and one parse budget shared by the whole export - each of them a divergence point whose failure mode is either a hole (an export ships what `--strict` would reject) or a false rejection of a valid file; (2) the precedents that preserve content - a `<base>` keeping its `target`, a reserved-id block retyped to inert JSON, a `<script>` losing an inert `href` - are attribute-level or type-level edits INSIDE the document both sides already parse, and none of them stands up a second parse pipeline in two languages; (3) it would not even END the loss, since a value that will not settle under reparse still has to be removed, so it trades a deterministic rule (no `srcdoc` survives, ever) for one whose outcome turns on parser quirks an author cannot predict; and (4) the AUTHOR does not lose the content itself - an offline export is a DERIVED artifact (the exporter parses a serialized copy and never mutates the live document), so the source file still carries the `srcdoc`. Ground (4) answers for the author and NOT for the recipient, who holds only the export and meets an unexplained frame with no toast behind it, so what was missing splits in two. The half taken first is notice BEFORE the export rather than a copy inside it: CMH-VAL-24 gives the author an authoring-time ADVISORY that Export Offline will empty the frame. The second half is now taken too (issue #1119): the cheap middle option between clearing and sanitizing, where the export keeps the nested markup beside the emptied frame as ESCAPED INERT TEXT (a collapsed `<details>` wrapping `<pre><code>`). It needs only ESCAPING on the exporter side - there is no second nested-document parser, so the ground-(1) drift argument does not touch it - NOTHING at all on the gate side, since the presence rule is unchanged and the two still agree by construction, and it lands content both sides already parse, exactly the ground-(2) precedent. The PLACEMENT rule is one sentence, and it is what settles the parked cases rather than a list of exceptions: the block goes where the FRAME is, so it is visible to exactly the reader the nested document was visible to. A `<template>`-parked frame renders nothing and neither does its block; a `<noscript>`-parked one renders nothing for a scripting-ON reader (that body is raw text in a `display:none` element) and renders for the scripting-OFF reader the fallback exists for, and the block follows it in both directions - so nothing is lost that was ever shown, and nothing is shown that was not. The bounds that keep it from adding content where none was lost are each an ANSWER rather than an omission. An EMPTY or WHITESPACE-ONLY `srcdoc` gets no block: there is no nested document to keep, and a `<summary>` announcing a preserved document over an empty `<pre>` is noise. That trim is safe HERE and would not be on the removal rule, because the attribute still goes on PRESENCE - what is PRESERVED and what is REMOVED are separate questions, and only the second one the gate sees. WHICH whitespace is a literal ASCII class (`_OFFLINE_SRCDOC_CONTENT_RE`, mirrored by the validator's `nested.strip(" \t\n\f\r")`) rather than either engine's default, for exactly the reason `_OFFLINE_REL_WS_RE` is: JS `trim()` also takes NBSP and U+FEFF while Python's `str.strip()` also takes U+001C-U+001F and U+0085, so the two disagreed in BOTH directions on real values (`&#xFEFF;` had the advisory promise a block the exporter never inserted; `&#28;` had it deny one it did). A frame in a FOREIGN namespace gets none either, since an `<iframe>` inside `<svg>` renders nothing in any browser (so its nested document was never visible) and an HTML block serialized into foreign content would not render either, while an `<iframe>` inside `<foreignObject>` IS HTML-namespaced, does render, and correctly gets one. Because the block is FLOW content and a frame is PHRASING content, a frame inside a `<p>` anchors its block after that PARAGRAPH rather than beside itself: left inside, the recipient's parser would close the paragraph at the `<details>` start tag, re-parent any text after the frame and leave a stray empty `<p>`, so the export would not be serialize/reparse stable - the very property that rejecting sanitization bought. `<p>` is the whole of that rule rather than a phrasing-host list, because it is the only element the parser auto-closes on a `details` start tag, and the walk that finds it stops at the first NON-HTML ancestor - a frame inside `<foreignObject>` keeps its block inside the graphic, both because moving it out would put the text somewhere the frame does not render and because `<p>` is not in button scope from an SVG integration point, so a `details` there closes no paragraph at all. Two frames in ONE paragraph share that anchor, so each block is inserted after any block already there rather than at the paragraph's own next sibling: otherwise they come out in REVERSE order and each nested document is paired with the wrong frame, which is the one thing a recipient auditing preserved markup has to be able to trust. And the text is never capped or truncated, because bounding the LAYOUT (the block is collapsed) beats reintroducing the very loss this ends. Two normalizations reach it, and both exist so the export is a FIXED POINT: CR and CRLF become LF (the HTML tokenizer does that to any text it reparses, so a script-built `srcdoc` carrying CRLF would otherwise come back different on the second export), and the file-wide blank-line normalization every offline export already applies to its whole serialization (`\n{3,}` becomes `\n\n`) reaches the block exactly as it reaches an authored `<pre>` - the block is treated as the code block it is rather than specially. A frame that did not RENDER keeps a block that does not render: if the frame or an ancestor carries the `hidden` attribute the block carries it too, or an export would newly EXPOSE markup nobody was ever shown - sharpest for a `<p hidden>`, where the paragraph re-anchor lifts the block out of the hidden container. Only the DECLARATIVE attribute is read, because the exporter parses a detached document with no stylesheets and no layout, so a CSS-hidden subtree is not knowable there and guessing would be worse than the bounded rule. The KEPT count in the toast is read off the FINISHED document rather than banked as each block is inserted, because a later pass can still take one away (the straddling-noscript strip removes a `<noscript>` whose body straddles its own end tag, and a block parked inside goes with it) - claiming markup the file does not carry would reintroduce the silent loss this ends, now with a positive claim behind it. It is counted by IDENTITY rather than by walking the class, exactly as `_offlineCountKeptNeutralized` counts a neutralized script: `cmh-srcdoc-export` is public markup a source can legitimately already carry (a previously exported file re-imported, say), so a class walk would report an author's own block as preserved markup and could claim more kept documents than there were emptied frames. A preservation also never costs the EXPORT: the frame is emptied first, so a failure degrades to the pre-#1119 behavior instead of turning Export Offline into an error. The block wears `cm-skip`, exactly like every other layer-injected node inside the content root, which is what keeps it out of the section-hash and document-hash walks on BOTH sides (`_cmhScanSkip` in the runtime, `_SKIP_CLASSES` in `tools/authoring/section_hash.py`) and out of the anchor and selection walks: without it an export would shift its own section hashes, flip an already-reviewed section to "changed", and invalidate the validated stamp the same file carries - trading one loss for a worse one - so the block is readable but deliberately not commentable. It also means a Markdown export omits the block, which loses nothing: an `<iframe>` has no Markdown representation either, so the nested document was never in a `.md` export to begin with. One consequence is deliberate rather than incidental: the offline copy used to be strictly LESS revealing than its source (the nested document was dropped), and now shows it. Nothing is newly PRESENT - every other export mode already carries the same bytes in the `srcdoc` attribute, and so does the source the recipient could have been sent instead - but it is newly VISIBLE in the artifact most likely to be forwarded, which is why the block is collapsed and labelled rather than inlined. Re-exporting an already-exported file is IDEMPOTENT by construction rather than by a guard, since the first export removed the attribute the second would read and the block it left is inert text no pass on either side reads, and a test pins it. The ELEMENT is kept (an author's `title`, sizing and relative `src` are content), and the export toast now carries BOTH counts - how many frames were emptied, and how many kept their markup - because unlike a network strip this changes content that worked offline. It also clears an `iframe`'s `srcdoc` UNCONDITIONALLY - a nested document carried as an ATTRIBUTE VALUE, which no pass here can see into (every walk visits ELEMENTS, and that markup never becomes elements) and which the strict validator's tag index reads as attribute TEXT, so an inline handler, a meta refresh or a network loader parked inside one used to ride through an export and past `--strict` alike; the offline CSP does not close it either, since a `srcdoc` frame is content the policy is INHERITED into rather than a fetch `frame-src 'none'` blocks, and the inherited policy still allows inline script, which can navigate the top-level document. The direction chosen (issue #996, settled the way #926 settled the meta-refresh one) is that an offline document may not carry `srcdoc` at all: the strip clears the attribute on PRESENCE - an empty or inert one included, so nothing the gate blesses is a file an export still changes - and offline `--strict` rejects any that remains (CMH-OFFLINE-05), which is what makes the two sides agree BY CONSTRUCTION; recursively parsing the nested document on both sides is the alternative, and keeping two independent parsers in step is precisely the drift these rows exist to prevent. The ELEMENT is kept (an author's `title`, sizing and relative `src` are content), and the removal is COUNTED in the export toast, because unlike a network strip it takes away content that worked offline. It also reads a script's own network LOAD from the whole attribute set `src`, `href`, and `xlink:href` rather than `src` alone - an SVG `<script>` never uses `src` (it loads through SVG2 `href` or the legacy `xlink:href`) and its body is EMPTY, so a `script[src]` selector never saw it and the inline egress scan, which reads `textContent`, had nothing to read; such a script rode into a zero-network file with only the CSP between it and the fetch, and the strict validator mirrored the same blind spot and certified it as offline-clean, so both sides now read the same three attributes (`_OFFLINE_SCRIPT_LOAD_ATTRS` and the validator's `SCRIPT_LOAD_ATTRS`, pinned to each other by a parity test), each script element is examined ONCE (one carrying two network attributes is removed, and counted in the toast, once), and a relative or `data:` reference is still left untouched. Three bounds on that widening are stated rather than implied. What COUNTS as a load is namespace-blind on both sides, but what is DONE about it is not: `src` loads on a script a browser RUNS and `href`/`xlink:href` load on an SVG one, so those elements are removed, while on an HTML script the same attributes are inert (in HTML and in XHTML alike) and only the ATTRIBUTE is removed - deleting the element would destroy running author code over a dead attribute, and clearing the attribute leaves the validator, whose flat tokenizer has no namespace to consult, nothing to complain about, so the two agree without either of them having to know a namespace. A `src` on a DATA BLOCK is the same shape and now gets the same treatment (issue #1144): HTML's "prepare the script element" returns before the fetch step for such a type, so `<script type="application/json" src="https://host/x.json">` requests nothing - the strip used to delete the whole element, destroying an author's data over an attribute no browser reads, while the gate refused the same document for a load that never happens. Both sides moved together on the same predicate (`_offlineScriptSrcFetches` / the gate's `src` arm, pinned by evaluating the REAL runtime function in a JS engine over one shared corpus, the whitespace class included - a Python re-implementation of the normalization was what let `trim()` and `str.strip()` disagree about a `&#xFEFF;`-padded type unnoticed, which once this predicate decides a FETCH is a document the gate blesses and the export then deletes): the gate stops reporting it, and the strip takes the dead attribute alone so an export still carries no network-looking reference and remains idempotent under its own `--strict`. The residual that pairing used to carry is now closed rather than paid (issue #1171). For a MIME-parameter type, `nomodule` on a classic script, a whitespace-only `type` or a non-JavaScript `language` fallback, the type-only `_offlineIsRunnableScriptType` said runnable, so the strip removed the whole ELEMENT AND ITS BODY though no browser requests any of them - an author's content deleted behind a verdict the gate raised for a request that never happens. The exporter's `_offlineScriptSrcFetches` now asks `_offlineScriptSrcIsFetched`, a mirror of the validator's `script_src_fetches`, and `test_the_python_and_js_script_src_fetches_predicates_agree` pins the two over a shared corpus of ATTRIBUTE SETS in a real JS engine, so the gate and the strip still call the same scripts loaders. WHICH question a pass asks is now explicit, because the two are genuinely different and the difference is MEASURED (CMH-VAL-08 records the engine evidence and the spec that re-measures it). A pass that decides whether a `src` is a real reference asks the FETCH question, which is namespace-BLIND and does NOT honour the legacy `event`+`for` pair: Chromium's preload scanner requests that script and then never runs it, so a strip that spared it would leave a live network reference in a file that promises zero network, and an earlier revision of this change did exactly that. A pass that decides whether CODE runs - the renderer/loader-shim strip, which deletes on what a body says, and the chart HOIST, which relocates an element - asks `_offlineScriptRunsInlineBody`, the mirror of `script_runs_inline_body`, and that is a THIRD question rather than a rename of the second. It layers two rules on the execution predicate, and both were measured: the insertion NAMESPACE must be one that defines `script` and runs it (HTML and SVG do; a MathML `<script>` is an inert unknown element whose body never executes), and an element that loads EXTERNALLY never runs its own child text. Asking the bare execution predicate there was a real defect this round caught: the hoist selects `script:not([src])` by local name in EVERY namespace, so it moved a MathML script into `<body>`, and an HTML serialization of that document RUNS it on reparse - the export would have granted execution the source never had, which is the one thing an exporter must never do. Execution stays namespace-SCOPED for the mirror-image measured reason: an SVG `<script nomodule>` with an inline body really does run, so reading `nomodule` there would delete or fail to order a script that works. The load strip is content-preserving in the one shape where the two questions genuinely split. A classic script carrying the legacy `event`+`for` pair with a network `src` is REQUESTED and then never run, so the dead ATTRIBUTE alone is taken and the element and its inert body stay - the same treatment the data-block and inert-`href` branches already give, reaching zero network without costing the author content. The renderer/loader-NAME pass makes the same split for the same reason: it removes a bundle-shaped `src` by FILENAME, and deleting the element there would silently undo the preservation for the one spelling whose URL happens to look like a renderer. A block the export itself NEUTRALIZED keeps the whole-element treatment, because it was runnable as authored. Two shapes keep the old whole-element treatment, and both are about PASS ORDER rather than about the type. An ACTIVE-DATA block keeps its `src` through this pass, because `_offlineActiveDataBlockIsRemovable` judges an import map by `hasAttribute("src")` and this pass runs FIRST: clearing the attribute here hid the block from the pass that owns it, so a map the SOURCE browser IGNORED (its `src` step fires an error and returns) survived and the export carried it LIVE, while the Python gate - reading the ORIGINAL attributes - still rejected the same document. An exporter must never add behavior the source did not have, and a strip that disagrees with the gate about the same bytes is the drift this row exists to prevent. A block THIS export NEUTRALIZED is the other: a reserved-id script the neutralization pass rewrote to `application/json` was RUNNABLE as authored, so its network `src` was a real load, and reading its rewritten type would hand a decoy that borrowed a layer id the data-block treatment from a type the export itself had just written - the strip is handed the neutralized set and removes those elements whole. The RENDERER strip that runs just before it takes the same decision: it removes a chart or mermaid bundle by its FILENAME, and a filename is not a reason to delete a data block whose `src` fetches nothing, so it is handed the same set and asks the same question - without that, an `application/json` block whose `src` ended in a chart bundle name was blessed by the gate and deleted by the export. (An SVG script is removed rather than cleared for the opposite reason: SVG2 ignores the body while `href` is present, so dropping the attribute would start EXECUTING it.) The strip now also walks `<template>` content for its LOAD passes - scripts, media, links, forms and styles - which `querySelectorAll` cannot reach but the validator's tokenizer reads plainly, so a network-loading element parked in a template no longer rides into an export its own gate then rejects; and the inline-egress scan, the reserved-id neutralize pass and the event-handler scrub follow the same walk (they did not at first, on the reasoning that template content never executes and the validator's script model skipped it too - but a second script can adopt the fragment and insert it, at which point a parked script RUNS, and the validator now reads template content through its own views, so following the walk costs no false content loss). And the two implementations' network-URL predicates (`_OFFLINE_NETWORK_URL_RE`, `NETWORK_URL_RE`) now allow exactly the leading characters a browser REMOVES before parsing a URL - C0 controls and spaces, U+0000 to U+0020 - instead of `String.trim()` on one side and nothing on the other: a value padded with those loads (and the validator used to bless the file the strip had cleaned), while one padded with NBSP or U+FEFF resolves as a relative reference and is left alone. The range is written as literal code points rather than `\s`, and the Python copy carries `re.ASCII`, because the two engines disagree about both (`\s` is Unicode-aware in Python and matches U+001C-U+001F; JS's excludes them but includes U+FEFF; and Python's `re.IGNORECASE` folds `s` onto U+017F where a JS `/i` regex never does). What they still share is a literal test, but it now runs on the value as the URL PARSER sees it rather than on the raw attribute: leading AND trailing C0-or-space stripped, ASCII tab/LF/CR removed from ANYWHERE inside the value, and every backslash mapped onto a slash, because for a special scheme the parser's relative and authority-slash states treat the two alike. So the spellings a browser normalizes INTO a network load are caught rather than read as relative references - a backslash authority in either position (`https:/\host/x.js`, verified fetching `https://evil.example/x.js` in a real Chromium, and the scheme-relative `\\host/x.js`), and a tab- or newline-split scheme or authority (`ht<tab>tps://host/x.js`). An explicit `file:` AUTHORITY counts too, because `file://host/x.js` is an SMB fetch off the machine on Windows. How many separators open that authority was CHECKED in a real Chromium rather than read off the spec, because the answer is not "two or more": exactly two, or FOUR-or-more, give a host, while THREE is the empty host of an ordinary local path - so `file:////evil.example/x.js` really does fetch and a third-slash test alone called it local. Two host spellings that stay ON the machine are excluded WHATEVER the separator count, since reporting either would delete an author's local reference and make the gate reject a file with no egress at all: `localhost`, and a Windows DRIVE LETTER, which the file-host state turns into a path rather than a host (`file://C:/x`, `file://c|/x` and even `file://c:evil.example/x` are all the local file `file:///C:/...`, which is why the drive test does not require a separator after the colon). `localhost` is matched as the URL PARSER compares a file host rather than as a literal, because the parser percent-decodes the host and lowercases it through domain-to-ASCII BEFORE the file-host state turns the exact string `localhost` into the empty host: `file://local%68ost/x` parses to href `file:///x` in a real WHATWG parser, exactly like `file://localhost/x`, so a literal test reported a purely local reference as egress and both sides now spell the host one alternation per character with BOTH hex rows per letter (a `/i` regex folds `%6c` onto `%6C` but never onto `%4c`, and `%4c` decodes to `L`). The same percent-tolerance is right for the FOUR-or-more-separator arm, where the long run opens a real HOST to Chromium (the same deviation above) and a real Chromium was MEASURED percent-decoding that host before comparing, so `file:////local%68ost/x` parses to host `localhost` - the same excluded host the plain spelling reaches. Nothing that decodes to anything OTHER than `localhost` can match, so the widening cannot smuggle a host past either side: `%2F` and `%00` are forbidden host code points that fail to parse, and a host that merely STARTS with `localhost` is stopped by the terminator that follows. The rule the whole `file:` arm now keeps is CANONICALIZATION STABILITY: a value and the href the URL parser canonicalizes it to must get the SAME verdict, or a spelling hides an authority only the parser sees. Three shapes broke it, and none of them is reachable by a test that reads only the START of the value, because the parser's path state runs AFTER the host is emptied. (1) What the `localhost` exclusion may be FOLLOWED by is the end of the value, a `?` or `#`, or a SINGLE path slash - never two: `file://localhost//evil.example/x.js` empties the host and keeps `//evil.example/x.js` as the path, so the parser canonicalizes it to `file:////evil.example/x.js`, the four-separator UNC form this same arm rejects, and a bare `[/?#]` terminator blessed it as local on BOTH sides (the backslash spelling `file://localhost/\evil.example/x.js` reaches it too, through the cleanup that maps `\` onto `/`). (2) A DOUBLE-DOT segment pops the segment before it - including the very label an exclusion just matched - so `file:////localhost/../evil.example/x` and `file:////C:/../x.js` canonicalize onto the four-separator form with a different leading label; a `..` anywhere in the path therefore makes the arm match REGARDLESS of the `localhost` and drive-letter exclusions, in every spelling the parser treats as a double-dot segment (`..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, `%2e%2e`, case-insensitively). (3) An EMPTY path segment IS that four-separator form, and it arrives from values the separator arms never look at - `file:///.//x.js` and `file:/a/..//x.js` both canonicalize to `file:////x.js` from a three-slash or slash-less value - so it gets an arm of its own that ignores the leading separator count entirely, reading only a `//` in the PATH (a `//` after a `?` is in the query, which cannot change the path). A fuzz of 421,560 values against a real URL parser measured the result at this revision: ZERO remain where the predicate says local while the value's own canonical form is egress. The cost is over-detection in the safe direction, and it is pinned in the corpus rather than left implicit: `file://localhost//C:/x.js` (canonically the LOCAL `file:////C:/x.js`), `file://localhost/a/../b.js`, a bare `file://localhost//`, and an authored `file:///C:/a//b.png` are all now reported, while the controls beside them - `file://localhost/a/./b.js`, `file:///C:/local/x.js`, `file://localhost/x.js?q//h` - stay local. Fail-CLOSED is the direction this predicate takes everywhere else. What the host spelling covers is PERCENT-ENCODING and CASE, which is the half of canonicalization a regex can model; the IDNA/UTS-46 half is an ACCEPTED, deliberate over-detection, so `file://<U+FF4C>ocalhost/x`, its percent-encoded UTF-8 `file://%EF%BD%8Cocalhost/x`, `file://LOCALHO<U+017F>T/x` and the soft-hyphen `file://local%C2%ADhost/x` all parse to href `file:///x` (measured) and are still reported. That residual is deliberate rather than an oversight - UTS-46 mapping cannot be written as a regex both engines agree on, and Python's `re.IGNORECASE` folds `s` onto U+017F where a JS `/i` never does, so attempting it is how the two drift - and the corpus pins those spellings as network so the boundary cannot move on one side only. A TRAILING DOT is deliberately OUTSIDE the exclusion, and that is the parser-faithful reading rather than an accepted over-detection - the file-host state special-cases the exact string `localhost` and `localhost.` is not it, so `file://localhost./x` keeps a NON-EMPTY host and on Windows resolves to the SMB path `\\localhost.\x`, which is egress even though it lands on the loopback, exactly as the scheme-relative `\\localhost\C$\x` is. Percent-encoding does not reach the DRIVE-LETTER exclusion the way it reaches the host one, because that test reads the raw buffer the file-host state reads and `%3A`/`%7C` decode to forbidden host code points that fail to parse at all. An EMPTY host stays local through the separator rule itself rather than through an exclusion: three separators do not open an authority at all, and an authority terminated at once is empty. Every arm also requires a NON-EMPTY authority, so a value whose authority is terminated at once by `?`, `#` or the end of the value (`//?q`, `https://`, and the Windows extended-length path `\\?\C:\x`, which the backslash mapping turns into `//?/C:/x`) is left alone - a special scheme fails to parse there and fetches nothing at all. The one attribute whose value is a LIST gets the same treatment at its own boundary, and that boundary was wrong twice over. HTML tokenizes `srcset` candidates on ASCII whitespace ONLY, while both sides split on the ENGINE's whitespace, which cut `"<U+0001><U+000B>//host/x.png 1x"` at the U+000B and hid a real load from BOTH of them - and drifted between them, because Python's `str.strip()` takes U+001C-U+001F while JS's `trim()` takes U+FEFF. And splitting on the COMMA is not what HTML does either: its parser collects a run of non-ASCII-whitespace as the URL, so a comma INSIDE that run belongs to the URL - `srcset="https://,host/x.png 1x"` really does request `https://,host/x.png` (measured in a real Chromium), while the comma-split tested the truncated `https://`, which the non-empty-authority rule above correctly calls local. Both readings were taken for a while, on the reasoning that a descriptor (`1x`, `320w`) can never match the predicate so the union cost nothing - but a `data:` URL may legally CONTAIN a comma (it separates the media type from the data), so `srcset="data:text/plain,https://host/payload 1x"` was comma-split into `data:text/plain` and `https://host/payload`, and the second half matched. That is fail-CLOSED and not a drift (both sides agreed), but it made an offline export clear a `srcset` that reaches no network and `--strict` reject a document with no egress at all, so both sides now run HTML's own srcset candidate STATE MACHINE instead of a union of approximations (#1084): skip a run of ASCII whitespace and commas, collect a run of NON-whitespace as the URL, then either strip that URL's trailing commas (which end the candidate with no descriptors) or run the descriptor tokenizer forward to the first comma OUTSIDE parentheses. Both cases the union existed for survive - a comma inside the URL run still belongs to the URL, and a comma that FOLLOWS the descriptors still separates two candidates even with no space around it (`local.png 1x,https://host/x.png 2x` is two), while a comma that abuts the URL RUN is not a separator at all (`a.png,b.png` is the single relative reference a browser resolves against the document) - and the two implementations move together, so the gate can never reject a file the exporter just produced. The deck gate (`deck/deck_validate.py`) reads the list through the same shared `srcset_candidate_urls`, because a THIRD reading of it was the same bug on a surface that then disagreed with both. What is deliberately NOT taken from HTML is descriptor VALIDATION: HTML appends a candidate only once its descriptor list parses cleanly, so it DISCARDS `https://host/x.png 1x 2x` (a repeated `x`) outright, while all three surfaces here keep the candidate and report the load. That over-inclusion is the fail-CLOSED direction and it is kept on purpose - the alternative is a second, larger state machine (the `w`/`x`/`h`/`d` grammar, its duplicate and range rules) to hold identical across two languages, which is the drift these rows exist to prevent, and the cost of getting it wrong would be a MISSED load rather than an over-strip. The descriptor tokenizer's paren handling is a two-state flag and NOT a nesting depth, matching HTML: a single `)` leaves the paren state however many `(` preceded it, so `x.png ((),https://host/y.png 1x` really is two candidates and the second really is fetched (measured), which is why a depth counter here would be a missed load rather than a tightening. The ASCII-whitespace SET the boundary rests on is pinned across the two languages as a VALUE, not only by verdicts, because a corpus can only ever exercise the characters it happens to carry. A SINGLE leading slash or backslash remains a path, so a relative reference written with backslashes is still left alone. Two limits used to be stated here rather than closed; both are now closed. The http/https arm no longer requires the two slashes: it CONSUMES the run of slashes after a special scheme rather than counting it, because the URL parser's special-authority states ignore that run, so the scheme-only `https:host/x.js` and the single-slash `https:/host/x.js` resolve to exactly the same host as `https://host/x.js` and are now caught on both sides (#961). The arm still requires a non-empty HOST, so a value whose authority is terminated at once stays local, and it moved TOGETHER with the CSS strips it mirrors (below) so the gate can never reject a file the exporter has just produced. And a relative reference REBASED by an injected `<base href>` used to be seen by neither - that one is now CLOSED (#924), by a rule of the BASE ELEMENT's own rather than by widening this predicate. A base loads nothing itself, so no pass on either side looked at one, and both sides leave a RELATIVE reference alone - which is the whole control case - so a single base element naming a remote host rebased every relative reference in the document onto it, and a relative image or script reference fetched off-host while both checks read it as local. The strip now clears a non-local `base` `href` through the same template-walking pass (a parked base starts rebasing the moment a script adopts the fragment), and the strict validator flags the same shape, so the exporter and the gate agree. THREE bounds on that rule are stated rather than implied. (1) A base is held to a STRICTER predicate than every per-resource pass: not this one, but the `_offlineIsNonLocalRef` / `offline_is_non_local_ref` the import-map rule already uses (any scheme, or an authority of two slashes or backslashes in either order, after the URL parser's own input cleanup, and already pinned across the two engines by the active-data parity test). Its blast radius is what earns the difference - one attribute re-points EVERY safe reference in the document - so precisely the two spellings the arm above defers to #961, the slash-less `https:host/` and the one-slash `https:/host/`, are caught here rather than deferred, along with a `blob:` or `data:` target; and `base-uri 'none'` cannot be leaned on to cover them, because a policy delivered in a `<meta>` does not bind a base element the parser already resolved before it. (2) The HREF alone goes rather than the element: a `target` is not egress, and a RELATIVE base reaches no network at all (a root-relative one resolves against the filesystem, which the ordinary local-path rules already cover), so removing either would be content loss. Clearing one IS counted in the download toast, unlike every other attribute pass here, because it is the only strip that re-points references which still WORK - author `<a href>` navigation included, which no other pass touches - so doing it silently would leave the author guessing why their links moved; and outside offline mode the gate's remediation names the real fix (make the base relative, or write the affected values out in full) rather than "remove it", which would break every link that depended on it. (3) The check is deliberately namespace-blind on both sides, exactly as the script LOAD attributes are - the validator's flat tokenizer has no namespace to consult, so scoping the runtime to the HTML namespace would make the exporter KEEP an SVG-namespaced `base` href the gate then REJECTS, and an SVG `base` is a meaningless element either way, so agreement is worth more than the theoretical over-strip. The validator's copy is NOT scoped to offline mode: the self-contained guarantee is not offline-only, and unlike an offline file a shareable one has no zero-network CSP behind it. What a base still does NOT reach on either side is markup carried as an `iframe[srcdoc]` attribute VALUE, which no offline pass parses at all (issue #991 tracks that whole nested-document surface, of which a parked base is one shape). In an offline export the zero-network CSP still blocks such a fetch and in a shareable one nothing does, which is why the predicate rather than the CSP is the layer this is fixed in. The offline strip also removes remote form `action` and `formaction` targets, removes refresh meta tags and remote preload/prefetch/prerender links - and WHICH `<link>` fetches is now one shared decision rather than two hand-copied ones (#1061): the relation set (`FETCHING_LINK_RELS` / `_OFFLINE_FETCHING_LINK_RELS`) and the `rel` tokenizer (`link_rel_tokens` / `_offlineLinkRelTokens`) are pinned to each other as TEXT and over one corpus, because the exporter's list was missing `apple-touch-icon-precomposed` outright - so the strip KEPT such a link while the gate reported it, and the export produced a file its own `--strict` run rejects - and the two sides tokenized the list with their own engine's whitespace, which disagree in BOTH directions (a JS `\s` splits on U+FEFF, Python's argument-less `str.split()` splits on U+001C-U+001F, and both split on NBSP and the vertical tab, none of which is HTML ASCII whitespace). Both now split on the ASCII class HTML actually tokenizes a `rel` list on and fold case ASCII-only, the way the CSS gates already spell their classes out (#961). The strip also strips network CSS `@import` and `url(...)` - in the same widened shape as the attribute predicate above, so a scheme-only `url(https:host/x.png)` or `@import "https:host/t.css"` is stripped and an empty authority (`url(https://)`, `url(//)`, which fetch nothing) is left in the author's stylesheet, and both replaces move with the validator's `CSS_NETWORK_IMPORT_RE` / `CSS_NETWORK_URL_RE` rather than after them (#961). Removing what the gate REPORTS is the whole point, so the import strip consumes the at-rule's prelude the way a CSS parser does (to its `;`, its block boundary, or the end of the sheet) rather than demanding a terminator right after the URL, and the value strip reads a quoted value as a CSS STRING rather than as "anything but a paren or a quote" - an `@import` carrying a media query or a `layer()` clause, and a quoted URL carrying a `)` or the other quote, used to be reported by the gate and left in the export. A third shape was worse than drift: a `url(` token the CSS tokenizer closes but the author did not (unterminated at the end of the sheet, or with a quote never closed or closed by the OTHER quote) was verified FETCHING in a real Chromium while the strip left it in place, and so is `@import"https://host/x.css"` written with NO whitespace after the at-keyword; both are now consumed. The strips are BOUNDED (they stop at `;`, `{`, `}`, the next `@`, and either side of a comment boundary) so a false hit costs the declaration it sits in rather than the stylesheet, and they run to CONVERGENCE with a space in place of a removed at-rule, since a deletion can otherwise splice two inert fragments into a live `@import`. What both sides still read is RAW text rather than tokenizer output, so a CSS escape, a comment before the URL, an embedded tab or a bare-string reference is missed by BOTH (a shared miss, not a drift; issue #1029) -, preserves benign inline scripts whose dynamic import comments contain `//` but no network literal, preserves custom canvas scripts that are not chart snapshots, and preserves only data and relative media references. Same-origin absolute URLs are stripped because an offline file must not beacon to its original host. Both strips decide `is this script runnable?` with the SAME predicate the Chart.js evidence scan uses, so they cover the whole HTML JavaScript MIME type set (`text/ecmascript`, `application/ecmascript`, `text/x-javascript`, `application/x-javascript`, `text/x-ecmascript`, `application/x-ecmascript`, `text/jscript`, `text/livescript`, `text/javascript1.0`-`1.5`, and the modern three) rather than only the modern three - a legacy-typed script still EXECUTES, so it must not keep a remote dynamic import or a stale renderer loader - while a genuinely non-executable block (`text/template`, `application/json`, transpiler-only `text/babel`/`text/jsx`) stays untouched data. `importmap` and `speculationrules` are NOT in that inert set: they are not JavaScript, but they are ACTIVE, and their own rule is below. The strict VALIDATOR carried the same narrow five-type set in its own independent Python copy (`_JS_TYPES`), so an offline file whose remote dynamic import sat in a `text/x-javascript` script passed `validate.py --strict` as offline-clean; that set now mirrors the runtime predicate exactly and a parity test pins the two implementations together in both directions, since a drift makes the gate bless a file the strip no longer protects. Three of the layer's reserved DATA ids (`embeddedComments`, `handledCommentIds`, `commentableHtmlLayer`) were exempted by ID ALONE, tested BEFORE the runnable-type test, so a decoy script that merely BORROWED one of them ran in the exported file untouched by BOTH strips - no aliasing and no obfuscation, which made it cheaper than every residual CMH-OFFLINE-05 lists - and invisible to the strict validator's own egress check, which never had such a skip and would then REJECT the very file the exporter had preserved it in. The exemption is now EARNED: a reserved-id script whose type would RUN is retyped to `type="application/json"` before anything reads the document, so both strips exempt it on the ordinary runnable-type test and the two implementations agree by construction rather than by a hand-kept id list. The neutralized set is those three ids plus `reviewedSections`, which the strip never exempted - so a runnable `reviewedSections` carrying egress used to be DELETED and is now kept as inert data instead, the one direction this change loosens. Retyping rather than DELETING is deliberate - these blocks hold review state and a reviewer legitimately quoting an egress shape must never lose their comment - so a legacy or hand-authored block carrying no `type` is REPAIRED into inert data (which also makes the exported file strict-valid and shields such a block from the renderer strip, which never had an id skip) instead of being executed or stripped. A script that keeps its bytes but loses the ability to run is a quiet change, so the download toast names how many were kept as inert data beside how many were removed, counted AFTER the strips so one script can never be reported as both removed and kept (a reserved-id block carrying a network `src` is still REMOVED, because a remote load is what the strip exists to take away). Three limits are stated rather than implied. `reviewedSections` was NOT in the old skip list, so a runnable one carrying egress used to be DELETED and is now kept as inert data instead. The vendored payload id is deliberately NOT in the neutralized set: it is infrastructure resolved by POSITION (CMH-OFFLINE-07), so a script that merely borrows that id is authored content and must clear the same egress scan as any other - neutralizing it would hand back the exemption that resolution rule exists to remove. And the exporter/validator agreement is about the EGRESS exemption only: a DUPLICATED reserved id, or a reserved block whose body is not valid JSON, is the source document's own pre-existing invalidity, which `--strict` still rejects because the export preserves the author's bytes rather than deleting them. A `<script type="speculationrules">` or `<script type="importmap">` block is a THIRD shape: ACTIVE without being JavaScript, so the JavaScript-MIME predicate never looked at either, and they get DIFFERENT rules because their risk is not the same shape. A speculation RULESET is removed OUTRIGHT: it exists only to make the browser fetch early, it shows a reader nothing, and it needs no URL literal at all to reach the network (a `"source": "document"` ruleset prefetches the links the document already carries), so no URL-shaped test could have gated it and a single-file export has nothing to pre-warm. An IMPORT MAP has a legitimate local use - it makes a relative module graph resolve - so it is removed only when it carries a reference the file cannot resolve on its own, decided by PARSING the JSON rather than scanning its text, because JSON spells one URL many ways (`\/`, `\u002f`, padding, an embedded tab the URL parser strips) and a text scan closes one spelling while leaving the rest. Every string in the parsed value counts, KEY as well as value (an import map's `imports` and `scopes` keys are references too), and a reference is non-local when it carries a scheme - not only `https:`, but `data:` and `blob:`, which map a bare specifier onto code the document never contained - or an AUTHORITY prefix, two of `/` or `\`, in either order, because for a special scheme the URL parser's relative and relative-slash states treat the two alike. The comparison runs after the URL parser's own input cleanup (ASCII tab and newline stripped ANYWHERE, leading C0-or-space stripped), so a padded or tab-split spelling cannot pass as relative either; an unparseable body, or a `src`, removes the block as well (a browser hard-fails such a map, and an external ruleset is unreviewable, so failing closed loses nothing), and the walk runs inside the same guard as the parse so a body nested deeply enough to exhaust the stack fails closed rather than throwing an engine message out of the export. Both types are matched EXACTLY after an ASCII-whitespace trim, because these are HTML keyword types and not MIME types: `importmap;charset=utf-8` is inert data a browser ignores, and deleting an author's inert block is the costlier error. Removals are counted in the dropped-scripts toast. The template walk this row added for the LOAD check now also carries the reserved-id neutralize pass, the inline-egress scan and the event-handler scrub, at any depth: template content does not execute on its own, but serialization preserves it verbatim and a second, benign-looking script can adopt the fragment and insert it, at which point a parked script RUNS. That costs no false content loss, because the strict validator now records template-parked scripts, style blocks and inline styles in SEPARATE views that only the offline checks read (every other check must keep ignoring inert template content, which is why the existing views are not widened) and applies the same rules to them. The kept-as-inert count is taken by RE-WALKING the document rather than by a containment or `parentNode` test - the only test that is right for a fragment, since `doc.contains` reports every template-parked block as gone and `parentNode` would report an orphaned one as kept. The active-data rules are mirrored in the validator from the same type list, pattern and JSON walk, pinned by a parity test that EVALUATES THE EXPORTER'S OWN SOURCE in node over a removed AND a kept corpus (a Python re-implementation would keep passing after any of the decision's four parts drifted, and could not catch an engine difference at all). Two more egress shapes were in NEITHER side (#992), so a document carrying either rode into a zero-network export the gate then certified clean. HYPERLINK AUDITING (`<a ping>` / `<area ping>`, on an SVG anchor as much as an HTML one) POSTs to every URL the attribute names on every click: the strip now removes it through the same template-walking pass as the other load attributes, and the gate rejects one in an offline document. It goes whatever it names - the meta-refresh reasoning - because a relative ping still POSTs, shows the reader nothing, and is meaningless in a single-file export, so accepting one would bless a file an export would change, and an unconditional rule is one the two sides cannot drift apart on. What "names no URL" means is decided by HTML's own tokenization rather than by either engine's idea of whitespace: the value is split on ASCII whitespace ONLY (tab, LF, FF, CR, space, written as literal code points on both sides), so an empty or ASCII-whitespace-only value is left alone by BOTH - the strip has no write path for it at all and the gate does not report it, which is what leaves the decoded attribute value unchanged (a character-reference SPELLING is not preserved, since the parser decodes &#9; to a tab long before either side reads it) - while a value a browser reads as a real target is caught by both. That boundary is the one place this rule could have drifted: `String.trim()` and Python's `str.strip()` disagree about NBSP, U+FEFF and U+001C-U+001F, so trimming would have made an NBSP ping a live relative beacon the gate silently blessed (it POSTs to `/%C2%A0`, measured in a real Chromium) and an empty-after-trim value one the strip removed from a file the gate had certified byte-clean. It is scoped to the two elements HTML gives the attribute any meaning on, which the validator's tokenizer can do exactly because it reads tag NAMES, so an author's `ping` bookkeeping on some other element is not silently deleted. The CSP most likely absorbs this one in a current browser (CSP Level 3 folds hyperlink auditing into `connect-src`, which the offline policy sets to `'none'`), but the strip and the gate are the layer that is not supposed to DEPEND on the CSP, and the directive's `ping-src` history makes that coverage version-dependent - which is why the browser evidence for it is taken on a copy of the export with the CSP meta REMOVED, and proved OBSERVABLE by a positive control (a freshly injected ping link on the same page must be seen leaving) rather than by a bare absence of requests. The SVG filter primitive `<feImage href>` / `xlink:href` fetches exactly like the SVG `<image>` and `<use>` the media list already covered, and simply was not in it; it now is, on both sides, with a relative and a `data:` reference left untouched as the control. ONE selector spelling reaches both namespaces: CSS compares a type selector case-SENSITIVELY for an SVG-namespaced element and case-INSENSITIVELY for an HTML one, so `feImage` is the portable spelling that matches the SVG primitive and an `<feimage>` authored outside `<svg>` alike (a current Chromium is laxer still and matches any casing, which is an implementation detail no test pins), the strip stays namespace-blind exactly as the validator's flat tokenizer is forced to be, and the gate looks the tag up as the lowercased `feimage` its parser records. What neither side reaches yet is a network `url(...)` inside an SVG PRESENTATION attribute (`filter`, `fill`, `stroke`, `clip-path`, `mask`, `marker-*`, `cursor`), which a browser does fetch, and (in current Gecko only) an EXTERNAL template referenced by a paint server's or filter's own `href` (`<filter>`, `<pattern>`, `<linearGradient>`, `<radialGradient>`) - shared misses rather than drifts, tracked as issue #1065. Two more egress shapes were in NEITHER side (#992), so a document carrying either rode into a zero-network export the gate then certified clean. HYPERLINK AUDITING (`<a ping>` / `<area ping>`, on an SVG anchor as much as an HTML one) POSTs to every URL the attribute names on every click: the strip now removes it through the same template-walking pass as the other load attributes, and the gate rejects one in an offline document. It goes whatever it names - the meta-refresh reasoning - because a relative ping still POSTs, shows the reader nothing, and is meaningless in a single-file export, so accepting one would bless a file an export would change, and an unconditional rule is one the two sides cannot drift apart on. What "names no URL" means is decided by HTML's own tokenization rather than by either engine's idea of whitespace: the value is split on ASCII whitespace ONLY (tab, LF, FF, CR, space, written as literal code points on both sides), so an empty or ASCII-whitespace-only value is left alone by BOTH - the strip has no write path for it at all and the gate does not report it, which is what leaves the decoded attribute value unchanged (a character-reference SPELLING is not preserved, since the parser decodes &#9; to a tab long before either side reads it) - while a value a browser reads as a real target is caught by both. That boundary is the one place this rule could have drifted: `String.trim()` and Python's `str.strip()` disagree about NBSP, U+FEFF and U+001C-U+001F, so trimming would have made an NBSP ping a live relative beacon the gate silently blessed (it POSTs to `/%C2%A0`, measured in a real Chromium) and an empty-after-trim value one the strip removed from a file the gate had certified byte-clean. It is scoped to the two elements HTML gives the attribute any meaning on, which the validator's tokenizer can do exactly because it reads tag NAMES, so an author's `ping` bookkeeping on some other element is not silently deleted. The CSP most likely absorbs this one in a current browser (CSP Level 3 folds hyperlink auditing into `connect-src`, which the offline policy sets to `'none'`), but the strip and the gate are the layer that is not supposed to DEPEND on the CSP, and the directive's `ping-src` history makes that coverage version-dependent - which is why the browser evidence for it is taken on a copy of the export with the CSP meta REMOVED, and proved OBSERVABLE by a positive control (a freshly injected ping link on the same page must be seen leaving) rather than by a bare absence of requests. The SVG filter primitive `<feImage href>` / `xlink:href` fetches exactly like the SVG `<image>` and `<use>` the media list already covered, and simply was not in it; it now is, on both sides, with a relative and a `data:` reference left untouched as the control. ONE selector spelling reaches both namespaces: CSS compares a type selector case-SENSITIVELY for an SVG-namespaced element and case-INSENSITIVELY for an HTML one, so `feImage` is the portable spelling that matches the SVG primitive and an `<feimage>` authored outside `<svg>` alike (a current Chromium is laxer still and matches any casing, which is an implementation detail no test pins), the strip stays namespace-blind exactly as the validator's flat tokenizer is forced to be, and the gate looks the tag up as the lowercased `feimage` its parser records. What neither side reaches yet is a network `url(...)` inside an SVG PRESENTATION attribute (`filter`, `fill`, `stroke`, `clip-path`, `mask`, `marker-*`, `cursor`), which a browser does fetch, and (in current Gecko only) an EXTERNAL template referenced by a paint server's or filter's own `href` (`<filter>`, `<pattern>`, `<linearGradient>`, `<radialGradient>`) - shared misses rather than drifts, tracked as issue #1065. One residual is now recorded as a MEASUREMENT rather than an omission: what SCHEMES these predicates recognize. Both read an http/https authority, a scheme-relative one and an explicit `file:` host as a network load, and read every OTHER authority-bearing scheme - `ftp:`, `ws:`, `wss:`, `filesystem:`, and a custom scheme with no registered handler - as local. That boundary was CHECKED in a real Chromium rather than argued from the URL standard, because the standard's `special scheme` set (`ftp`, `file`, `http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`) is wider than what a browser will actually fetch: from a `file:` document, raw TCP listeners behind every AUTOMATIC SUBRESOURCE channel the strip covers recorded connections for http and https and NONE for any of the others - `net::ERR_UNKNOWN_URL_SCHEME` for `ftp:`, `ws:`, `wss:`, `gopher:` and a custom scheme (Chromium removed FTP support in 88, and `fetch("ftp://...")` throws `URL scheme "ftp" is not supported`), and `Not allowed to load local resource` for `filesystem:`. So widening either predicate would buy no egress protection at all while costing real content: the exporter would DELETE an author's reference and the gate would reject a file with no egress in it, which is the same over-detection trade the `localhost` and Windows drive-letter exclusions above already make. The controls are part of the evidence rather than decoration, and they are PER CHANNEL rather than aggregate: an aggregate control is satisfied by the first `img`, so a channel that is dead by construction hands every candidate a free zero forever - the first draft of the probe did exactly that with an at-rule import written after a qualified rule (the CSS parser drops it), a `source` element inside a media element that already carried `src`, and `background` on a `div`, which is not a loading attribute there. So the http control now gets its own listener per channel and every channel is asserted LIVE, while each candidate gets one listener for all channels together, since for a candidate the only question is whether ANYTHING connected. FIVE limits of that evidence are stated rather than implied, so the boundary is not read as wider than what was measured. (1) A SCRIPTED `WebSocket` really does connect in `ws:`/`wss:`, and no attribute carries it, so nothing URL-shaped could gate it; the export's `connect-src 'none'` closes it, and that is now measured on the real exported file against a raw listener in BOTH directions (blocked with the policy, connecting with the policy removed) rather than asserted as a substring of the policy text - a `connect-src` that still spelled `'none'` beside another source would pass a substring check while the channel reopened. (2) A scheme with a REGISTERED protocol handler is a different case from the unregistered one measured here: a handler turns a navigation into a fetch of the handler's own https template. It cannot be REGISTERED from a `file:` document at all (that needs a secure origin and a user gesture), and a reader's machine may already carry an OS-level one, so both shapes are recorded as unmeasured rather than covered. (3) DNS-only channels - `preconnect` and `dns-prefetch` - leak a NAME rather than open a connection, so a TCP probe cannot see them at all, and one in a candidate scheme SURVIVES the link pass for the same reason everything else in this residual does, which is tracked as issue #1076; they stay in the probe's markup so a future engine that started connecting would trip the control assertion, but they are not claimed as measured, and neither are the other channels a headless page cannot drive (a `track` whose cue mode never leaves `disabled`, a same-origin-only SVG `use`, an icon or manifest fetched by browser UI, and the superseded `link rel=prerender`). (4) A scheme handed to an EXTERNAL application is not a network load at all, so it is left alone on purpose: stripping it would delete an author's `mailto:` or `tel:` link and the launch is still a reader's own click. (5) The measurement is CHROMIUM's, and nothing is claimed for other engines: `ws:`/`wss:` were not observed as subresource-fetchable in the engine under test, `filesystem:` was refused there as a local resource from a `file:` document's opaque origin (which is a statement about that context rather than about the scheme), and FTP removal is an implementation choice rather than a spec guarantee - so `ftp:` is the row to re-measure first if the boundary is ever revisited. What this predicate is NOT is the thing that protects a file already on disk: an exported file carries its own zero-network CSP, which refuses these subresources whatever a future engine decides, so re-measuring changes what a NEW export strips rather than retroactively rescuing an old one. `offline-clean` therefore means no automatic browser egress under the strip and that policy together, not the absence of every authority-shaped token from the file. The probe's channel list is worth more than a scheme check on its own: building it MEASURED the SVG PRESENTATION-attribute gap this row already records below as issue #1065, and refined it. `fill`, `stroke`, `mask`, `clip-path` and `marker-end` taking a `url(...)` value really do fetch over http from a `file:` document; `filter`, in the same list, does NOT resolve externally in the Chromium under test, either as a presentation attribute or as a CSS value - so the Chromium half of #1065 is the paint set, and `filter` stays in scope on the Gecko evidence rather than on a Chromium fetch. The five that do load are pointed at every candidate scheme here in the meantime, where they stay inert, so whoever fixes #1065 already has a harness that drives them. Both predicates move TOGETHER if it is - the shared corpus in `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` carries these schemes with their expected verdicts on both sides (with the slash-run and backslash spellings the URL parser normalizes for the ATTRIBUTE predicate, since `ftp:`/`ws:`/`wss:` are special schemes exactly as `https:` is, and without them for the CSS gates, which are prefix matchers over raw stylesheet text and never normalize), and the probe re-runs the browser measurement on every CI pass, so a one-sided widening fails rather than drifting. The `<image>` strip clears `src` and `srcset` beside the two `href` spellings, for the mirror-image reason (#1165): HTML tree construction RENAMES an `<image>` start tag to `img`, so the HTML spelling really fetches through those two and is already cleared by the `all("img")` pass, while an SVG-namespaced `<image src>` fetches nothing - but the shared egress index the validator reads deliberately does not carry the namespace, so it reports `<image src>` in either, and a strip that cleared only the HTML one would have the gate reject a file this export just produced. Clearing both keeps the over-detection IDENTICAL on the two sides, the same construction the universal `background` read uses, and a relative `<image src>` is left untouched as the control. The two SPECULATIVE-CONNECTION relations, `preconnect` and `dns-prefetch`, are removed UNCONDITIONALLY rather than only when their `href` parses as a network URL, and offline `--strict` rejects a `<link>` carrying either one on its REL ALONE, before the href is read (#1076). Every other fetching relation on this row deletes a reference only when it would really fetch, because deleting a local one would take an author's CONTENT away; these two take nothing - unlike a stylesheet or an icon they show a reader NOTHING, their whole purpose being to make the browser reach out early, which is the same reasoning that removes a `speculationrules` block outright. So a hint in a scheme the per-resource predicate reads as local (`<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="ftp://evil.example">`), and a relative, same-document or href-less one, all go too. That predicate is the wrong LAYER for them rather than merely too narrow: their leak is a NAME RESOLUTION rather than a connection, so the TCP-listener probe that settled its scheme boundary (#993) structurally cannot see one - which is why both are parked in that probe's unobserved list. It was MEASURED rather than assumed, with an instrument that can see a lookup: Chromium's own NetLog, read as HOST_RESOLVER EVENTS rather than as raw text (Chromium logs an ordinary request's full URL in its `URL_REQUEST` entries, so a substring search over the file would report a host as resolved on a log that captured no resolver activity at all - the exact vacuity the control exists to rule out). The result at this revision (Chromium 149, from a `file:` document AND an `http:` one, with Playwright's `--disable-background-networking` REMOVED and `NetworkPrediction` enabled, since measuring with the speculative machinery switched off would make every zero meaningless) is ZERO resolver activity for a `preconnect`/`dns-prefetch` host in ANY scheme - the `http:` and `https:` CONTROL hints included - while an ordinary image reference to an http host in the same document does produce a resolver job. The same result was measured once by hand on the full headed binary; CI runs the headless engine, so that half is a recorded observation rather than something the committed test re-verifies. A control that measures zero cannot license a boundary: the instrument cannot separate "this scheme is inert here" from "this build does not drive the hint at all", so no measurement supports keeping such a hint in any scheme, and the safe rule that needs no engine to be right is to remove both outright. The measurement is committed as a spec that re-runs on every CI pass with its positive control, and it fails LOUDLY if a hint host ever does reach the resolver - not because the rule would then be wrong, but because it would have become load-bearing and this row must be re-read. It is a TRIPWIRE and a record rather than a regression test (it measures the engine, not the exporter, so it passes on the pre-change build too, and the product test beside it is the red-first one), and it lives in the `heavy` Playwright project because it launches its own browser with the measurement's own flags. What goes is the HINT, not necessarily the ELEMENT: a `rel` that mixes a hint with a content relation (`rel="alternate preconnect"`, `rel="stylesheet preconnect"`) names a reference a reader USES, so the speculative TOKENS are dropped from the list and the element is removed only when nothing else is left - deleting it whole would be exactly the silent content loss this rule's justification denies. What remains is then judged as the relation it also is, so a surviving network stylesheet is still stripped by the loader pass and the gate reports BOTH defects rather than one per run, while a non-fetching relation with a network href (`rel="alternate"`) is left alone by both sides. Both sides read the list through the SHARED ASCII tokenizer and one shared relation set (`_OFFLINE_SPECULATIVE_LINK_RELS` / `SPECULATIVE_LINK_RELS`, a strict subset of the fetching set, pinned to each other and evaluated in node over one corpus that also checks what the strip WRITES BACK on a mixed rel), so the strip and the gate agree by CONSTRUCTION rather than by two predicates staying in step, and a `<link>` whose rel is not one of the two - relative href and all - is author content that survives untouched. The check is namespace-blind on both sides, exactly as the script LOAD attributes and the `base` href are, since the validator's flat tokenizer has no namespace to consult and scoping the runtime to the HTML namespace would make the exporter KEEP a hint the gate then REJECTS. WHICH `(tag, attribute)` pairs the strips must cover is no longer kept in step by hand either: `tests/test_egress_list_parity.py` (CMH-BUILD-22, issue #1179) reads the strip passes out of this partial and asserts every pair the strict gate reports has one, so the drift this row exists to prevent - a gate that rejects the file the export just produced - fails a test instead of waiting for the next spelling to expose it. That reading is scoped to `_stripOfflineNetworkLoads` and follows the one pass that delegates (`_offlineStripScriptLoad`), and every strip that is a rule of its own rather than a media load (`ping`, a form target, `srcdoc`, the speculative rels, `referrerpolicy`, the CSS reads) is named in that test, so a NEW strip has to be classified before it can land - which is the moment to ask whether the two gates need it too. The legacy `lowsrc` is deliberately NOT stripped, and that is now a recorded decision rather than an omission: measured in Chromium it is not fetched at all, so there is nothing to strip, and the deck gate's contrary rule (the only one of the three that had one) was retired to match. The offline export also neutralizes the SVG PRESENTATION ATTRIBUTES the strict gate reads (issue #1186, `clip-path` / `mask` / `fill` / `stroke` / `marker-start` / `marker-mid` / `marker-end` / `cursor` / `filter`): each value goes through the SAME `_offlineCssNoNetwork` reading the `[style]` strip uses, so a network `url(...)` becomes `url("data:,")` while a local `url(#clip)` survives byte-identical, and the strip and the gate cannot drift apart because they share one pattern.
