| CMH-OFFLINE-05 | Offline exports add a restrictive Content Security Policy meta tag as defense in depth: inline runtime/styles and data images/fonts are allowed, and all network egress, form posts, and embedding are blocked through `default-src 'none'`, `connect-src 'none'`, `form-action 'none'`, `frame-src 'none'`, and `object-src 'none'`; the one embedding shape that policy does NOT reach is an `<iframe srcdoc>` - `frame-src 'none'` blocks a `src` LOAD, but a srcdoc frame is content the policy is INHERITED into rather than a fetch, and the inherited policy still allows inline script, which can navigate the top-level document - so the offline strip clears the attribute unconditionally and this gate REJECTS any offline document that still carries one (CMH-OFFLINE-04 records the direction and why parsing the nested document on both sides was rejected as the alternative). The gate reads it off the SHARED EGRESS TAG INDEX like every other offline rule, so a `<template>`-parked frame, a `<noscript>` fallback and a self-closed foreign element are judged exactly as the exporter's namespace-blind element walk judges them, and PRESENCE is the test - an empty or inert `srcdoc` is cleared by the export too, so anything narrower would bless a file an export still changes. Event-handler attributes are removed, and a reopened offline file with injected dynamic imports makes zero HTTP(S) requests. Event-handler attributes are removed EVERYWHERE, template content included, and the strict validator rejects any `on*` attribute in offline mode for the same reason, so a hand-authored offline file cannot keep the one channel the CSP cannot close (`script-src 'unsafe-inline'` allows an inline handler, and no meta-delivered policy restricts the navigation it can perform) while passing the gate the export is measured by. The validator reads those handlers off the SHARED EGRESS TAG INDEX (`_find_event_handler_attrs_egress`), not off a second collection of its own in the document parser, because the strip walks `querySelectorAll("*")` on a DOMParser document where SCRIPTING IS OFF - a walk that reaches two shapes the document parser's start-tag scan did not: a self-closed FOREIGN element (`<svg><rect onload=.../></svg>`, whose start-tag handling returns before any per-attribute bookkeeping) and the markup inside a `<noscript>`, which is raw TEXT to a scripting-ENABLED parse and is exactly what the reader who cannot run the layer at all really gets. The CSS strip (`all("style")` / `all("[style]")`) walks that same DOMParser document, so it reaches the fallback's stylesheets too; the export therefore already scrubs a network `@import` / `url(...)` from a `<noscript><style>` and from a fallback `style=` attribute, and the strict validator now reads the same fallback CSS view (CMH-VAL-21), which is what keeps the gate from rejecting a file the export just produced. Reading the fallback as markup is only HALF the question, though, because a `<noscript>` body has TWO readings and the export re-parses with just one of them: the `DOMParser` every strip walks has scripting OFF, so the body is MARKUP; the reviewer who opens the exported file has scripting ON, so it is RAW TEXT that ends at the FIRST `</noscript`. The two agree exactly while the SERIALIZED body carries no such end-tag-open - one reader then sees inert text and the other the markup the strips already scrubbed - and disagree the moment it does, because everything past that seam is live markup to the reviewer while the strips never saw it at all. Measured in chromium, two shapes really do ride an unguarded export out as a LIVE `on*` handler, both because the serializer writes them VERBATIM: a comment (`<noscript><!-- </noscript><img onload=...> --></noscript>`) and a raw-text `<style>` child. The seam cannot be reconciled from the exporter - escaping it would change what the scripting-disabled reader is shown - so such a body is DROPPED whole, the count is named in the export toast rather than being silent content loss, and the pass runs after the handler scrub and the CSS strip, since either can take a seam away with the attribute or declaration that carried it, and walks `<template>` content like the other passes. Four bounds are stated rather than implied. The predicate reads the SERIALIZED body (`innerHTML`) rather than modelling which node types a serializer writes verbatim, so it also catches an attribute-value seam on an engine that predates the escaping of `<` and `>` inside an attribute value (Chrome 116, Firefox 118, Safari 17) - an export runs in whatever browser the reviewer opened the document with, not in a pinned build step. The cost of reading the bytes instead of modelling them is that a seam drawn by ordinary NESTED markup is dropped too, even though what follows it is content the strips DID scrub and the gate accepts (`_TagAttrParser` reports no failure for it); the exporter is deliberately the stricter of the two, since that direction can only remove more, never emit a file the gate rejects. Only an HTML-namespace fallback is judged at all: an `<svg><noscript>` is an ordinary foreign element that switches no tokenizer on either side, so both readings agree about it seam or no seam, and removing one would be pure content loss. The same asymmetry governs what may be MOVED: the chart hoist skips any script with an HTML `<noscript>` ancestor, because such a script is a real element to this scripting-disabled parse but inert TEXT to the reader, so hoisting it into the body would not relocate author code, it would start executing code the source document never ran (the chart EVIDENCE scan is left alone, where a false positive only costs bytes). And all of this is about a `<noscript>` in the BODY: one in the HEAD is not an ordinary element to that parse - the "in head noscript" insertion mode allows only `link`, `style`, `meta`, `basefont`, `bgsound`, `noframes`, comments and whitespace, and anything else POPS the fallback and REPROCESSES that node, and everything after it, under the "in head" rules - so it becomes a head SIBLING (a `<script>`) or ends the head and lands in the body (a `<p>`, a line of prose) - so a `<script>` parked there is promoted out of the fallback inside `DOMParser` itself, before any pass can see it, and the export activates code the source never ran; a promoted node is indistinguishable in the DOM from one the author wrote as a head sibling, so no POST-parse rule can tell the two apart and the head fallbacks are judged BEFORE the parse instead: on the source string, read the way the reviewer's scripting-ENABLED tokenizer reads it (a start tag, then raw text to the first `</noscript`). One whose body that insertion mode would take apart is dropped WHOLE and counted in the download toast, exactly as a straddling one is; one carrying only what the mode allows is untouched, so this is not a blanket head-fallback removal, and the strict validator mirrors the same three sets (`OFFLINE_HEAD_NOSCRIPT_OK`, `OFFLINE_HEAD_ELEMENTS`, `OFFLINE_RAW_TEXT_ELEMENTS`, pinned to the runtime's regexes by a parity test) so the gate rejects exactly what the strip removes rather than certifying a file the export changes. Because the two are hand-mirrored SCANNERS rather than one shared literal, the sets are not what the parity rests on: a corpus of documents and fallback bodies - every non-obvious verdict in it measured in a real chromium `DOMParser` first - is answered by the gate and then re-answered by the exporter's own source running in node, and the two must agree. That is what a set comparison structurally cannot do, and it is how the one real divergence was found: a Python `re.IGNORECASE` folds `s` onto U+017F where a JS `/i` never does, so `</noſcript>` closed a fallback for the gate and not for the browser, in BOTH failure directions at once. What the two model is the parser's reading rather than the bytes': character data is judged after removing a U+0000 and any character reference that decodes to ASCII whitespace (`&Tab;`, `&#9;`, `&#x20;`, ...), because a NUL or such a reference before a fallback keeps the parser in the head while one inside a body leaves the fallback standing (measured); a leading BOM is dropped when a browser DECODES the file, so a real load never reads one as character data (`DOMParser`, which takes a string and does not decode, is the exception - measured), and reading one as content used to turn the gate off at position 0 for exactly the hand-authored file it exists to catch; every end tag "in head" routes to "anything else" ends the head, `</br>` included; and a `<head>`, `<html>` or `<noscript>` start tag INSIDE a fallback is not a pop (and a `<head>` start tag INSIDE a fallback IS a pop while an `<html>` or a nested `<noscript>` is not (an `<html>` is processed with the in-body rules, which only merge attributes, and a `<noscript>` is the parse error the spec says to ignore; a `<head>` is one the spec also says to ignore, but a real chromium pops on it - measured - and the browser that does the promoting is the one that matters). A tag name is folded ASCII-ONLY, as HTML folds one, because `String.toLowerCase`/`str.lower` read `lin<U+212A>` (KELVIN SIGN) as `link` while a browser does not, and that element really does pop a head fallback (measured), so a Unicode fold would hide the promotion, an `<html>` is processed with the in-body rules, which only merges attributes). Four bounds are stated rather than implied. `<template>` content is skipped on both sides, since a fallback parked there is parsed in its own fragment and never reaches the insertion mode at all. Anything the model cannot resolve fails CLOSED and the fallback goes - a truncated tag, a raw-text child (`<style>`, `<noframes>`) the fallback never closes, and the fallback's OWN missing close, where the body runs to the end of the document and is cut to there (a scripting-disabled parse pops and promotes it just the same, so keeping it would fail open on the very shape this rule exists for). The head is ended the way the tokenizer ends it (an explicit `</head>`, `</html>`, `</body>` or `</br>`, a start tag outside the head content set, or non-whitespace character data), so a document whose head this model ends EARLY carries its later fallbacks past BOTH sides together rather than past one of them - the two agree by construction in either direction. And the EXPORTER runs the pass to a FIXED POINT while the gate does not, which is not a drift but the difference between rewriting and judging: removing a fallback splices the bytes on either side of it together, and that can put a later fallback in head scope the walk had already stopped short of (`&#9`, a cut, then a `;` fuse into a whitespace reference and the head runs on - measured, the once-stripped document really does parse with the second fallback's script live in the head), so the exporter iterates until a pass drops nothing while the gate answers about the document in front of it, which is the finished file the exporter has already settled. And the start-tag boundary is the layer's existing `_cmhTagEnd` (mirrored as `_offline_tag_end`), which opens an attribute value at a quote only directly after `=`: a browser instead reads `<meta a=x=">` as an unquoted value that ends at the `>`, so a fallback written after one is not seen - by either side, which is why it is a bound rather than a drift, and rewriting that shared boundary belongs with the shareable exporter that owns it. The strict validator already failed CLOSED on the seam itself (`_TagAttrParser._flush_noscript`, whose fallback parse reaches it truncated or in a non-data state), so until this the exporter produced a file its own gate rejects - the self-contradiction the offline parity work exists to remove. Shareable is deliberately unaffected: it makes no zero-network promise and preserves the author's bytes by design (CMH-EXP-19). (Template-parked handlers were already covered by the scan this replaces and stay covered, since the index records every start tag.) Both new shapes rode into a file `--strict` then certified as offline-clean; asking the same egress question every other offline resource check asks is what keeps the gate and the strip from drifting apart again, and the `^on` test stays the exporter's literal one because agreeing exactly is the point: the strip really does remove `once`/`onward`, so a validator that were cleverer than it would bless an attribute the export takes away. Because the predicate is literal, the message claims only what the predicate DECIDES - that the name begins with `on` and the export scrubs it - rather than asserting that every match runs code. Both spellings are pinned against the real JS engine by a parity test, as every other offline predicate pair is, and a second test pins the validator's REACH (a source-level pin on the scrub's own walk, with the executed round trip carried by the offline Playwright spec) so a drift in where each side looks cannot hide behind an agreeing name test. One bound is stated rather than implied: the offline rules (this one included) are skipped for a document classified NonShareable, while the exporter runs the offline strips on that path too - a pre-existing gap tracked as issue #988. The META REFRESH rule is settled in the same both-directions way, and the direction chosen is THE VALIDATOR REJECTS EVERY `meta[http-equiv=refresh]` in offline mode rather than the exporter keeping a relative one. Three reasons, in order: the strip already removes every one whatever its target, so a file carrying a relative refresh is a file an export would silently change; a refresh is a TOP-LEVEL NAVIGATION, the channel no meta-delivered policy can restrict, and an injected `<base href>` rebases a relative target onto the network, so "relative" is not a safety property of the value on its own (that rebasing is a wider, still-open gap - issue #924 - which every other relative reference the offline checks accept is also exposed to; rejecting the refresh outright is what takes this ONE channel out of its reach rather than a claim the gap is closed); and a document whose whole promise is that opening it does nothing but render has no legitimate use for a declarative navigation away from itself. Keeping a relative one in the exporter would have had to defend all three. The network-target parser (CMH-VAL-08) is kept, now deciding only WHICH message the rejection carries - the one that names a beacon, or the generic one - so its whole false-positive corpus stays live as message-discrimination coverage instead of being deleted with the rule it used to gate. That parser no longer keeps a URL pattern of its own: the target goes to the SHARED `is_network_url` (issue #979), because a bespoke copy that only picks a message is exactly the code nobody re-widens when the shared predicate moves, and it had already drifted in both directions - missing a four-or-more-separator `file:////host` (a REAL AUTHORITY to Chromium, and the separator arithmetic is empirical because Chromium DEVIATES from the spec here: measured in Chromium 149 that URL parses to host `host` and re-serializes as `file://host/...`, where a spec-conformant parser takes the WHATWG file-host state's EMPTY host and leaves `//host/...` as the path; that pair of counted arms is the BASE-INDEPENDENT set: the same Chromium gives a zero- or one-separator spelling host `host` parsed ABSOLUTE, but against the `file:` base a document actually has those inherit the base's host and are local, so they carry no authority of their own - issue #1229 SETTLED that, and the CMH-VAL-08 row records the measurement), and every slash run of three or more that the shared `/{2,}` arm counts fail-CLOSED, while naming a local Windows drive path a beacon. (`frame-ancestors 'none'` is emitted and required by the validator for when the file is SERVED, but it is inert in a meta-delivered policy, so it is not what blocks embedding here.) What the validator demands of that policy is settled in the same both-directions way (CMH-VAL-08): it is not enough that the required token is PRESENT, since a browser reads the whole source list, so each `'none'` directive must be exactly `'none'` and each of `script-src`/`style-src`/`img-src`/`font-src` may carry only source expressions that provably cannot fetch, and only a meta a browser really APPLIES counts (in the head, outside an inert `<template>`, outside `<noscript>`, and BEFORE anything that can fetch or execute, since a meta-delivered policy is not retroactive). The exporter emits exactly the required tokens and inserts the meta as `head.firstChild`, so what it produces passes that gate unchanged and a hand-authored file cannot buy itself a widened policy the export would never have written. What that CSP CANNOT do, stated explicitly rather than implied away: it does not restrict TOP-LEVEL NAVIGATION, so an inline script the export deliberately preserves (CMH-OFFLINE-04) could beacon the entire document - every reviewer comment with it - by assigning `location.href`, a channel neither the strips nor a request-level test would have seen. No policy delivered in a `<meta>` can close it: `navigate-to` was dropped from CSP Level 3 and is implemented by no shipping browser, and `sandbox` (like `frame-ancestors`) is IGNORED when the policy arrives in a meta tag, which is the only delivery a `file://` document has. So the guarantee is enforced where it can be and bounded where it cannot. (1) The loader strip now also removes a runnable inline script containing a DIRECT scripted navigation to a network URL literal - a `location.href` assignment, a `location.assign`/`.replace` call, an assignment to a prefixed or statement-position `location`, or a prefixed `open(` call, through a REPEATABLE `window`/`self`/`top`/`parent`/`globalThis`/`document`/`frames` chain that also tolerates optional chaining (a single prefix was not enough: typing `window.` in front of the sink cleared the earlier pattern) - the same way it removes one carrying a remote dynamic module load. The URL literal is recognized in the literal prefixes a browser resolves to a network host, and in the spellings that NORMALIZE into one of those before anything resolves them - by the URL parser, or by the JavaScript parser that produced the string. The prefixes are scheme plus slashes, protocol-relative (slashes only), and SCHEME-ONLY - a quoted `https:`/`http:` with NO slashes after it, which a browser resolves to the same host. On top of any of them the literal may carry the leading C0-or-space padding the URL parser strips (`" https://evil"`), an ASCII tab, LF or CR ANYWHERE inside the scheme or between the two authority slashes (`"ht<tab>tps://evil"`, `"/<tab>/evil"`), which the parser removes from its whole input and which an ordinary string literal can carry as a real character, a BACKSLASH in place of either authority slash - four source backslashes (`"\\\\evil"`), since a literal spends two per runtime backslash, or an escaped slash (`"\//evil"`) - which for a special scheme the parser treats exactly like a slash, a JavaScript LineContinuation - a backslash followed by a line terminator - which evaluates to NOTHING in an ordinary and a template literal alike, and an ESCAPING BACKSLASH before any literal element (`"\https://evil"`, `"htt\ps:evil"`, `"https\://evil"`), because a backslash before a character that begins no escape sequence is a NonEscapeCharacter and evaluates to that character - the cheapest spelling of the lot, one keystroke and no decoder, and the one that would otherwise have defeated every other shape at once. The padding stops one code point short of the class the network-URL predicates allow: U+0000 is deliberately EXCLUDED, because the HTML parser replaces a NUL in script data with U+FFFD (which the URL parser does not strip), so a NUL-padded literal can never navigate and matching it would only make the validator, which reads the RAW text, reject a document the exporter - which reads the PARSED text - preserves. None of these needs aliasing, computed access or runtime assembly - just the URL spelled with one extra character - and while the check insisted on the exact raw spelling the whole channel was open to a one-token change and the strict validator agreed with the strip and blessed the file too. The authority branch deliberately does NOT require a host character after the two slashes: a sink assigned a quoted protocol-relative prefix concatenated with a host assembles a real beacon and the check fails CLOSED on it, at the price of also removing a host-less `"//"` or `"/\"` reference a browser would resolve locally - the same over-match direction this row already owns, and the reason a future reader must not "tighten" it by demanding a host. Backslash PARITY is load-bearing and is pinned by its own controls: a literal spends TWO source backslashes per runtime one, so THREE source backslashes leave a single runtime backslash and a local path where FOUR leave the two an authority needs, and an EVEN run before a scheme is a real backslash the browser resolves locally rather than an escaping one - which is why the branch is spelled `(?:\\?\/|\\\\)` rather than a naive `[\\/]{2}`, and why the escaping-backslash tolerance is a single optional `\\?` rather than a run. (The attribute-side network-URL predicates now agree about a backslash authority - they normalize the value the way the URL parser does before testing it - so the remaining divergence is narrower and deliberate: this check also recognizes a SCHEME-ONLY spelling, which the attribute predicates still require the two slashes for, because widening those alone would make the gate reject a file the exporter just produced. #961 moves that pair together; do not "reconcile" it by loosening this one.) Every added run is separated from its neighbour by a mandatory literal element, and each run's own two alternatives are told apart by their SECOND character (the line-terminator branch keeps only U+2028 and U+2029, because a backslash before LF or CR already falls inside the class beside it), so no input has two parses of a run. The two AUTHORITY alternatives can both begin with a backslash, but both are fixed-width, so choosing between them costs a bounded retry rather than a split of the input: the tail cannot backtrack superlinearly. Recognition is a LINEAR SCAN driven from the `location`/`open` anchors rather than one pattern: the earlier pattern carried the prefix chain as an unbounded repetition in front of the sink, so it re-entered that chain at every position a prefix could follow and a long NEAR-match cost QUADRATIC time (`window . ` repeated measured 2.3s at 18 KB and 174s at 144 KB, 4x the time for 2x the input). That was cheap to trigger, because the same predicate also runs over the vendored payload's INFLATED bytes, where a few hundred base64 bytes buy megabytes of near-match; the damage is bounded to an Export Offline that appears to hang, but an export that appears to hang is indistinguishable from a broken feature. The scan recognizes exactly the shapes the pattern did, pinned against it in BOTH directions, and its SCALING is pinned at 10x steps rather than at one fixed size, which is why the quadratic term survived the earlier backtracking guard. Linearity is a property of the WHOLE predicate, not just the sink search: the LOCAL-BINDING regex that decides whether the script declares its own `location` is the other full-text pass, and it carried the same class of defect one level down - its `function` alternative joined two unbounded whitespace runs around an OPTIONAL identifier (`function WS* IDENT{0,100} WS* \\(`), so a run never followed by an identifier was split every possible way and each split re-ran the bounded `[^)]{0,400}location` search, costing QUADRATIC time in the RUN's length (0.13s at 5 KB, 22.5s at 80 KB through the public predicate). The optional identifier and its own trailing run are bound inside one group now, so a run has a single parse and a failing split costs nothing; the recognized language is unchanged, since the old spelling with zero identifier characters is the new group skipped. Its scaling therefore grows the RUN rather than a repeat count, because a fixed gap repeated n times stays linear and hides exactly this term. The strict validator runs the same scan, with every shared literal BYTE-IDENTICAL and the walk that joins them pinned by evaluating the exporter's own source in node, so a hand-authored offline file with that shape is not blessed as offline-clean either; every metacharacter whose meaning differs between the JS and Python engines is spelled out rather than shared, because `\w` is ASCII-only in JS but Unicode-aware in Python and U+FEFF is JS whitespace but not Python's, which made the two copies disagree on real inputs. The IDENTIFIER-BOUNDARY class inside that scan is spelled as the COMPLEMENT of the boundary characters for the same cross-engine reason: a JavaScript identifier is not ASCII, so an ASCII-only class read every non-ASCII identifier character as a BOUNDARY, and a purely local binding whose name merely ENDS in `location` behind one (`<non-ASCII letter>location.href = <url>`, which navigates nothing) was deleted whole by the export and REJECTED by `--strict` - the false-positive direction that silently destroys an author's content, and the one this check is meant to avoid above all. It cannot be fixed by reaching for `\w` (ASCII-only in JS, Unicode-aware in Python) and Python's `re` has no Unicode property escape, so the class lists every ASCII character that cannot appear in an identifier EXCEPT `.`, plus the exact whitespace set the scan already uses, and reads everything else as an identifier character. The `.` exception predates this spelling and is load-bearing rather than an oversight: a member-expression dot must CONTINUE the chain, so `cfg.location.href = <url>` reads as some other object's `location` and stays benign, and making it a boundary would delete that script. That settles the ASTRAL case in both engines at once rather than needing a second rule: a supplementary code point is a surrogate PAIR to `charAt` and a single code point to Python, and neither reading is in the boundary list. That rule is one instance of the UNIT MODEL this pair now commits to, recorded here rather than left implicit in two languages whose string indices count different things. The model is NOT that the two copies count nothing - they do count - but that every length or index comparison in the pair is unit-INSENSITIVE, so a JavaScript index (UTF-16 code units) and a Python index (Unicode code points) cannot reach different verdicts on the same input. What is FORBIDDEN is the one shape that is not: an engine-native count BOUNDING a span of arbitrary source text, however it is spelled - the distance between two source positions, the width of a slice, a bounded regex quantifier, or an explicit counter. The bounded 400-character window the tokenizer replaced was exactly that forbidden shape, and it split the two engines in the direction that costs an AUTHOR content: a window of 198 supplementary code points is 203 characters to Python and 401 code units to JavaScript, so on `var {/*<198 astral>*/ location} = {}; location.href = <url>` the validator saw the binding and accepted the document while the exporter saw none, read the unprefixed sink beside it as the document's own `location`, and DELETED a script that navigates nothing (#1112). Replacing the window with a tokenizer removed that shape rather than moving it. The comparisons that DO survive fall into five CLASSES rather than a list of sites - stated as classes deliberately, because a site list goes stale the moment a helper is renamed and a class an author can test their new line against does not. (a) An advance or width over an ASCII token the code just matched - the anchor match width that selects the sink arm (`m[0].length === 4` against `after - at == 4`), the anchor restart, every `startsWith`-then-advance (`//`, `/*`, `*/`, the HTML comment opener, `${`, `=>`, `++`, `--`, `...`), and the `pos >= len(name)` guard - is safe because the token is ASCII, so its width is the same number in either model. (b) The single-token peek after a declaration keyword (`_offlineShadowDeclStarts` / `_offline_shadow_decl_starts`, `after.length === 1` against `len(after) == 1`) is safe ONLY because each engine's peek is exactly one unit OF THAT ENGINE - a lone surrogate to `charAt`, a whole code point to Python - and both classify as an identifier character. This is the one class that is merely unit-INSENSITIVE rather than unit-IMMUNE, so it is the one a well-meaning edit can break: making the JS peek astral-aware (`String.fromCodePoint`) without mirroring the Python side re-opens #1112 at this exact site, and any change to `_offlineShadowIdentChar` on one side must be mirrored on the other. (c) The fixed-width ESCAPE advances in the quoted, template and regex skips (`j += 2`, and `j += 3` for the CRLF LineContinuation in the quoted and template skips, which the regex skip does not have) are the one place the two engines legitimately land on DIFFERENT positions: on an astral escape JavaScript steps past the backslash and ONE code unit and Python past the whole code point. They reconverge because the character JavaScript is left standing on is a lone low surrogate, and every delimiter either loop tests for - a quote, a backtick, a `$`, a `[`, a `]`, a `/`, a backslash, a line terminator - is ASCII while a surrogate is at least U+D800, so the leftover is skipped as an ordinary character and neither the regex `in_class` flag nor a literal's end can be flipped by it. (d) The backwards prefix tail (`OFFLINE_NAV_PREFIX_MAX`) is safe because the slice is only ever tested with `endswith` against ASCII prefix names, so a code-unit slice and a code-point slice end in the same characters. (e) A comparison that ORDERS two positions in the same string, or tests one against that string's length (every loop bound, and the regex-versus-division position test), is invariant because both operands live in one index space, whichever one it is. Note the sharp edge on (e): ordering and equality are invariant, SUBTRACTION is not - `a > b` answers the same in both models where `a - b > 400` does not, and that subtraction is precisely the forbidden shape above rather than an instance of this class, so (e) never licenses measuring a distance. (`OFFLINE_SHADOW_MAX_DEPTH` bounds the frame stack by DEPTH rather than by characters, so it is outside this question entirely.) Classes (a), (c), (d) and (e) are unit-IMMUNE - respelling any of them in code points changes no verdict on any input - which is why the corpus that pins this has real GUARDS only for (b) and carries the others as illustrations that the shapes are reached and agreed on. If a bound over arbitrary source text is ever genuinely needed again it is spelled in UTF-16 CODE UNITS - what the exporter, and therefore the shipped document, actually runs - and mirrored EXPLICITLY on the Python side, which must then count units rather than characters, instead of being assumed. Because no verdict depends on such a bound, the window width decides nothing and no ASCII input changed verdict when this was settled. Non-ASCII WHITESPACE is deliberately carved back out, so a real sink sitting one exotic space into a script is still seen; and because widening the identifier side can only ever REMOVE matches, never invent one, the cost is bounded to the residual direction this row already owns - a non-ASCII character that is not a legal IdentifierPart (an em dash, a curly quote) in the boundary slot now suppresses the match, which an author who wants that already has cheaper ways to get. The ASCII-only CASE FOLD is untouched and must stay that way: it exists so Python's Unicode folding cannot fold a non-ASCII letter ONTO `location` (the dotless i, the long s), which is the OPPOSITE failure, and both directions are pinned by benign samples in the same corpus. Removing a script is content loss, so the export now NAMES the count in its download toast instead of dropping it silently. (2) The export emits `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">` (replacing any authored referrer meta, since the last one declared wins) and drops per-element `referrerpolicy` attributes, so a navigation that does happen - a reader clicking an authored link, which stays allowed because it is user-initiated and carries no document data - leaks no referrer. This is precautionary: browsers already suppress a `file://` referrer, so it earns its keep mainly when an export is later SERVED over http, and a preserved script can still set `.referrerPolicy` on an element it creates at runtime. (3) The RESIDUAL is documented, not papered over, in BOTH directions. The strip reads RAW SOURCE for a literal shape, so it MISSES: an aliased sink (`var l = location; l.href = <url>` - no URL obfuscation needed), computed access (`location["href"]`), a sink chain carrying an IDENTIFIER ESCAPE (`window.locatio\u006E.href`, `window.\u006Fpen(...)`, `location.hre\u0066`, the `\u{...}` form of each, and the same escape in a name's FIRST character) - a UnicodeEscapeSequence that decodes to a legal identifier character may appear inside an IdentifierName and names exactly the same property, so an escape in ANY identifier of the chain, at any position in it, steps around a scan whose anchor, prefix names and tails are all matched as literal text. The one shape that survives the escape is a prefix name separated from its `.` (or `?.`) by WHITESPACE, because the backwards walk skips that run and finds a legal boundary at it, so the literal remainder of the chain qualifies on its own - `windo\u0077 . top.location.href` is stripped where the tight `windo\u0077.top.location.href` is not; that is incidental to the escape rather than a defence (the same whitespace makes an arbitrary `zzz . location.href` match), and the corpus pins both so the residual cannot be read as a narrower claim than it is. The same literal matching cuts the OTHER way in the local-binding shadow rule, and that direction costs an AUTHOR content rather than letting a beacon out: an escaped `var`/`let`/`const`/parameter/catch `location` declaration does not register as a shadow, so an unprefixed sink beside it is no longer suppressed and a script that navigates NOTHING is deleted whole (`const l\u006Fcation = { href: "" }; location.href = <url>` goes, where its plain spelling stays). Both directions are residual by DECISION rather than by oversight. Recognizing each name as literal-or-escaped per character is possible without backtracking, but it turns a plain literal anchor search into a per-position automaton over every inline script (the exporter runs this same scan over the vendored payload's INFLATED megabytes) to close a channel the computed access above already leaves open for a shorter edit - which is equally what caps how much further hardening the URL LITERAL is worth, because an attacker who will not write an encoded scheme can write an encoded sink name instead, trivia between the sink and the URL (a comment, or parentheses around the literal), a URL a browser NORMALIZES that raw source cannot READ - the padding, tab-split, backslash, LineContinuation and escaping-backslash spellings above are all matched now, and what is left is the MULTI-character escape that ENCODES one of those characters (`"\u0068ttps:evil"` for the scheme, `\x68`, an octal), plus a `javascript:` wrapper that assigns the real URL at runtime. The two are residual for DIFFERENT reasons, and the distinction matters because it is what says how far the channel is really closed: an encoding escape needs a string-literal DECODER, since it can sit at any position in several spellings and only the literal's own quoting context says whether a backslash starts one, which a regex over raw source structurally cannot do - whereas the single-character cases (a backslash that ERASES itself, or that stands for the very next character) are decided by backslash parity alone, which is why they are closed rather than excused. The `javascript:` wrapper is different again: it is perfectly visible and is left out as a deliberate TRADE rather than a visibility limit - the URL is not in the source at all, and matching the wrapper would buy nothing, since a script able to write it already runs arbitrary code in that document, a URL ASSEMBLED at runtime, a BARE unprefixed `open(<url>)` (a real global sink, deliberately unmatched because raw source cannot tell it from a local `open` helper and deleting the wrong script is the costlier error), any UNPREFIXED `location` sink in a script that declares its own `location` binding (a declaration keyword, a destructuring declaration, a function, method or arrow parameter, a catch binding, or a `function`/`class` declaration name), since `const location = { href: "" }; location.href = <url>` navigates nothing and deleting that script would be exactly the content loss this strip must not cause - the PREFIXED sinks are never suppressed that way, because `window.location` names the real one whatever a local binding shadows, and an attacker gains nothing since aliasing was already a cheaper bypass. That last point is also the DECISION the shadow arm rests on, recorded here rather than left implied: the arm is a FALSE-POSITIVE REDUCER, not a security boundary. An author who wants an unprefixed sink ignored already has the aliasing bypass above, which is cheaper than any spelling of a fake declaration, so an arm that wrongly reports a SHADOW gives a hostile author nothing new, while one that wrongly reports NO shadow deletes a script that navigates nothing and makes `--strict` reject the very document the exporter just wrote. That asymmetry sets the bar, and the rule now TOKENIZES the declaration instead of matching a bounded CHARACTER WINDOW over raw source: one left-to-right pass with no backtracking, skipping comments, string and template literals and regex literals, and tracking declaration lists, parameter lists and destructuring patterns as binding contexts, mirrored helper for helper in the exporter and the validator. What that closes in the direction that costs an AUTHOR content, all of which the window MISSED and therefore deleted: an arrow parameter (parenthesized, bare or destructured), a method or `constructor` shorthand, a generator in all three star spellings, a nested destructuring or a default that spends a `}`/`]`/`)` inside the old window, a comment between `catch (` and the name, a non-ASCII function name, a `for` head declaration, a REST binding (`function f(...location)`, `const {a, ...location}`), a computed or quoted method name, whose name slot is a bracketed key or a string literal rather than an identifier, a `using` declaration, a named `import`, and a binding at ANY distance into the list (the 400-character bound is gone). What it closes in the direction that preserved a BEACON, all of which merely MENTIONED the name: a `location` in a block or line comment, in a string, in a regex literal, in a parameter or destructuring default (`function f(a /* location */)`, `function f(q = location)`), as a property KEY renamed away (`const {location: renamed} = opts`), as a method or accessor NAMED `location`, as a member access, call or index head (`o.location = 1`), inside a computed KEY (`const {[location]: renamed}`), after a declaration a line break has already ended (`let x` then `location.href = <url>` on the next line), after an `import` or `using` used as an EXPRESSION rather than a declaration, in a string a LineContinuation spans (a backslash before CRLF escapes both characters, and reading only the CR ended the literal and handed its text to the tokenizer as code), beside a CALL whose `)` is followed by a block on the next line (ASI makes that a call and a block, not a method definition), and a non-ASCII identifier character in the boundary slot, since `\u03c0location` and `location\u03c0` are now read as the ordinary names they are rather than as `location` behind a boundary. What stays residual, and the same decision explains each. Erring toward DELETING a script (the tokenizer sees no shadow where there is one): an ESCAPED declaration (`const l\u006Fcation`), for the reason the escaped SINK is missed above - both names are matched as literal text; a method whose name is a RESERVED word (`{delete(location) {}}`), since the same word list is what stops `if (location) {` being read as a method; a method written in Allman style, whose `{` is on the line after its `)`, since a `{` on the next line is how an ordinary call followed by a block is told apart from a method body; and a binding introduced by `eval`, `with` or the `Function` constructor, which exists only at run time and is invisible to any tokenizer. Erring toward KEEPING one (a shadow reported where nothing is declared): the arm asks whether the script declares a `location` ANYWHERE, not whether that binding is in scope AT the sink, so one declared inside another function still suppresses an unprefixed top-level sink; a call followed by a block on the SAME line, INSIDE a block, object literal or class body, is read as a method definition - that is not valid JavaScript, but it is text this scan still has to answer for, and the enclosing brace is what a genuine method shorthand shares with it; and a declaration list left dangling by ASI is ended at the line break only once it has bound a name, so the bare `let\nlocation = <url>` shape (a keyword with its name on the next line) is still read as a declaration. None of these buys an author anything the aliasing bypass did not already give them, which is the whole reason the arm can be a false-positive reducer rather than a boundary. Also residual: a bare `location = <url>` that follows something other than `;`, `}`, `)`, `>` or a line break (so `x = location = <url>`, `a = 1, location = <url>` and a same-line `{ location = <url> }` are missed - the delimiter set is deliberately narrow so a purely local binding such as a parameter or destructuring default is never deleted), and any OTHER navigation sink - notably a synthesized anchor click (`document.createElement("a")` + `.click()`) and a script-injected `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`, both of which beacon exactly as well and neither of which the CSP can stop. It also MISSES anything in a script carrying one of the layer's reserved DATA ids - it did, rather: that skip was tested BEFORE the runnable-type test, so a decoy runnable script that merely BORROWED `embeddedComments`, `handledCommentIds` or `commentableHtmlLayer` bypassed BOTH strips, and the strict validator (which never skipped those ids) then rejected the file the exporter had preserved it in. The exemption is now EARNED rather than claimed: such a script is retyped to inert `application/json` data before either strip looks (CMH-OFFLINE-04), so it can beacon nothing at all, the reviewer text those ids exist to protect is still never read as code, and the exporter and its own `--strict` gate agree. It also removes MORE than beacons: any preserved script that scripts a top-level navigation to a network URL literal goes, whether the author meant it maliciously or not (an SSO redirect, a help-popup window.open), because raw source cannot tell them apart and either one is a document-wide leak from a file that promises zero network; and it OVER-MATCHES outright, since a script whose COMMENT or STRING merely spells one of these shapes is removed whole - the normalized spellings widen that slightly, so a code SAMPLE quoting a line-wrapped or backslash-spelled navigation now goes too - and accepting the scheme-only literal widens that slightly, so a script that ASSEMBLES a URL from a bare scheme constant at the sink (`location.href = "https:" + "//" + host`) or quotes one of these shapes as a code SAMPLE now goes too - while a script that merely COMPARES against such a constant (`location.protocol === "https:"`, `location.href === "https:x"`) still survives, which the corpus pins. That is why the export now names the number of dropped scripts in its toast. So this strip raises the cost of the obvious beacon; it is NOT a boundary, and no boundary exists for navigation. A document whose author is hostile can already run arbitrary code in the original file, which has no CSP at all. Per-script hashes (dropping `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`) were considered and rejected for this: the decisive reason is that hashing cannot stop a script the exporter deliberately PRESERVES, since the exporter would simply hash it too; an attacker able to append a script to the file can also edit the meta tag beside it; and a single post-hash rewrite would brick every export. The layer's own script is subject to the same strips, so a guard test fails if the runtime's source or BUILT bytes (code or comment) ever contain one of the stripped shapes - they once did, and every offline file silently shipped with an empty JS region. (4) The residual is NARROWER than it was on the two shapes CMH-OFFLINE-04 added, but it is not empty and it now cuts BOTH ways. A speculation ruleset is gone unconditionally, and an import map survives only when every reference in it is relative, so there is no URL spelling left to smuggle one past - what remains is the OVER-match: an import map that legitimately remaps a network URL onto a local file (a network `scopes` key, or an `imports` key naming a CDN URL) is removed WHOLE, taking its still-usable local entries with it, and so is one whose body is not valid JSON or which carries any member the browser would have ignored. That direction is deliberate - a preserved fetch is worse than a deleted map that resolves nothing offline - and the removal is named in the download toast rather than left silent. | CMH-OFFLINE-06 | The Offline export inlines Chart.js only on EVIDENCE that the document needs it, not on the SHAPE of a canvas. The exporter's chart-canvas selector (`figure.chart canvas, canvas.cmh-chart`) is a deliberate superset - it must never provision less than a renderer draws, and an author may attach their own Chart.js to any canvas - but a canvas whose `data-cmh-chart-points` / `data-cmh-chart-source` yields a usable point is drawn by the runtime's own 2D renderer (`setupInteractiveCharts`) and never calls Chart.js, so a document whose charts are all built-in previously carried roughly a megabyte of dead library in every offline file. The library is now inlined (with its MIT notice) only when the document has a chart canvas the built-in renderer will NOT draw - mirroring that renderer's own bail conditions, so empty, unparseable, or point-less data still counts as needing the library - or a runnable script that mentions the `Chart` global. That evidence is deliberately lopsided, because the two failure directions are not symmetric: a false positive costs bytes, a false negative ships a chart that never renders. So it matches any mention of `Chart` (catching indirect construction such as `const C = window.Chart; new C(...)`), covers every executable script MIME type rather than only the modern three, is read from the document BEFORE any script is stripped (so a script the loader strip removes cannot take the evidence with it), and skips only three things: the review layer's own script (identified by its version declaration AND its position outside the content root, so an author script quoting a public hook still counts), the layer's own id-bearing data blocks (reviewer comment text is not evidence), and a library this exporter inlined on a previous pass (removed by its own `data-cmh-offline-lib` marker and value, not by recognizing its bundled text, so a re-export can never accumulate a second copy). A script that merely names a bundle file is no longer stripped when it uses the global, and a `<head>` script that references the global is hoisted below the inlined library so it cannot run before it. Two shapes stay out of reach, both unchanged from before: an author script loaded from a relative `src` (its body cannot be read, and such a document is not self-contained anyway) and a chart canvas outside the content root (the shape gate and the author-time payload-carry decision are both scoped to that root). | `tests/49-offline-export.spec.js` - `CMH-OFFLINE-06: Export Offline omits Chart.js for a document only the built-in renderer draws` (also pins marker-based removal of a previously inlined library and a library-free re-export), `CMH-OFFLINE-06: Export Offline still inlines Chart.js when the document constructs a Chart on a built-in canvas` (direct, aliased-with-bundle-name, and module construction, each reopened offline), `CMH-OFFLINE-06: evidence covers a head-placed legacy-typed constructor and unusable built-in data`; `Export Offline embeds vendored mermaid and Chart.js for zero-network reopen (CMH-OFFLINE-01, CMH-OFFLINE-02)` pins the shipped-example shape; `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `test_the_selector_set_matches_the_runtimes_exactly` pins the decision function's chart selector to the author-time payload-carry selector; source: `assets/js/68-export-offline.js` - `_offlineDocNeedsChartLib()` |
| CMH-OFFLINE-07 | Re-running `Export Offline` on a file a previous Offline export produced works, including when it contains a mermaid diagram or a chart the built-in renderer does not draw. An Offline export CONSUMES the vendored `cmhVendoredRichLibs` payload and removes it, so the file it emits carries the libraries inline and no payload at all - a re-export therefore had nothing to re-inline from and threw `Offline export is missing the vendored mermaid bundle`, showing an error toast instead of downloading. The exporter now captures the already-inlined library bytes and their MIT notice BEFORE the renderer strip removes them and falls back to those copies, reusing what is already local. Capturing and re-emitting, rather than leaving them in place, keeps the strip's exactly-one-copy and library-before-init ordering guarantees, so a re-export carries exactly one copy of each library, one mermaid init shim, and one MIT notice per library, and still renders with zero network. Re-emitting a captured script GRANTS IT EXECUTION and the document is UNTRUSTED, so the `data-cmh-offline-lib` marker alone is NOT proof this exporter wrote it. FOUR provenance gates make a forgery grant no capability the source document already had: the script sits OUTSIDE the authored content root and RUNS WHERE IT IS (CMH-SIZE-05 moved where this exporter writes, from `<head>` to the tail of the machinery fence, so the boundary is now the same RULE payload resolution applies - a `<head>` copy still qualifies unconditionally, which is what keeps a legacy offline file re-exportable, while a BODY copy counts only against a single resolvable content root and a contested one is refused by the layer's shared export precondition before the offline pipeline even runs; and because the boundary now reaches the body, the gate also asks the execution question the strips ask, so a copy parked in an HTML `<noscript>` or a MathML `<script>` - inert where it sits, executable once re-emitted - is never promoted. The gate's job is unchanged, keeping a copy inside authored content, which is preserved AS content by the same predicate in the strip beside it, from being captured; it was never a strength claim about `<head>` in particular); it carries EXACTLY the attribute shape the exporter emits - the marker and nothing else, which is stricter than any denylist and rules out `src` (whose inline text never ran), any `type` (so inert `application/json`/`text/plain` data is never promoted to code, and a MIME-parameter type such as `text/javascript;charset=utf-8`, which does not execute because HTML matches a type's essence, cannot masquerade as runnable) and `nomodule` (skipped by every module-supporting browser, so its body never ran, yet re-emission would drop the attribute and run it); its text passes the same network-import check the loader strip applies to every other surviving script, since capture runs BEFORE the strips and re-emission AFTER (a strip-PARITY gate, not an egress proof - the zero-network CSP is the enforcement boundary); and its bytes cannot open a script-data escape, which would otherwise re-serialize into an element the parser never closes and swallow everything after it in the machinery fence. The adjacent MIT notice naming the same library is required as a LICENSING condition, not authentication (the wording is a public constant a forgery can copy), so the security argument rests only on the four gates; a blank notice counts as none. The last qualifying match in DOCUMENT order wins, so a copy planted earlier - including one an older version left in the head - cannot displace the genuine one. The stale-notice sweep that keeps a re-export at exactly one notice per library is scoped by the SAME boundary predicate (`_offlineOutsideContentRoot`) as the capture gate, so the two can never disagree about where authored content ends: a notice this exporter wrote is removed wherever it put it, and one an author quoted inside their own content is left alone. Deliberate limits: the gates do not try to prove the bytes ARE the library (an author can already put arbitrary executable code in a head script without the marker, and the export preserves benign inline scripts by design, so a pinned digest would buy nothing while `crypto.subtle` is unavailable in the `file://` documents these exports open in), and an offline file produced before the MIT notice existed carries no notice, so it still fails loudly rather than being redistributed unlicensed - but with its OWN message, because the bundle IS in the file and only the licence blocks re-emitting it: it names the missing notice and the action that works (re-export from the source document that still carries the vendored payload) instead of the generic missing-bundle error, which sent the user looking for a payload the file was never going to have. That specific message is claimed only when licensing was the SOLE blocker and only for the library that could not be re-emitted: the flag is per library, and a copy the four gates rejected marks the library as refused for PROVENANCE, so a document holding both an unsafe copy and a notice-less one falls back to the generic message rather than name a cause the exporter cannot prove. It asserts nothing it cannot verify either - the gates authenticate no provenance, so it never claims who wrote the file. Synthesising the notice is not an option: with the payload consumed there is no licence text to emit, which is why the copy is refused. Because these messages name a cause and an action, EVERY Offline export failure toast is announced assertively (`role="alert"`) and stays on screen long enough to read, rather than in the 3s confirmation toast that fitted the one-line generic error. Only the export-build exit is reachable by any document, so that is the one the tests drive; the base-load and shareable-assembly catches keep the same treatment (`_getBaseHtml` swallows every fetch failure and falls back to its pristine snapshot). The shareable-assembly catch is no longer defence in depth: since the embedded-comments block is resolved STRUCTURALLY (CMH-EXP-16), a document whose region is missing, or which carries one that cannot be located reliably, throws there and gets the same assertive toast. A payload always wins over a captured copy, and a document with neither still fails loudly (CMH-SIZE-01). Winning is not a trust exemption: gates 3 and 4 above are CONTENT gates, so the payload's inflated bytes clear the same two checks through one shared predicate before they are appended, and a refusal names the library and the remedy rather than reporting a missing bundle (CMH-OFFLINE-08). | `tests/49-offline-export.spec.js` - `CMH-OFFLINE-07: re-exporting an already-offline document reuses its inlined libraries`, `CMH-OFFLINE-07: a forged inlined-library marker is never re-emitted as executable code` (one discriminating case per gate, plus five licensing cases: the specific unlicensed-copy message, a gate-rejected copy beside a notice-less one falling back to the generic message, a marker outside the head NOT masking the licence, per-library flags that do not cross-talk, and a both-libraries document naming the library it could not re-emit - every case also asserting the failure toast is assertive and still SHOWN, by its `show` class rather than a bounding box the opacity fade never removes, and the licensing case re-asserting it past the 3s default), `CMH-OFFLINE-07: an inlined library is captured from the machinery region, and the boundary fails closed` (the position gate's new boundary: a copy in the fence IS a candidate and travels exactly once while an authored marked copy inside the content is neither captured nor stripped, a copy that is inert where it sits - parked in an HTML `<noscript>` or a MathML `<script>` - is never promoted to running code, a fence pair parked in a `<noscript>` never becomes the insertion anchor, and a contested content root aborts the export naming the duplicate id rather than capturing from a region it cannot tell apart from content), `CMH-OFFLINE-07: the last qualifying inlined library wins over one planted before it` (a notice-less capture neither travels nor displaces the winning copy), `CMH-OFFLINE-07: the vendored payload wins over a copy already in the document`; | CMH-OFFLINE-08 | The Offline export treats the vendored `cmhVendoredRichLibs` payload as INFRASTRUCTURE and carries every library with its MIT notice as one unit. THREE ways the old code trusted a payload block are closed, and a FOURTH that position and uniqueness never addressed. (1) The payload was resolved by document-order id lookup, so an AUTHORED decoy payload block planted inside the content region came first and won - `tools/authoring/vendored_libs.py` places the real one after the content, immediately before `</body>` - and its compressed bytes were inflated and inlined into an export whose own CSP is `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`, so document-supplied code ran in a file the recipient believes is a clean skill-generated export. The payload is now a payload-id script OUTSIDE `#commentRoot`, and EXACTLY one of them, resolved from the DOCUMENT BEING EXPORTED rather than the live DOM. AMBIGUITY IS NOT ABSENCE: absence is the ordinary re-export case (an earlier export consumed the payload) and legitimately falls back to the copies already inlined in the file, so a document that HAS a candidate but cannot single one out - two of them, or a boundary that cannot be pinned down because zero or several elements carry the content-root id - THROWS instead of reporting no payload, which would otherwise quietly hand the export to document-supplied bytes. (A document whose content needs neither library never resolves a payload at all; it just strips.) The payload id is matched as an attribute VALUE, never written as an id-attribute selector literal, because this source is inlined into every export and a literal would make an exported file look like it still carries a payload block to anything scanning its text. What position and uniqueness authenticate is stated in the source: they defeat an author of the CONTENT REGION, who can no longer displace the genuine payload without becoming visibly ambiguous; they prove nothing against an author of the WHOLE FILE, who can simply omit the genuine payload - against that adversary the argument remains CMH-OFFLINE-07's (capture grants no capability the document did not already have) plus the zero-network CSP. (2) The consume-and-strip removed only the FIRST payload block, so a second one survived into a file that is supposed to carry the libraries inline and no payload at all. EVERY infrastructure block is now stripped, including one parked in a `<template>` (which `querySelectorAll` does not descend into, yet serialization preserves and a script adopted out of a template runs; containment is judged at the outermost template ELEMENT, since a fragment is inside no element) - while a payload-id script INSIDE the content root is preserved as authored content, because a document may legitimately show one as an example (the authoring tool refuses to cut it for the same reason) and deleting it would drop content and shift every comment anchor measured after it. Preserving it is not a free pass, and it is not invisible either: the payload id no longer exempts a script from the network-import strip NOR from the chart-evidence scan, so an authored script that borrows the id faces the same strip as any other and still provisions the library it calls (otherwise it would survive into an export whose Chart.js was judged unnecessary, and break at load). `vendored_libs.apply()` also now collapses a rich document to exactly one payload copy (the UNUSED branch already did), so a finalized document can never be born in the ambiguous state the runtime refuses. Since CMH-SIZE-05 the exporter applies the SAME boundary RULE - outside the authored content root - to every block it recognizes as its own: the payload, the inlined-library capture gate, the inlined-library strip, and the stale-notice sweep. The last three share one predicate built per document (`_offlineOutsideContentRoot`); payload resolution keeps its own resolver because its NULL-ROOT policy is deliberately different (no resolvable root makes a payload-bearing document AMBIGUOUS and throws, while for the other three it simply means nothing in the body is recognized as machinery), and both bottom out in the one `cmhContentRootState` primitive, so the rule cannot drift even though the two null policies stay distinct on purpose. AMBIGUITY STAYS LOUD: a document whose content root is CONTESTED is refused by the layer's shared export precondition (`_CMH_CONTESTED_ROOT_ERROR`) before the offline pipeline runs at all, and the capture gate's own contested branch is defence in depth behind it; neither degrades into treating an unverifiable region as machinery. (3) A library could ship with NO MIT notice: the notice was required only where a copy already inlined in the document was captured, so a payload whose notice text was stripped (by a minifier, or deliberately) re-emitted the library bytes with no notice - a silent MIT compliance break. Bytes and notice now travel as ONE unit at the point of use: whichever source is chosen (payload first, an already-inlined copy as the fallback), a missing notice fails the export naming the NOTICE and the remedy, not a bundle the document does carry, with no cross-source fallback on the notice alone (that would let anyone who can strip a notice force document-supplied bytes). A payload notice counts only when it is a STRING, since coercion would turn `{}` into `[object Object]` and emit that AS the notice; the emitter itself now throws rather than silently skipping an empty notice; and a captured copy with no notice is recorded only when nothing better is known, so a planted noticeless marker cannot displace a licensed copy under the last-wins rule and turn a legitimate re-export into a permanent refusal. (4) The payload's INFLATED BYTES were inlined with no content scan at all. They are appended as an EXECUTABLE script AFTER `_stripOfflineRichRenderers` and `_stripOfflineNetworkLoads` have already run, so nothing downstream ever looked at them, while the sibling captured-copy path did gate its bytes (CMH-OFFLINE-07, gates 3 and 4). The boundary above answers an author of the CONTENT REGION; against an author of the WHOLE FILE the earlier argument was that they "can already run script in the document anyway" - true of the SOURCE document, and the weaker claim this row now retires, because the export exists to strip egress out of the file it PRODUCES. An ordinary authored script carrying a remote dynamic import or a direct scripted navigation to a network URL literal is DELETED by the loader strip, so routing the same code through the payload did grant a capability the authored path does not have: egress inside a file whose whole promise is zero network. The decision is therefore to GATE rather than to keep the boundary: whichever source `_offlineInlineRichLibs` chooses, its bytes clear the same network-egress scan and script-data escape check through ONE shared predicate (`_offlineLibBytesUnsafe`), applied at the point of use - the last place before the bytes become a script - so the payload and capture paths cannot drift apart. This is a strip-PARITY gate, not an egress proof, exactly as CMH-OFFLINE-07's gate 3 is: it recognizes the same literal forms the strip does, and the zero-network CSP remains what enforces no subresource egress. A refusal is loud and SPECIFIC - it names the library, says its bytes MATCHED the egress pattern the strips apply to every runnable inline script or the script-data escape pattern (claiming only what each deliberately literal predicate decides, per CMH-OFFLINE-05 - both are supersets, and the escape half refuses an inert start tag as readily as an element-closing one rather than reasoning about tokenizer states), gives the remedy (re-run the authoring finalize step to refresh the vendored payload) and downloads nothing - rather than the generic missing-bundle message, which would send the user looking for a payload the document plainly carries. There is deliberately NO fallback to a captured copy when the payload is refused: the payload WINS over a captured copy by design, so a fallback would let anyone who can edit the payload invert that precedence at will and turn a loud refusal into a silent substitution of another attacker-chosen source. The cost of failing closed is stated rather than hidden: an upstream `mermaid` / `Chart.js` bump whose bytes tripped the literal predicate would make the export fail for every ALREADY-FINALIZED document in the wild, not just red this repo's build - `test_the_vendored_bundles_pass_the_offline_capture_gates` pins the shipped bundles, which is what keeps such a bump from ever being published, but it protects nothing already shipped. The legitimate path is never refused: the shipped bundles already satisfy both gates, so a dependency bump that broke that property trips a Python test rather than silently turning a valid export into a refusal. | CMH-OFFLINE-10 | Offline mode GATES the referrer surface the Offline export hardens, which until #1061 the export did alone. No CSP delivered in a `<meta>` can restrict TOP-LEVEL NAVIGATION (`navigate-to` was dropped from CSP Level 3 and `sandbox` is ignored in a meta-delivered policy), so a reader's click is not blockable and the only thing left to control is that the navigation carries no PROVENANCE. The export therefore removes every `referrerpolicy` attribute and replaces any authored referrer `<meta>` with `no-referrer`, while a hand-authored offline document carrying `referrerpolicy="unsafe-url"` validated with no error at all - the CMH-OFFLINE-04 drift shape, in the direction where the gate blesses a file the export would have changed. What the rule is worth is stated rather than overclaimed: a document opened from `file://` sends no `Referer` at all whatever its policy says (the Referrer Policy standard's "strip url for use as a referrer" returns no referrer for a non-HTTP(S) source), so the leak this closes is the one an exported report meets once someone SERVES it, over http(s), where `unsafe-url` hands the full document URL to whatever the reader clicks; the parity argument stands on its own either way. The gate is a CONTRACT check rather than a byte-for-byte mirror of the strip, exactly as the offline CSP rule is (the export REPLACES the policy meta unconditionally while the gate accepts any applied policy that MEETS the contract): what is reported is exactly what a browser would HONOUR as a policy weaker than `no-referrer`. The two readings are therefore SEPARATE grammars rather than one shared parser, and each was MEASURED in a real Chromium rather than read off the two specifications. `referrerpolicy` is an ENUMERATED attribute: the value is matched ASCII case-insensitively against the current tokens and nothing else, with NO whitespace trim and NO legacy alias, because `referrerpolicy=" unsafe-url "` and `referrerpolicy="always"` were both measured as the invalid value state, which sets no policy and leaves the document's own in force - trimming or folding there reported an attribute that weakens nothing. A referrer `<meta>` is the opposite: its WHOLE content value is ASCII-lowercased and HTML's legacy aliases ARE folded (`content="always"` sent the full URL cross-origin and `content="never"` sent nothing), but it is neither split on commas nor trimmed - `content="no-referrer, unsafe-url"`, `content=" unsafe-url "` and `content=" origin-when-crossorigin "` were all measured setting NO policy, so reading the meta with the HTTP header's list grammar reported documents a browser treats as carrying none. The attribute rule is SCOPED to the elements HTML gives `referrerpolicy` any meaning on (`a`, `area`, `iframe`, `img`, `link`, `script`, the first of which reaches its SVG spelling by tag NAME; the SVG-only fetchers SVG2 also lists the attribute on are deliberately EXCLUDED, because a real Chromium exposes no `referrerPolicy` on `image`, `use` or `feImage` at all - the IDL attribute is absent, so nothing there honours it), the way the `ping` rule is scoped to `a`/`area`, because the attribute anywhere else controls no request and reporting `<div referrerpolicy="unsafe-url">` would only cost an author content; and an `a`/`area` whose `rel` carries `noreferrer` is skipped, since HTML sets that navigation's referrer to `no-referrer` whatever the attribute says. The `http-equiv="referrer-policy"` pragma is deliberately NOT checked - it is not an HTML pragma directive and the same measurement showed Chromium ignoring it entirely, so it can weaken nothing; the export still strips it, which is the same canonicalizing over-reach the CSP meta gets. EVERY permissive meta is reported rather than only the effective last one: the flat tag index cannot tell a live meta from a `<template>`-parked one, so letting a later `no-referrer` suppress an earlier permissive meta could be masked by an inert meta - a false NEGATIVE - while the cost of the over-report is a remediation ("remove it") that is correct for every one of them, since the export removes them all. Presence is deliberately NOT required, unlike the CSP rule: a document that declares no referrer policy at all weakens nothing, and it is what every hand-authored offline file carries. Both rules read the shared EGRESS index, so a `<template>`-parked element, a `<noscript>` fallback and a self-closed foreign element are judged alike, matching the strip's own template-walking element walk - and the export's referrer meta pass now walks templates too, so it cannot emit a file this gate then rejects. Scoped to offline mode, like every other rule whose counterpart is an offline strip: a shareable export runs no such strip and makes no zero-network promise. | `tests/test_validate_self_contained.py` - `test_offline_mode_rejects_a_permissive_element_referrer_policy`, `test_offline_mode_accepts_an_element_policy_a_browser_does_not_honour`, `test_offline_mode_rejects_a_permissive_referrer_meta`, `test_offline_mode_accepts_a_referrer_meta_a_browser_does_not_honour`, `test_the_referrer_surface_is_left_alone_outside_offline_mode`, `test_the_referrer_policy_readings_match_what_a_browser_honours`; `tests/49-offline-export.spec.js` - the referrer assertions of `a preserved inline script cannot beacon by navigating the offline file to a remote URL (CMH-OFFLINE-05)` (a `<template>`-parked referrer meta pins the export's template walk); source: `skill/tools/validate/checks/resources.py` - `REFERRER_POLICIES`, `REFERRER_POLICY_LEGACY`, `REFERRER_POLICY_ELEMENTS`, `referrer_policy_attr()`, `referrer_meta_policy()`, `assets/js/68-export-offline.js` - `_ensureOfflineCsp()`, `_stripOfflineNetworkLoads()` |

| CMH-KQL-10 | Editing a KQL query regenerates its `Run in Azure Data Explorer` link, so the button can never execute pre-edit text. The query is encoded INSIDE the href, so re-highlighting only the `<code>` inner would leave a stale payload behind - silently, since nothing validates it. `kql_highlight.refresh_block()` recovers the cluster and database from the existing link's own ADX path (`kusto_link.decode_query()` is the inverse the tests verify the rebuilt payload with) and rebuilds both the code and the href, preserving the `figure.cmh-kql` frame, the caption, the `cm-skip` cluster copy affordance and the link attributes. `content_replace.py` applies it to every KQL figure in the fragment, so the agent edit loop keeps code and link in step; a figure that is not a runnable ADX block is left exactly as authored. The run link and the `language-kusto` code block are both located by the SHARED class-token reading (CMH-VAL-21 clause 11), so what the VALIDATOR calls a run link (CMH-KQL-05/07: any anchor carrying `cmh-kql-run` as a class token) is exactly what the rewriter can rebuild - a validator-clean figure whose link carries an extra class, a single-quoted or unquoted class, a character-referenced class, or `href` written before `class` is rebuilt rather than silently keeping its pre-edit query, and a `cmh-kql-run-ish` class (or a `language-kustomize` label) is not matched at all. The run link's start tag is RE-SERIALIZED from its parsed attributes, so `target` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"` survive, an `href` spelled inside another attribute's value is never the one rewritten, the figure this tool emits round-trips byte for byte (a HAND-WRITTEN link is NORMALIZED instead - names folded to ASCII lower case, values re-quoted and re-escaped from their decoded form, an inert trailing `/` dropped - all equivalent to a browser), and a duplicate `href` (which a browser ignores) is not left behind as a stale pre-edit payload. That re-serialization goes through the ONE shared writer (`_browser_attrs.serialize_start_tag`, CMH-VAL-21) and is ROUND-TRIP FAITHFUL for a VALUELESS attribute: it is written back as `name=""`, not as a bare name. The bare name dropped the `/` HTML uses to terminate an attribute name, so an authored `data-a/=onclick` was written as `data-a =onclick` and re-parsed as `data-a="onclick"` - a value the authored figure never had (#1195). An absent value IS the empty string to a browser, so the quoted empty value is the same attribute and cannot be terminated by the next name's `=`. EVERY run link in the figure is refreshed, because the validator's own gate accepts and checks more than one. What counts as an element is what the validator's PARSED views count: a start tag written inside an INERT region - an HTML comment (terminated or not), a raw-text body, or another tag's quoted attribute VALUE - is a decoy and is skipped rather than rewritten in place of the live one, at BOTH levels (`content_replace`'s figure scan and `refresh_block`'s link and code-block scans), and the tag names are terminated HTML's way (ASCII whitespace, `/` or `>`) in the anchor scan AND in the three copies of the code-block pattern (`kql_highlight`, `content_extract`, `highlight_document`), so a custom element such as `<a-run>` or `<pre-run><code-run>` is not an element to re-serialize or to read a query from. A comment ends where the validator's own parser ends one (`-->`, the legacy `--!>`, the abrupt `<!-->` / `<!--->`, or the end of the input when unterminated), and an end tag's quoted attributes are tokenized with it, so neither can hide a live element. An anchor written inside the code block's own body is content, not a control, so the edits stay disjoint and the splice cannot corrupt the block. The block the query is READ from (`content_replace`) and the block it is WRITTEN back to (`refresh_block`) are the same block - the figure's first KQL-labelled one - so a second, non-KQL code block in the figure cannot have its text encoded into the ADX link and written over the query. | `tests/test_kql_dispatch.py` - `AdxLinkRegenerationTests` (`test_the_run_link_encodes_the_query`, `test_editing_the_query_regenerates_the_link`, `test_refresh_preserves_the_frame_caption_and_cluster_affordance`, `test_refresh_is_a_no_op_for_an_unchanged_query`, `test_refresh_refuses_a_figure_it_cannot_understand`), `RunLinkShapeTests` (`test_every_validator_clean_run_link_shape_is_rebuilt`, `test_a_rebuilt_run_link_keeps_its_other_attributes`, `test_the_ordinary_single_class_run_link_still_passes`, `test_a_class_that_merely_contains_the_token_is_not_a_run_link`, `test_the_kusto_code_label_is_read_by_the_same_token_rule`, `test_a_code_label_that_merely_contains_the_kusto_name_is_not_a_kusto_block`, `test_a_kql_labelled_block_is_a_kusto_block`, `test_a_duplicate_href_is_not_left_behind_as_a_stale_payload`, `test_a_duplicate_attribute_keeps_only_the_first_as_html_does`, `test_a_valueless_attribute_cannot_fuse_with_the_next_one`, `test_every_run_link_in_the_figure_is_refreshed`, `test_a_run_link_inside_a_comment_is_not_the_run_link`, `test_a_kusto_block_inside_a_comment_is_not_the_code_block`, `test_tag_shaped_text_inside_an_attribute_value_is_not_a_tag`, `test_a_kusto_block_inside_an_attribute_value_is_not_the_code_block`, `test_a_comment_opener_inside_an_attribute_value_does_not_open_a_comment`, `test_an_unterminated_comment_runs_to_the_end`, `test_an_anchor_inside_the_code_body_is_content_not_a_control`, `test_a_custom_element_is_not_an_anchor`, `test_a_custom_element_block_is_not_a_code_block`, `test_a_preceding_unrecognized_block_does_not_hide_the_kusto_block`, `test_find_kusto_code_tolerates_an_empty_input`, `test_the_code_block_pattern_matches_content_extracts`); | CMH-HL-14 | Runtime keyword lookup is per LANGUAGE, mirroring each author-time config exactly, rather than one approximate bucket shared by the 23 languages in the `hash` and `c` families. The shared set both OVER-colored (a lowercase `true` in Python, `true`/`false`/`null` in R, `bool` in Objective-C were keywords at runtime but not at author time) and UNDER-colored (Python's capitalized `True`/`False`/`None` are author-time keywords the case-sensitive shared lookup never matched). Splitting was measured on the BUILT `commentable-html.js` (not on the raw keyword text) at 9,346 bytes, 736,669 to 746,015 or about 1.27 percent - cheap against a divergence visible in every Python block - so the approximation is removed rather than documented. Lookup order is per-language, then per-family, then the broad fallback, and a short alias (`py`, `js`, `rb`) resolves to the canonical name. The runtime identifier token mirrors the author-time `_IDENTIFIER_RE` INCLUDING its optional leading `@`, without which Objective-C's `@interface` / `@property` would split into a bare `@` plus a word no exact set contains - so the split would have colored LESS than the approximate bucket it replaced.
