| CMH-RESP-10 | A wide table never breaks a word mid-token. Table cells use `overflow-wrap: break-word`, NOT `anywhere`: the two break identically once a line is being laid out, but they differ in INTRINSIC SIZING, which is exactly what table layout depends on. `anywhere` participates in min-content sizing, so every cell reports a min-content width of roughly ONE CHARACTER and the table algorithm collapses a column to that and shreds its text even while other columns still have spare room. Reported against a 14-column table that rendered `NAMESPACE MOVE` as `NAMES` / `PACE` / `MOVE` and `computeservice-as-tvm-paros` as `computeservic` / `e-as-tvm-paros`. `break-word` is ignored for min-content, so a cell keeps its longest-word width and is only broken when there is genuinely nowhere left to go. | `tests/79-wide-table-wrap.spec.js` - `a wide table does not break words mid-token (CMH-RESP-10)`, which pins BOTH the computed property and the observable consequence (each cell is at least as wide as its longest word); source: `assets/css/50-content.css` |
| CMH-RESP-11 | A table that is genuinely too wide for its container scrolls horizontally inside its own box instead of pushing the whole document sideways. This is the necessary other half of CMH-RESP-10: `break-word` is IGNORED for min-content sizing (which is exactly what stops a column being collapsed and its text shredded), so a table whose columns cannot fit reports a min-content width larger than its container and escapes it - a worse defect than the shredding it cures. Every author table is therefore rendered inside a `.cmh-table-scroll` box. The wrapper is a real ELEMENT rather than `display: block; overflow-x: auto` on the table itself, because `display: block` wraps the rows in an anonymous table box that shrink-to-fits and collapses a fitting table's columns to their content width (measured: a 2-column table fell from 400px to 99px) - the same collapse the old `@media (max-width: 700px)` rule inflicted on phones, which this replaces. The wrapper carries the table's margins, since `overflow-x` makes it a block formatting context that would otherwise trap them and change the spacing around every table, and it adds no text nodes so no stored comment offset moves. A wrapper that ACTUALLY scrolls is focusable (`tabindex="0"`), named, and carries the scroll hint on `aria-description`, following the same ownership convention as the gallery-card scroll affordance; ownership is tracked PER ATTRIBUTE in `data-cmh-scroll-a11y` so an author's own label is never clobbered while the region still gets its tab stop (refusing to touch an author-labelled wrapper would leave a scrolling region no keyboard user can reach - the barrier this removes). One that fits carries no attributes and so adds no dead tab stop. The wrapper takes an explicit `width: 100%`, which matters in a FLEX parent (a gallery card row, a deck slide): a scroll container's automatic minimum size is 0, so a width-less wrapper would shrink to min-content and collapse the table (measured 900px -> 252px) - the same failure that ruled out `display: block`. The state is re-measured on resize and on late content via a `ResizeObserver` on both the wrapper and every table it directly holds, and a `MutationObserver` contains a table ADDED after startup (author content scripts run after the layer's JS region, so a document that builds a table at runtime would otherwise escape containment). A `.cm-skip` table is contained too - `cm-skip` only means "outside the comment text-offset coordinate system" and is used by author content, and the layer itself never creates a table - while a table that IS a draggable widget part is left to the widget layer, and a wrapper THE LAYER created and that a move or removal emptied is pruned (an author's own empty `.cmh-table-scroll` is left alone: it may be a mount point a later script fills). Attribute ownership is by VALUE, not by mere presence, so a regenerated caption refreshes the label the layer wrote instead of the stale value later looking like an author edit and being preserved for good. Because the wrapper becomes the flex/grid ITEM, the table's resolved item placement (`order`, `grid-column`, `grid-row`, `align-self`, `justify-self`, the `flex-*` trio) is carried onto it, so an author's placement keeps applying. A focused scroll region owns the arrow keys in a deck, which would otherwise change slides and leave the clipped columns unreachable by keyboard. Print reverts the wrapper to `overflow: visible` (paper cannot scroll, so clipping there would lose content) and keeps `anywhere` to make the table fit the sheet. `_clipContainersFor()` substitutes the wrapper for a table clip container with `closest` (an INNER table of a nested pair sits in a `td`, levels below the box that clips it), so CMH-RESP-02 bubble clipping still measures the box that actually clips. | `tests/79-wide-table-wrap.spec.js` - `a table too wide for its column scrolls in its own box, not the page (CMH-RESP-11)`, `wrapping a table leaves a normal table full-width and never double-wraps (CMH-RESP-11)`, `a table wrapper takes keyboard focus only while it actually scrolls (CMH-RESP-11)`, `a table in a FLEX parent keeps its width and is not collapsed (CMH-RESP-11)`, `a table added after startup is contained too (CMH-RESP-11)`, `an author-labelled wrapper keeps its label AND still gets the tab stop (CMH-RESP-11)`, `an author table inside a cm-skip host is contained too (CMH-RESP-11)`, `a table's grid placement survives being wrapped (CMH-RESP-11)`, `arrow keys scroll a focused table box instead of changing deck slides (CMH-RESP-11)`, `removing a table cleans up its wrapper, but an author mount point survives (CMH-RESP-11)`, `a regenerated caption refreshes the wrapper's own label (CMH-RESP-11)`; `tests/29-overflow.spec.js` - `a long unbroken token in a table cell scrolls inside the table's box instead of overflowing`; `tests/39-responsive.spec.js` - `every table fits the viewport and scrolls internally when wide` (each example report at 360px and 390px); `tests/76-diagram-gallery.spec.js` - `frames only diagram containers and leaves a stray table alone (CMH-CONTENT-19)` (the wrapper is not turned into a gallery card); source: `assets/js/61-table-scroll.js`, `assets/css/50-content.css`, `assets/css/92-print.css`, `assets/js/95-startup.js` |
| CMH-RESP-12 | A floating control (the hover bubble, the Add Comment buttons, the whole-diagram button) is bounded by the INTERSECTION of EVERY recognised clip container around its target, not just the nearest one. Clipping composes, so a diagram host inside a scrolling `.cmh-table-scroll` wrapper (CMH-RESP-11), inside a `figure.chart`, or inside a `.cmh-diff-raw` is itself clipped by that outer box: a target the OUTER box has scrolled out of view hides the control exactly as a target scrolled out of the nearest one does, and a target that is only partly visible clamps the control to the intersection instead of to a box that reaches past the outer one. `_clipContainersFor()` walks the whole ancestor chain (one selector built from both the gallery-card and the generic vocabularies of CMH-RESP-02) and `_clipAwareRect()` / `_floatingBounds()` intersect every box it returns; a single `closest()` returned only the FIRST match, so the inner box SHADOWED the outer scroller and the control floated over unrelated content - the defect of issue #769 in reverse. The `TABLE` -> `.cmh-table-scroll` lift is kept as a SUBSTITUTION inside the walk (the wrapper is the box that scrolls; the table itself can be wider than its visible box), and the walk subsumes the gallery-card preference the old resolver hard-coded: a `<figure><pre class="mermaid">...</pre></figure>` card is bounded by the figure's scroll card (the card's inner `pre` ships `overflow:visible` and grows to the diagram, so it is filtered out below), which is exactly the box the old preference picked - now reached by rule rather than by a special case. An empty intersection in `_floatingBounds()` falls back to the viewport, as before, because `_clipAwareRect()` has already hidden the control in that case. Only a box that CLIPS joins the chain, decided by computed overflow (`_clipsItsContent()`: an `overflow-x` or `overflow-y` other than `visible`, and never a `display:contents` element, which generates no box at all and whose empty rect would hide every control inside it). Overflow is the only mechanism consulted - a box that clips solely through `clip-path` or paint containment is not detected, which no shipped container uses and which the single-container resolver did not detect either. A gallery card's inner `pre.mermaid` deliberately ships `overflow:visible` and grows to the diagram it holds, and an author can set `overflow:visible` on any recognised container: bounding a control by a box its content plainly spills out of would be a NEW defect introduced by counting more boxes, so the filter is what makes honouring the whole chain safe. Every selector list is `filter(Boolean)`ed before it is joined, since an absent vocabulary would otherwise leave an empty token (`", table, ..."`) and one invalid selector makes `closest()` throw for every floating control in the document. | `tests/51-charts-mobile.spec.js` - `a floating control honours the WHOLE chain of nested clip containers, not just the nearest (CMH-RESP-12)`, `a recognised container that does not clip does not bound the control (CMH-RESP-12)`; `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `test_the_clip_layer_derives_its_containers_from_the_shared_constant` (the walk selector is built from both vocabularies and the resolver queries it); source: `assets/js/20-mermaid.js` - `_clipContainersFor()`, `_clipAwareRect()`, `_floatingBounds()` |

The obvious fix is ruled out: scrolling the header (`overflow-y: auto` plus a floor on the list) makes it a CLIPPING context, and the Export and More dropdowns are absolutely positioned inside it, so it would clip both menus. The header is split instead, at a seam that already exists in it. The three CHROME rows - the title row, the ribbon and the primary actions - are the ones that own the menus and the ones a reviewer needs at all times, so they stay `flex: none` and pinned, which keeps the menus' ancestry `overflow: visible`. The three rows that grow TRANSIENTLY and own no popup - the search row, the document-info lines and the identity row - move into a new `.head-aux` block that is `flex: 0 1 auto; min-height: 0; overflow-y: auto`, making it the one region the header's shrink lands in. The ORDERING under pressure is deliberate and the region carries NO floor of its own: a floor there would only ever bind when the header cannot fit at all, and there it would force the pinned chrome to overlap the cards instead (measured at a 24px host root font: with a 48px floor the header spilled 7px over the list, without one it does not spill at all). `.list` takes a `min-height: min(96px, 30vh)` floor so that shrink is taken from the header rather than from the cards, and a viewport 480px tall or less spends the header's (doubled) vertical padding on the same budget. 480px rather than 320px is deliberate: the trim helps any short window, including a short desktop one, and nothing about it is phone-specific. 96px is a card's meta line plus the start of its body - a usable scroll window, deliberately NOT "one card": a rendered card measures ~250px at this viewport, taller than the whole pane minus the pinned chrome, so no header can promise a whole one. The list floor is capped against the viewport (`30vh`) so it YIELDS below 320px instead of letting the pinned chrome overrun the list; measured, the full containment guarantee then holds all the way down to 640x240 - well under any device - and what is NOT promised below 320px is the 96px window itself, which scales with the viewport instead. The residual is a host document with a very large ROOT FONT, which inflates the pinned chrome rather than the viewport: at 640x320 in the comfortable preset with both transient rows open, nothing overlaps up to a 24px root, and at 32px the chrome exceeds the header box by 69px - unfixable without scrolling the chrome, which is the one thing this design refuses to do because the menus live there. Measured after the fix, all twelve states - with a card AND with the empty first-time list - keep the list fully on screen (96-120px visible, layout == visible) with zero pane overflow, and `.head-aux` keeps a 68-85px scroll window. Bounding a region has consequences, and each is handled rather than left. (1) `overflow-y: auto` alone computes the INLINE axis to `auto` too, so a long localized "Generated on" line would grow a horizontal scrollbar inside the header and spend the very budget this buys; the axis is pinned to `hidden` and `.cm-side-info > span` wraps instead. `hidden` rather than `clip` on purpose: the two compute identically here, but a browser without `clip` support drops the declaration entirely and falls straight back into the scrollbar this exists to prevent. Both halves are load-bearing and tested - the wrap is what stops the overflow existing, the pinned value is what a fallback lands on. (2) The region's clip edge is pushed out to the header's padding box with a negative inline margin and matching padding, so a control's focus ring is not shaved off and the scrollbar sits flush with the pane as the list's does; A `scrollbar-gutter: stable` was tried here and REJECTED by measurement: it would stop the rows shifting inline the moment the region starts scrolling, but on a classic-scrollbar platform it reserves that width permanently, which narrows the region enough to wrap the metadata onto another line and grow the header - measured in the pinned Linux renderer pushing a grown reply editor's Save button off screen (CMH-GROW-02). A shift that only happens once the region is already scrolling is the smaller cost. The `.cm-side-info` divider deliberately STAYS on the row rather than moving onto the region: on the region it would sit above the search row instead of directly above `Generated on`, which is the placement CMH-SIDE-03 pins, and the cost of leaving it - that it scrolls with the metadata it introduces - is cosmetic and only visible once the region is already scrolling. (3) The `set name` link's OVERLAID 44px tap target (CMH-RESP-14) overhangs its box by `(44px - link height) / 2`, and the identity row is the region's LAST child, so at phone width the region reserves that overhang inside its scrollport - without it the target was clipped AND a viewport with room to spare carried ~14px of scrollable overflow for a region with nothing to scroll. The header hands its own bottom padding to the region there, so a portrait phone pays nothing for the reservation (the space lands where the header's padding already was, and the border below it does not move) while a landscape phone gets that padding back as list. (4) The region is a scroller whose `.cm-side-info` lines have nothing focusable in them, so it takes a keyboard tab stop, `role="group"` and an accessible name WHILE it actually scrolls and gives them back when it does not (`assets/js/49-head-aux.js`), the same conditional treatment `61-table-scroll.js` gives a scrolling table wrapper (CMH-RESP-11), rather than leaving a region no keyboard user can scroll or a dead tab stop on a desktop. `group` rather than the landmark `region`, matching that precedent, so a landscape phone does not gain a landmark inside an already-complementary pane; the name is what is ALWAYS in the region rather than an enumeration of two rows that are hidden most of the time. A tab stop the layer adds also needs the layer's own focus ring - the UA default is what `assets/css/80-focus.css` exists to replace - and it is INSET, because the region now spans the pane's whole padding box and an outset ring's end segment would land on the viewport edge unpainted, exactly as `#commentList` already reasons. (5) Both floors carry an explicit `box-sizing: border-box`, as CMH-RESP-14's controls do, because the `border-box` reset lives in the document theme rather than the layer: under a reset-free host the padding would otherwise be ADDED to each floor and the region would overlap the list by ~43px, re-creating the defect. Revealing a row inside a bounded region also has to SCROLL it: the search toggle and the `set name` button focus their own field, which the browser scrolls in, but the identity NUDGE - the first way a reviewer meets the editor, opened for them when they save a first comment - deliberately opens it WITHOUT focus, so it was revealed 68.7px below the region's fold; `_identityEditing()` now scrolls the editor into view itself. Because the header can now shrink, the pane's own vertical overflow is no longer the metric that catches a deficit - it moves INSIDE the header, where the pinned chrome would paint over and hit-test above the cards - so the guard measures the header's own overflow and the gap between the primary row and the list as well. On a desktop viewport `.head-aux` does not scroll at all and the layout is unchanged. | `tests/72-followups.spec.js` - `the side pane header never pushes the comment list off the bottom on a landscape phone (CMH-RESP-16)`, `the side pane header's bounded region stays reachable on a landscape phone (CMH-RESP-16)`, and `enlarging the side pane's controls does not starve the comment list on a landscape phone (CMH-RESP-14)` (retargeted onto the visible-height metric); source: `assets/template.shell.html` - `.head-aux`, `assets/css/10-layout.css` - `.cm-sidebar header`, `.cm-sidebar .head-aux`, `assets/css/20-chrome.css` - `.cm-sidebar .list`, `assets/js/49-head-aux.js`, `assets/js/43-identity.js` - `_identityEditing()` |
| CMH-CONTENT-21 | Every runtime DOM mutation inside the content root is TEXT-NEUTRAL on an unedited document, and the slot-permutation that guarantees it lives in ONE place. The sort bug behind CMH-CONTENT-20 was a class, not a one-off: any pass that APPENDS elements instead of permuting them through their existing slots strands the whitespace text nodes an author leaves between them, making the elements textually adjacent - a change no later undo can reverse, which silently drifts the document and section content hashes and falsely raises the not-validated banner. The audit (#977) checked every other path that moves or injects nodes in `#commentRoot` and found the six named ones text-neutral: the table-scroll wrapper inserts its box AT the table's position (`61-table-scroll.js`), checklist controls and the code-line gutter are `cm-skip` and are inserted WITHOUT moving a sibling (`36-checklist.js`, `26-highlight.js`), an editable note's whole `[data-cmh-note]` subtree is excluded from the hashed text before AND after the runtime rewrites it (`37-notes.js`), and deck mode only toggles classes and appends `cm-skip` chrome to `document.body` (`95-startup.js`). The audit did find TWO real defects in the print appendix and fixed both test-first. First, the print appendix (`83-print.js`) materializes every open comment as real prose at the end of `#commentRoot` on `beforeprint`, so for as long as a print preview was open the document hash - and with it the validated banner and every section review badge - reflected the REVIEWER's notes rather than the document. Runtime-injected chrome is now excluded from the scan by IDENTITY (`CMH_HASH_EXCLUDED`, via `_cmhScanSkip`) rather than by a class - a set kept deliberately SEPARATE from the export-tail set `CMH_INJECTED_CHROME`, which is populated partly by a heuristic sweep where an over-capture merely costs a stale tail, whereas an over-capture here would silently subtract DOCUMENT text and produce the very false banner the hash exists to prevent: the appendix cannot simply wear `cm-skip`, because the print stylesheet hides `body > .cm-skip` and a document with no `#commentRoot` roots the layer at `<body>`, which would hide the appendix from the very print it exists for; and identity is the right test anyway, since the Python hasher reads the SOURCE file (which can never contain injected chrome) while an author element wearing the id would be wrongly dropped. Second, the appendix was resolved with `getElementById`, so an author element that happened to carry `id="cmhPrintComments"` was treated as the layer's own - overwritten on `beforeprint` and DELETED on `afterprint`, or immediately when the document had no comments to render - and, never having been registered as injected chrome, its authored prose moved the hash too; it is now resolved through a private reference to the element this module created (`_ownPrintAppendix`), the same resolve-your-own-control-by-identity rule as CMH-CORE-21. The ONE intentional exception is a draggable widget/triage-board card MOVE (`35-widgets.js`), where the arrangement IS the content: on a board that is not `cm-skip` the hash legitimately moves, and `Reset moves` restores every recorded child - the whitespace between the cards included - so the hash returns EXACTLY to its load value. The shared guard is implemented rather than rejected: `cmhPermuteChildrenInSlots` (the DOM writer) and `cmhPermutedChildNodes` (the pure reader used by the canonical-hash scan) in `00-preamble.js` are the single copy of the slot math, and both `_reorderBody` and `_cmhCanonicalChildNodes` are rewired onto them; each fails SAFE (declining anything that is not a permutation of nodes currently parented by the element, since an untouched DOM is always text-neutral). The persisted sort map is also re-homed onto a null-prototype object per CMH-SEC-02, so the runtime has one convention for a document-reachable state map rather than two. | `tests/96-dom-text-integrity.spec.js` - `the table-scroll wrapper does not move authored text`, `checklist control injection does not move authored text`, `editable notes do not move authored text`, `the code-line gutter and fallback highlighter do not move authored text`, `a cm-skip draggable board is hash-invisible, and Reset moves restores a plain board`, `deck navigation and the overview grid do not move authored text`, `sorting permutes rows through their slots, leaving authored whitespace in place`, `a polluted Object.prototype cannot inject a persisted sort`, `a crafted ::tableSort payload cannot pollute Object.prototype`, `an array ::tableSort payload is discarded, so a sort still persists across a reload`, `materializing the print appendix does not move the document hash`, `an authored element carrying the appendix id is neither clobbered nor hashed away`, and one per shipped example document, `the shipped report-triage.html hashes the same live as on disk` through `the shipped deck-showcase.html hashes the same live as on disk` (the LOAD-TIME catch-all: the live `window.__cmhReview.docHash()` is compared to the Python `document_content_hash` of the file on disk, so a NEW LOAD-TIME stranding mutation is caught even with no case written for it - an EVENT-driven pass still needs its own trigger test, which is exactly why the print appendix went unnoticed until it was fired explicitly); source: `assets/js/00-preamble.js` - `cmhPermuteChildrenInSlots()`, `cmhPermutedChildNodes()`; `assets/js/62-sortable-tables.js` - `_reorderBody()`, `_loadTableSortState()`; `assets/js/84-section-review.js` - `_cmhCanonicalChildNodes()`, `_cmhScanSkip()`; `assets/js/83-print.js` - `_ownPrintAppendix()` |

| CMH-PERSIST-01 | The document's `localStorage` namespace is `data-comment-key` for the JSON comment array, plus the sidecar keys `<key>::deleted` (embedded-delete tombstones), `<key>::commentSort`, `<key>::diffLayout`, `<key>::diffSyntax`, `<key>::tableSort`, `<key>::cl` (checklist state), and `<key>::note` (editable-notes state). | CMH-PERSIST-02 | `data-comment-key` is origin-scoped and must be unique per document; reusing it intentionally shares comments, tombstones, and UI state, and changing it starts a new namespace with no automatic migration. `new_document.py --key auto` derives a stable key from the document IDENTITY (`--key-from-source`, then `--source`, then the `--out` path), never from `--label`, so two documents that merely share a label do not collide; with no identity source it requires an explicit `--key`. | source: `assets/js/`; `tools/authoring/new_document.py` - `resolve_key()`; `tests/test_new_document.py` - `test_resolve_key_auto_same_label_distinct_identity_does_not_collide`, `test_resolve_key_auto_without_identity_requires_explicit_key`, `test_key_auto_derives_stable_key_from_out_path`, `test_key_auto_without_identity_exits_2` |
| CMH-PERSIST-03 | `mergeCommentSets()` de-dupes ids WITHIN the persisted array as well as across the embedded set, keeping the latest by timestamp (`updatedAt` then `createdAt`) regardless of array order, so a corrupted `localStorage` array that repeats an id renders and re-persists the newest version of that comment once, never twice. | `tests/47-hardening.spec.js` - `duplicate persisted comment ids dedupe and the newest-timestamp entry wins (CMH-PERSIST-03)`, `the newest duplicate wins even when it appears first (CMH-PERSIST-03)`; source: `assets/js/` - `mergeCommentSets()` |
| CMH-PERSIST-04 | `mergeCommentSets()` bounds startup work against an untrusted `embeddedComments` array or a poisoned `localStorage` array under a matching `data-comment-key`: the merged result is capped at `CMH_MAX_COMMENTS` (new ids stop being admitted once reached; an id already present may still be replaced by a newer duplicate), and any comment whose `start`/`end` is present but not a finite, non-negative, ordered, in-range number (per `CMH_MAX_OFFSET`) is dropped before it ever reaches `backfillContext()`'s or `restoreHighlights()`'s per-comment document walk. Comments with no offset anchor (document/image/widget/mermaid/diff) are unaffected. `restoreHighlights()` additionally requires a finite `start`/`end` before treating any comment as a text anchor, so a malformed entry with neither a recognized `anchorType` nor offsets (one that `mergeCommentSets()` lets through as trivially sane) cannot still drive a per-comment `rangeFromOffsets()` document walk. | CMH-SEC-04 | Accepted risk (by design, not a finding) - scoped to ONE thing: the runtime's automatic load of the mermaid diagram library from a version-pinned jsDelivr URL (`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@<version>/dist/mermaid.esm.min.mjs`) on the online render path. `build.py` pins that import to the single-sourced `dev/package.json` version (never a floating tag such as `latest`), so the pin fixes WHICH version loads; because it is a dynamic ESM `import()` it cannot carry a Subresource Integrity hash, so the accepted residual risk is trusting jsDelivr to serve untampered bytes for that one pinned URL, not merely the version. This is accepted because the dependency is on a top-tier, world-wide CDN (so this marketplace is only ever collateral, never a target) and Export Offline still produces a fully zero-network FILE. Since CMH-SIZE-08 that export DOWNLOADS the pinned UMD build (`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@<version>/dist/mermaid.min.js`) instead of reading bytes the document embedded, so the export path now depends on jsDelivr's AVAILABILITY at export time - but NOT on its trustworthiness, and that distinction is the point: unlike the render path's dynamic `import()`, which cannot carry an integrity hash, the export verifies what it downloaded with SubtleCrypto against a SHA-384 hash recorded at build time from `assets/vendor/mermaid.min.js`, and refuses to inline anything that does not match. The integrity guarantee this row accepts the loss of on the render path is therefore ENFORCED on the export path, and `tools/build.py --vendor-bytes` restores a build whose documents export with no network at all. The decisions are recorded in #451 and #1260. NOT part of this accepted risk and still in scope for review: Chart.js, which never auto-loads from a CDN on the RENDER path (it may load from one only on explicit per-document opt-in that requires a pinned version PLUS SRI/crossorigin, CMH-CHART-03). | CMH-SEC-06 | The offline threat model: what an offline export promises, what it does NOT, and how a review should triage a gap. A review that raises something this row puts out of scope cites it and dismisses it rather than opening an issue - but read the LIMITS below before doing so, because several classes stay fully in scope. **How the two layers relate (this refines CMH-OFFLINE-05, it does not contradict it).** The parser-level strips are the PRIMARY mechanism and the product promise: an Export Offline artifact is meant to carry no network references at all, and CMH-OFFLINE-05's browser tests deliberately prove the strip ALONE by re-testing with every CSP meta removed. The zero-network CSP `_ensureOfflineCsp` stamps (`default-src 'none'`, `connect-src 'none'`, `frame-src 'none'`, `object-src 'none'`, `img-src data:`, `font-src data:`, `form-action 'none'`) is defense in depth BEHIND that. The consequence is for SEVERITY, not for correctness: when the strip misses a spelling in a class the CSP does cover, the browser still blocks the load, so the gap is a tidiness defect and NOT A VULNERABILITY. **Non-goal (1) SCOPE - the enforcement boundary for triage.** The offline promise covers the commentable-html layer's own emissions; exhaustively hardening arbitrary authored input HTML against every exotic spelling is explicitly not a goal. So a NEW, previously unpinned way to spell a fetch in a CSP-covered class (an SVG paint or presentation attribute, `imagesrcset`, `iframe[srcdoc]`, a CSS escape or `image-set()`, an `ftp`/`ws` authority, a `noscript` raw-text boundary, a foreign-content parse divergence) does not earn its own issue unless a user can actually observe something. Enumerating such spellings is unbounded and was the largest single source of a supercritical backlog. The `iframe[srcdoc]` case in that list additionally has a SETTLED disposition rather than an open question: an offline document may not carry one at all, and issue #1080 weighed sanitizing the nested document against clearing it outright and confirmed the clear-outright rule (CMH-OFFLINE-04 records the four grounds and CMH-VAL-24 the authoring-time warning that now announces the cost), so a proposal to parse and rewrite a nested document has a recorded answer to engage with rather than an open question to raise - and where a proposal genuinely IMPROVES on the recorded grounds (the escaped-inert-text option CMH-OFFLINE-04 records as an open follow-up is the worked example), it is a finding like any other. **This is NOT a licence to regress:** any strip behavior a test already pins - every shape CMH-OFFLINE-05's specs assert with the CSP removed - is a REQUIREMENT, and breaking it is a defect, never a dismissal. **Non-goal (2) TRUST - a trusted author is not a threat actor.** This follows from CMH-SEC-01 (authored content is trusted, unsanitized HTML) and CMH-OFFLINE-04 (benign inline author scripts are preserved by design under `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`). A finding whose attacker is the document's own author, and whose payoff is a capability that author already has by writing an ordinary inline script (suppressing a layer control with a class, forging markup the tolerant parser reads differently from a browser), grants nothing new and is out of scope. **LIMIT: the STRIP-ENFORCED channels, where no CSP directive helps at all.** The speculative-connection link rels (`preconnect`, `dns-prefetch`, `prefetch`, `prerender`, dropped by the `link[href]` pass) leak DNS/TCP rather than fetching a subresource - `prefetch-src` was dropped from the spec, `connect-src` does not cover them, and `default-src 'none'` never sees them - and `<base href>` is neutralized by its own pass precisely because a meta-delivered `base-uri 'none'` does not bind a base the parser already resolved (`base-uri` and `frame-ancestors` are therefore NOT counted as enforcement anywhere here). For these the strip is the only enforcement in existence, so a gap or missed spelling in them IS a real egress bug, fully in scope, and must never be dismissed by citing this row. **The residuals a meta-delivered CSP cannot close are TWO, acknowledged rather than papered over.** (a) TOP-LEVEL NAVIGATION, exactly as CMH-OFFLINE-05 records it (`navigate-to` was dropped from CSP Level 3 and ships in no browser; `sandbox` is ignored in a meta-delivered policy). (b) WEBRTC: `RTCPeerConnection` ICE/STUN is governed by no shipped directive and `connect-src` does not cover it, so author script can emit UDP the policy never sees - shown empirically under this exact policy, where image, SVG, `srcdoc`, CSS and `a[ping]` fetches were all blocked and STUN was not. Both follow from preserving author scripts by design, so "no network" is a promise about what the LAYER emits and what these layers enforce, NOT a sandbox around hostile author code: a recipient still needs the file to come from an author they trust, because the export is not a sanitizer. The literal navigation pattern is BEST-EFFORT against the obvious spellings, never a completeness promise - deciding statically whether arbitrary JavaScript navigates is undecidable - so a further evading spelling (an optional call, a tagged template, an aliased or shadowed binding, a non-ASCII identifier) is a KNOWN INSTANCE of that residual rather than a new defect. **Always in scope, whatever the above says:** a change that weakens the CSP or the strip; EVIDENCE THAT AN ENFORCEMENT CLAIM IN THIS ROW IS INACCURATE (a channel asserted to be handled that is not - that invalidates the non-goal itself and must be raised, never dismissed by citing this row; the panel reviewing this row disproved two such claims already); a regression of any pinned strip behavior; a false POSITIVE where a strip deletes or rejects benign authored content; and any drift that makes the exporter emit a file its own `--strict` run rejects. | `tests/test_offline_threat_model.py` - `test_the_offline_csp_still_enforces_every_directive_the_threat_model_names`, `test_the_spec_declares_the_offline_threat_model_and_its_non_goals`, `test_the_threat_model_names_both_non_csp_coverable_residuals`, `test_an_inaccurate_enforcement_claim_is_never_dismissible_by_citing_this_row`, `test_strip_enforced_channels_are_named_and_really_are_strip_enforced`, `test_the_row_does_not_authorize_regressing_pinned_strip_behavior`; source: `assets/js/68-export-offline.js` - `_ensureOfflineCsp` |

| CMH-A11Y-13 | A toast is never invisible-but-operable behind a modal dialog, never an operable control OUTSIDE one, and a dialog a toast action opened never strands focus. | CMH-PRINT-06 | An eligible flat (non-deck) document prints / Save-as-PDF as a SINGLE continuous no-break page rather than paginating onto A4/Letter sheets, so no page break cuts through a section, table, chart, diagram, or code block - and it does so GENERICALLY across print destinations, not just Chromium's native "Save as PDF". On print entry (`beforeprint` / print-media) `83-print.js` measures the full content and injects a dynamic `@page { size: pageW pageH; margin: PAD }`. The page WIDTH is a shareable standard page (US Letter, 816px) rather than the on-screen reading column (~1280px on a wide screen), so the honored output is a standard-sheet-width PDF. Crucially the injected print CSS sets `html,body,.app { width: auto }` - it does NOT force a fixed body width - and takes the inset from the `@page` margin: this is progressive degradation. A browser that HONORS the custom `@page` size (Chromium's native vector "Save as PDF") fills the pageW-wide page as one tall page; a driver that IGNORES it (Microsoft Print to PDF, physical printers, browsers without custom-`@page` support) reflows the content into its OWN real Letter/A4 printable area and paginates normally, NEVER forced to an oversized width it would then downscale (the old bug: poor quality, side whitespace, stranded diagrams). The HEIGHT is measured at the exact content width the honored page renders at (pageW - 2*PAD) - a narrower column reflows taller and scales charts/diagrams to fit - so the measurement is accurate (no `.app`-overflows-body box-model skew, no double-counted page margin) and needs only a small safety band. Content that genuinely cannot fit the shareable width (a wide table) grows the page so nothing is clipped. Because Chromium LOCKS the `@page` to the measurement taken at `beforeprint` (screen media) and ignores later updates, the height is also measured proactively under stable screen media (a ResizeObserver on chart canvases plus a short settle) and cached as a floor. Documents that contain a block-stacking container - a multi-column gallery (`.visual-grid`) or a grid/flex widget such as a kanban board - are intentionally LEFT ON NORMAL PAGINATION (CMH-PRINT-04): their print-time grid->block reflow and async chart resize cannot be measured before the `@page` lock, so they page normally (content never clipped) instead of risking a bad single page. The injection never leaks into an export: the final rules are `@media print` (inert on screen), emptied on `afterprint`, and exports rebuild from the pristine on-disk/snapshot HTML. Content taller/wider than Chromium's ~200in page clamp also falls back to pagination. | `tests/70-print-pdf.spec.js` - `CMH-PRINT-06: an eligible flat document prints as a single continuous no-break page`; source: `assets/js/83-print.js` |
| CMH-PRINT-07 | The printable-height cap applies to BOTH mermaid host shapes, and it DERIVES that host set from the one shared diagram vocabulary rather than re-typing half of it. The runtime renders diagrams into `pre.mermaid` AND `div.mermaid` (`CMH_MERMAID_SEL` in `assets/js/03-selectors.js`; see CMH-CHART-12), so a document that authors its diagrams as `div.mermaid` gets the same 8.4in cap as a `pre.mermaid` one instead of an unconstrained SVG that overflows the printed page or splits across a break. The cap exists in TWO surfaces that must agree - the `@media print` stylesheet (`92-print.css`, what is printed) and the `measureCss()` string (`83-print.js`, applied under screen media to measure single-page height for CMH-PRINT-06) - and both had been scoped to `pre.mermaid` alone. Capping a host in one but not the other either prints an oversized diagram or measures a height the print never produces. `measureCss()` now builds its selector from `CMH_MERMAID_SEL` (contributing nothing at all, rather than a dangling comma, if that vocabulary is ever empty - an invalid selector would make the browser drop the whole cap), and the stylesheet - which as plain CSS cannot reference the constant - is PINNED two-directionally to it, so neither PRINT surface can drift back to half the vocabulary. | `tests/68-print.spec.js` - `CMH-PRINT-07: print caps a div.mermaid diagram exactly like a pre.mermaid one`, `CMH-PRINT-07: the measure CSS caps both mermaid hosts, so the measured page matches the print`; `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `RuntimeParityTests.test_the_print_measure_css_derives_its_mermaid_hosts_from_the_shared_constant`, `RuntimeParityTests.test_the_print_stylesheet_caps_exactly_the_shared_mermaid_hosts`; source: `assets/css/92-print.css`, `assets/js/83-print.js` |
| CMH-PRINT-08 | The wide-diagram scroll-fade edge mask is an ON-SCREEN cue only. It fades a scrollable diagram host's left and right 18px to signal that the diagram scrolls horizontally inside its own box; paper cannot scroll, so a host carrying `.cmh-diagram-scroll-fade` at print time prints with NO edge mask - for BOTH `pre.mermaid` and `div.mermaid` hosts (`CMH_MERMAID_SEL`; see CMH-RESP-09) - instead of a printed diagram whose left and right edges are washed out for an affordance the reader cannot use. The on-screen cue itself is unchanged. It is expressed by declaring the mask `screen`-only at its single source (`assets/css/70-kql.css`) rather than by adding a print-scoped reset in `92-print.css`: the cue is a pure screen affordance, and a reset would be a redundant SECOND rule naming the same host set - the shape that let `div.mermaid` fall out of the tall-media cap while `pre.mermaid` kept it (CMH-PRINT-07). A mask changes no layout, so the CMH-PRINT-06 measured single-page height is unaffected (measurement runs under screen media, where the cue still applies, exactly as on screen). The rule is pinned two-directionally to the shared diagram vocabulary: every scroll-fade mask rule must sit in a media context whose every comma branch names `screen` (a media list is a union, so `screen, all` would still match paper), must declare the prefixed and the unprefixed property (Chromium aliases the two, so only a textual pin can catch a dropped one), and the union of the hosts they fade must equal that vocabulary - so the fade can neither leak back into print nor fade one host shape while leaving the other unfaded. | `tests/68-print.spec.js` - `CMH-PRINT-08: print drops the diagram scroll-fade mask on both mermaid hosts`; `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `RuntimeParityTests.test_the_diagram_scroll_fade_mask_is_screen_only_on_exactly_the_shared_mermaid_hosts`; source: `assets/css/70-kql.css` |
| CMH-PRINT-09 | A TALL-NARROW diagram (rendered viewBox aspect w/h <= 0.5) prints at the printable COLUMN WIDTH instead of a sliver beside an empty band. The tall-media cap (CMH-PRINT-04/07) binds on HEIGHT alone (`max-height:8.4in;width:auto`), so for a diagram at least twice as tall as it is wide it sets the printed WIDTH to `8.4in * aspect` - measured at 42% of the column for a `769 x 2197` flowchart, leaving 58% of every row it occupies empty, while the same diagram fills the column on screen. The runtime marks such a host `.cmh-diagram-tall` from the rendered SVG's intrinsic viewBox aspect (`assets/js/20-mermaid.js`; intrinsic, so it is independent of the container width and of the on-screen narrow scale-up, and it changes nothing on screen), and BOTH print surfaces key a width-bound override off that marker: the `@media print` stylesheet (`92-print.css`, what is printed) and the screen-media measurement mirror (`measureCss()` in `83-print.js`), so the measured single continuous page matches what prints instead of reserving the shrunken height (CMH-PRINT-06). The host is also allowed to fragment (`break-inside:auto`), so a diagram taller than a page flows across pages rather than reserving one whole; that is effective because print already resets every `#commentRoot` descendant to `overflow: visible`, so the host is not the scroll container it is on screen (a box with clipped overflow would be monolithic and could not fragment). Wide and normal-aspect diagrams, figures, and images keep the 8.4in cap unchanged, and so does a tall-narrow diagram inside a .cmh-diagram-gallery card - a card is a compact uniform THUMBNAIL bounded by its card rather than a diagram stranded beside an empty column, and a gallery document is deliberately left on normal pagination, so width-binding one measured 77in and would have spent whole sheets on a single thumbnail. Conversely a `figure` WRAPPING a tall-narrow diagram is relaxed to `break-inside:auto` along with the host, because the figure rule would otherwise re-impose on the wrapper exactly the atomicity the host rule just relaxed. Two bindings are load-bearing beyond the obvious `width`, and each has its own red-first test. (1) `max-width` must be re-bound on both surfaces: such a diagram is usually ALSO `.cmh-diagram-narrow`, whose screen rule pins the SVG to `max-width: min(100%, var(--cmh-diagram-cap))` (CMH-MMD-10) and OUT-SPECIFIES the measurement mirror's cap, so measurement sized the page to that narrow cap while print used the full column and the single continuous page spilled onto 3 sheets. (2) The measurement mirror ALONE additionally bounds the diagram to the honored page's content width: that string is applied at two different widths (the wide reading column when the height cache is refreshed, the capped print content width at print time) and the larger result wins, and unlike a height-capped diagram a width-bound one is proportionally taller at the wider column - so without the bound the cache floor stamped ~9in of trailing blank onto the page, moving this issue's wasted space to the bottom of the sheet. Geometry note: on a PAGINATING driver a diagram taller than a whole page necessarily starts at the top of a page, so a partial page can still precede it - no CSS can both fit such a diagram on one page AND print it at column width. What the fix removes is the wasted width: the printed diagram now fills the pages it occupies (~36% ink versus ~14% for the sliver, with no full-height empty band beside it), and on the single continuous page (the Save-as-PDF path) nothing is stranded at all. Scope note: the 0.5 threshold is the issue's reported shape, not the full extent of the cap's mis-scaling - the cap shrinks the printed width for every aspect below roughly `column / 8.4in` (~0.87), so a diagram between 0.5 and that bound knowingly keeps a partial side band and stays on the fit-one-page cap, which is the conservative choice because the width-bound path trades page-fit for width. | `tests/70-print-pdf.spec.js` - `CMH-PRINT-09: a tall-narrow diagram prints at column width instead of a sliver beside blank space`, `CMH-PRINT-09: a tall-narrow diagram that is also narrow-scaled still measures the page it prints`, `CMH-PRINT-09: the width-bound override covers a div.mermaid host and never a deck`, `CMH-PRINT-09: entering print classifies a tall-narrow diagram before the page is measured`, `CMH-PRINT-04: reports print with no blank/stranded pages and dense widgets/galleries survive`; source: `assets/css/92-print.css`, `assets/js/20-mermaid.js`, `assets/js/83-print.js` |

| CMH-VAL-23 | Declarative shadow DOM is rendered content rather than an inert template to the validator and TOC generator. A browser-eligible HTML host (the standard attachShadow host set or a valid autonomous custom element) may attach its first `<template shadowrootmode="open">` or `"closed"`; that root contributes rendered prose and headings, including a shadow-rendered report title when its outer host is top-level, while an ineligible or foreign-namespace host, a second declaration on one host, an invalid mode, or any declaration inside an outer ordinary template contributes nothing. Script/style bodies inside a rendered shadow heading remain non-visible raw text and cannot become prose or a title. The supported authoring shape is intentionally bounded: every declarative root must carry `shadowrootserializable` so file-based Save/Shareable/Offline snapshots preserve open and closed roots through `getHTML({serializableShadowRoots:true})` (a browser implementing `Element.getHTML` is required for shadow-DOM export), and a shadow host may neither be `#commentRoot` itself, mix light-DOM children with the shadow template, nor use active `<slot>` distribution (a slot parked inside a nested inert template is ignored). Document-scoped metadata, ids, content-region markers, light-DOM links/charts/mermaid blocks, and layer state inside a shadow tree stay outside the document tree and cannot satisfy document-level checks; offline security still inspects its serialized script/style/inline-style content through the template-only views. The density pass applies the same namespace and document-root boundaries. The TOC lists only the first heading per outer light-DOM shadow host and links it to that host (injecting a collision-free host id when needed), because fragment navigation cannot target an element inside either open or closed shadow roots; nested shadow headings resolve to the outer light-DOM host, shadow ids do not shift light-DOM slugs, and shadow `id="commentRoot"` / `nav.cm-toc` markup cannot establish or replace document scope. Rewriting is refused when `#commentRoot` is itself the host because the inserted light-DOM TOC would be hidden and violate the supported shape. The runtime side TOC derives a serializable closed root's label when a light-DOM heading host has no text, honoring valid-mode and first-root-only semantics. Runtime Markdown and section-review/hash walkers remain deliberately light-DOM-only because review/comment anchors do not cross a shadow boundary. | `tests/test_validate_references.py` - `test_reference_inside_a_declarative_shadow_root_warns`, `test_declarative_shadow_root_prose_is_collected`, `test_shadow_script_and_style_text_is_not_prose`, `test_an_ineligible_hosts_shadow_template_stays_inert`, `test_an_autonomous_custom_element_can_host_a_shadow_root`, `test_only_the_first_declarative_shadow_root_on_a_host_is_rendered`, `test_a_declarative_shadow_root_inside_an_inert_template_stays_inert`, `test_a_title_rendered_by_a_declarative_shadow_root_satisfies_report_kind`, `test_a_shadow_h1_under_a_top_level_host_satisfies_report_kind`, `test_shadow_raw_text_alone_does_not_satisfy_report_kind`, `test_a_declarative_shadow_root_must_be_serializable_for_exports`, `test_a_shadow_host_cannot_mix_light_dom_children`, `test_shadow_slot_distribution_is_rejected_as_unsupported`, `test_a_slot_inside_an_inert_nested_template_is_not_distribution`, `test_comment_root_cannot_itself_be_the_shadow_host`; | CMH-VAL-24 | Outside offline mode an `<iframe srcdoc>` draws an authoring-time WARNING that Export Offline removes the nested document from the frame, so an author meets that cost while they are still authoring instead of in a transient toast after the export has already emptied the frame. This is the second half of the settled `srcdoc` trade (issue #1080, recorded in CMH-OFFLINE-04): sanitizing the nested document was implemented, weighed and rejected, so the frame really does reopen empty and the only remaining gap was notice. The notice SURVIVES the recipient-side half that followed (issue #1119, CMH-OFFLINE-04): the export now keeps the nested markup beside the emptied frame as escaped inert text, so what the message says changed - the frame stops RENDERING the nested document, and the markup is preserved as text - but the notice itself does not go, because an author who needs the frame to keep rendering still has to author the snippet as content instead. Saying it was 'removed outright' after that would send them off to duplicate by hand exactly what the export already preserves. What the notice promises is bounded by what the exporter really keeps: an EMPTY or whitespace-only value keeps nothing (there is no nested document), and that case is trivially visible to this tokenizer, so it is BRANCHED rather than glossed - a gate that describes behavior the exporter does not have is the one-sided rule CMH-OFFLINE-04 exists to prevent. The exporter's other bound, a frame in a FOREIGN namespace, is invisible to a flat tokenizer with no namespace to consult, so the wording carries it instead of branching on it: what is kept is what could have RENDERED, and an `<iframe>` inside `<svg>` renders nothing. WHICH whitespace counts as empty is the literal ASCII class the exporter uses (`nested.strip(" \t\n\f\r")` against `_OFFLINE_SRCDOC_CONTENT_RE`) rather than `str.strip()`, because the two engines' defaults disagree in both directions - `str.strip()` also takes U+001C-U+001F and U+0085, JS `trim()` also takes NBSP and U+FEFF - so a `&#xFEFF;` value had this notice promise a block the exporter never inserted and a `&#28;` value had it deny one it did. PRESENCE is the test, exactly like the offline-mode error - an empty or inert `srcdoc` warns too, because the export clears those as well - so nothing here parses the nested document and the exporter and the strict gate still agree by construction. It is read off the same shared EGRESS index the offline rule uses, so a `<template>`-parked frame, a `<noscript>` fallback and a self-closed foreign element are all named exactly as the export will really empty them. It is an ADVISORY (CMH-VAL-18, prefix `offline export advisory: `), never an error and never a blocking warning: it reports what a DIFFERENT mode's export would REMOVE, so the notice never fails `--strict`, never withholds the `commentable-html-validated` stamp, and never blocks a fail-closed caller such as `retrofit`. Blocking would have made DELETING the nested document the only route to a clean handoff - the very loss the notice exists to announce. That classification answers the CONTENT-LOSS question and is deliberately NOT a ruling that a nested document is SAFE outside offline mode: no check here can see inside an attribute value, so a network load parked in a `srcdoc` escapes the self-contained errors that would refuse the same load written as an element - a gap that predates this notice and is not decided by the advisory channel. It is now CLOSED by its own rule rather than left open: CMH-VAL-25 reads the nested document as a fragment and reports the loads inside it as BLOCKING findings (issue #1125), so the two findings on one frame answer different questions - this one what an offline export would REMOVE, that one what the frame FETCHES - and a frame that reaches no network still draws this advisory alone. An offline document reports the ERROR alone, so the two halves never double-report the same frame, and the branch is deliberately "not known to be offline" rather than "known to be shareable": a MISSING or malformed layer descriptor lands here too, which is harmless because the descriptor rule already errors on it independently. The message is collapsed onto one line before truncation, because a `srcdoc` carries a whole document and is almost always multi-line while a report line is printed line-oriented (the offline ERROR shares that treatment), and it says the offline copy shows whatever local `src` the frame also carries rather than promising an empty frame - the export clears only a NETWORK `src`. | `tests/test_validate_self_contained.py` - `test_a_srcdoc_warns_that_an_offline_export_will_remove_it`, `test_the_srcdoc_offline_warning_reaches_a_parked_frame`, `test_a_frame_without_a_srcdoc_draws_no_offline_warning`, `test_an_offline_document_reports_the_srcdoc_once_as_an_error`, `test_a_srcdoc_is_not_an_error_outside_offline_mode`, `test_the_srcdoc_notice_is_an_advisory_not_a_blocking_warning`, `test_the_srcdoc_advisory_reports_on_one_line`, `test_a_srcdoc_document_still_passes_strict_and_is_still_stamped`, `test_the_srcdoc_advisory_says_the_markup_is_kept_as_inert_text`, `test_the_srcdoc_advisory_promises_nothing_kept_for_an_empty_value`, `test_the_srcdoc_emptiness_test_is_the_exporters_ascii_class_not_the_engines`; the exporter half the wording describes is pinned by `tests/49-offline-export.spec.js` - `CMH-OFFLINE-04: an iframe srcdoc carries a nested document neither the strip nor the gate can inspect`, so a reader of this row reaches the test an exporter regression would fail |
| CMH-VAL-25 | The self-contained guarantee reaches INSIDE an `<iframe srcdoc>`: outside offline mode a network reference carried in the nested document is a BLOCKING finding at the SAME severity the byte-identical reference written as an element draws - an error, except a loading `link`, which is a warning at both levels (a non-advisory warning fails `--strict` and withholds the stamp just the same). It was the one spelling that escaped (issue #1125) - every rule above reads ELEMENTS, and a `srcdoc` carries a whole document as an attribute VALUE, so the tag index reads that markup as attribute TEXT and `<iframe srcdoc="&lt;img src=https://evil.example/x.png&gt;">` validated clean while `<img src="https://evil.example/x.png">` beside it was refused. That let a shareable file carry the `commentable-html-validated` stamp and still phone home, which is precisely what the stamp tells a recipient it will not do. The nested value is read as a FRAGMENT through the SAME shared tag index (`_find_tag_attrs_egress`) every other rule here reads - the fragment lookup `_tag_attr_index` already serves for a KQL figure's inner HTML - and the SAME predicates are applied to it (`is_network_url` for `img` `src`/`srcset`, `script` `src`/`href`/`xlink:href`, `iframe` `src` and a LOADING `link` `href`; the stricter `offline_is_non_local_ref` for a nested `<base href>`, which rebases every relative reference in the nested document). So a nested element gets exactly the verdict the identical top-level element gets, and there is no second notion of what a load is. The type-keyed `src` rule CMH-VAL-08 records (issue #1144) reaches in here too: an inert data block's `src` is no more a load inside a frame than outside one, while a script a browser RUNS still is. The cheaper option the issue sketched - scanning the RAW `srcdoc` TEXT for a network-looking URL - was weighed and REJECTED: it cannot tell an `<a href>` (navigation, exempt at the top level), a `data:` URI, or a URL written in prose from a real load, so it would BLOCK benign nested markup, and a false rejection is the one failure mode a gate that withholds the validated stamp cannot afford (the over-match trade CMH-OFFLINE-05 accepts is a best-effort pattern over UNDECIDABLE scripted navigation; a fragment read here is decidable, so accepting that trade would be a choice rather than a necessity). Reading the fragment costs no two-parser drift either, which is the whole reason this is takeable where sanitization was not (CMH-OFFLINE-04): shareable mode runs NO exporter strip pass over the nested document, so this gate is the ONLY implementation of the rule and has nothing to stay in step with. It is scoped to the not-offline branch because offline mode already rejects a `srcdoc` on PRESENCE, which is strictly stronger - so the two never double-report one frame and offline behavior is unchanged. Frames are found off the same shared EGRESS index, so a `<template>`-parked frame, a `<noscript>` fallback and a self-closed foreign element are all judged alike, and a frame nested inside a frame is walked to a bounded depth. The SEVERITY mirrors the top level element for element as well: a network `link` is a WARNING there, so the nested spelling is a warning too (a non-advisory warning fails `--strict` and withholds the stamp just the same, but a plain run must not report the nested spelling of a reference more harshly than the identical top-level element). Four residuals are recorded rather than implied. (1) What it MISSES: a reference the nested document builds at RUNTIME (an inline script that assembles a URL, a nested `fetch`) - the element-level read is a fetch-shape test, not an interpreter - and the same shareable-only CSS-spelling residual CMH-VAL-08 records (a bare remote string in `image-set(...)`, a CSS escape, a URL hidden by a comment), because the nested read applies the SAME shared patterns. This residual USED to be far wider and to cost nothing, because shareable mode checked none of the media/CSS set at the top level either, so the nested read carried exactly the top-level residual rather than adding one. That is no longer so, and the nested set moved WITH the top-level one rather than lagging it (issue #1145): the two share `_MEDIA_LOAD_ATTRS` rather than restating it, so `video`/`audio`/`source`/`track`/`object`/`embed`/`input type="image"`/SVG `image`/`use`/`feImage` (including the `<image src>`/`<image srcset>` pair added in #1165, which a browser fetches because it renames the start tag to `img`) and the legacy `background` attribute are all reported inside a frame now, at the same severity their top-level twins draw, a nested `meta http-equiv=refresh` to a network target, and a nested `<script type="speculationrules">` (read on its TYPE alone, the way the top-level rule reads it, so the nested body is never parsed as JSON), and nested CSS egress in BOTH of its spellings - a `style=` attribute (through `_find_inline_styles_egress`) and a `<style>` BODY (through `_find_fragment_styles`, a scripting-disabled parse of the nested text, which is the pass that buffers style bodies at all and is also the right egress view for a `<noscript>` fallback). The `<style>` body needs that separate parse because the shared attribute index deliberately does not buffer ordinary style bodies - it would hold a second copy of the whole layer stylesheet for every cached document - and the raw-text alternative is the false-rejection trade this row rejected above; it FAILS CLOSED on its own flag rather than the attribute parse's, since it is a second, independently-failing parse and an empty style list from a parse that blew up must mean "could not look", never "this fragment has no stylesheet". The work stays bounded because a nested document is physically contained in its parent's attribute value: each distinct nested value now costs a FIXED TWO passes (the cached attribute index, plus this one uncached style pass) rather than one, and two is a constant, so a wide or deep nest is still linear in the text it actually carries. So the nested read is now NARROWER than the top-level rule in no place that the top-level rule itself is not. (2) The ONE deliberate strictness difference: a nested Chart.js CDN `src` is not exempt. The top-level exemption exists for a single documented opt-in - the loader that draws THIS document's `<canvas>` charts, whose version and SRI `check_charts` audits when the document renders one - and a copy parked inside a nested document can never be that loader, because a frame cannot draw into its host's canvas. So the exemption has nothing to exempt rather than being withheld. A network `src` on a frame that ALSO carries a `srcdoc` is reported rather than treated as shadowed, at both levels: `src` is the documented FALLBACK an engine without `srcdoc` support navigates, and Export Offline clears `srcdoc` unconditionally (CMH-OFFLINE-04), so it is exactly the reference that survives into a copy where nothing shadows it. (3) What it deliberately does NOT do: the top-level LOCAL-path `img` warning ("run tools/inline_images.py") has no nested counterpart. This is an EGRESS gate, not a portability advisor, and a relative reference in a demo frame is not a load. (4) It fails CLOSED, and both paths are pinned by mutation: a nested fragment whose parse blows up, and nesting past the depth budget, are REPORTED rather than read as "loads nothing". The walk is bounded by the DOCUMENT rather than by the branching factor - a frame's content is physically contained in its parent's attribute value and shrinks by a round of entity escaping per level, and a value is tokenized twice per batch of lookups - once for the cached attribute index and once for the uncached style-body pass, a fixed constant rather than a growing one - so a wide or deep nest costs work linear in the text it actually carries. | `tests/test_validate_self_contained.py` - | CMH-VAL-27 | Outside the layer views, "will a browser execute this?" is answered by the BROWSER's rule per NAMESPACE and per script TYPE, never by tag name. `_flush_raw_captures()` used to drop the capture's insertion namespace when it finalized a `<script>`/`<style>` into `parser.scripts`, so every consumer downstream of it judged execution by the tag name plus `type` and `src` alone - the same fail-OPEN class CMH-VAL-19 closed for the layer views, still open one step further out. The mermaid SVG control is written as a CLASSIC script for that reason, so no test asserts the unverified fact in either direction. The whitespace-only `type=" "` case is deliberate rather than an oversight and must not be "simplified" into the `type=""` branch: the algorithm tests the RAW value against the empty string BEFORE it strips, so only a literally empty value takes the classic branch. `script_code_runs` takes `ns` with an `"html"` default for the one caller whose elements are HTML by construction, and that caller passes it explicitly anyway so the reason lives at the call site; any caller iterating `parser.scripts` must pass that record's own `ns`. The comment scanner ends a quoted string at a NEWLINE as JS itself does, because without that a regex literal far above the scanned region - one carrying a quote inside a character class - opened a string state that ran for hundreds of lines and left 65 comment lines and 5 block comments standing; its tripwire checks the WHOLE file, since the scanner is stateful and an upstream desync is what reaches the region. | CMH-BUILD-23 | No name is declared more than ONCE in the runtime bundle's shared scope. The `assets/js/NN-*.js` partials are concatenated into one classic script inside one IIFE, so every partial's top-level `function` / `class` / `const` / `let` / `var` binding shares a single scope. A redeclared `function` is LEGAL there and the LATER declaration silently wins, so a duplicate survives the whole suite as dead code (issue #1183 shipped two identical `_cmhCommentableLink` declarations that way, baked into `SHAREABLE.html` and every built example); a duplicate `const` / `let` / `class` is the opposite failure - a bundle-wide SyntaxError that renders every report as inert HTML, reported against a line in a multi-megabyte artifact rather than against the identifier. A delimiter-aware walk (strings, template literals with `${}` nesting, line, block and Annex B HTML-like comments, regex literals, ASI, and the brace/paren/bracket stack) collects every shared-scope binding from BOTH the concatenated partials and the BUILT layer, and names the identifier, its kind, and every partial and line that declares it. The walk FAILS CLOSED rather than guessing: a destructuring binding (whose names it does not unpack), an identifier escape, a mismatched closer, and a delimiter stack that unwinds out of the shared scope are each REPORTED, not skipped. Its result is then cross-checked against a REAL JS engine: where `node` is on PATH (CI always has it) the bundle body is run as a script whose first statement is a `throw`, so V8 instantiates the scope - creating every top-level function binding - before executing a single statement of the runtime, and every name V8 hoists must be one the walk found; V8 must also PARSE the body, which is what independently settles the duplicate `const`/`let`/`class` half, since that is a SyntaxError. Two engine-free cross-checks back it up: the stack must come back empty and the shared scope must be the bundle's outer wrapper (asserted structurally, not by byte offset), and a plain COLUMN-0 regex must not find any name the walk already knows declared MORE often than the walk did - which is #1183's exact shape, both copies at column 0. So an under-count of a column-0 declaration reds the gate instead of quietly narrowing it, and the controls make a walk that stopped reporting fail rather than pass vacuously. The walk is a heuristic, not a parser, and the layering above is what bounds it rather than any claim to see every binding; the DOCUMENTED exclusion is HOISTING out of a nested BLOCK - a `var` written inside a block or a `for` header, and an Annex B `function` declared inside a block (this bundle is sloppy mode), both bind in the same function scope but are not tracked, because telling a block brace from a function-body brace is the cost and the runtime already has ~100 nested `var`s. A duplicate SHARED-SCOPE `var` is refused as a policy, since a second initializer silently overwrites the first and two partials claiming one name is an accident either way. | `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `test_no_declaration_in_the_bundle_is_made_twice`; source: `assets/js/*.js`, `skill/dist/commentable-html.js` |
| CMH-BUILD-24 | The tutorial capture's mermaid route is VERSION-AGNOSTIC about the URL and STRICT about the bytes, so a mermaid bump can neither break screenshot capture nor silently render it from the wrong release. `tools/capture_tutorial.mjs` aborts every remote fetch to stay hermetic and registers one narrower route that serves mermaid's version-pinned jsDelivr import from the local `node_modules/mermaid/dist`. That route is the only thing standing between the capture and the catch-all abort, and the URL it must match is single-sourced from `package.json` and restamped into the shell on every build - so a route that pinned a LITERAL version (`mermaid@11.16.0`) stopped matching the moment the dependency moved, mermaid never loaded, and `npm run shots` failed on a `waitForMermaid` timeout that pointed at nothing. Being version-agnostic about the URL would on its own trade a loud failure for a SILENT one - the local entry module's relative chunk imports resolve back through the same route, so the render is internally consistent at whatever version happens to be on disk, and the committed PNGs would be rendered from a mermaid that never ships - so `assertInstalledMermaidIsPinned` refuses to capture at all when the installed mermaid differs from the `package.json` pin, naming the fix. The refusal DECISION is extracted into `tools/mermaid_pin.mjs` so it is exercised directly rather than asserted about as source text: agreement proceeds, a STALE install is told to run `npm ci`, and a lockfile that has moved ABOVE the pin is told to bump the pin and re-vendor instead (advising `npm ci` there would loop, since `npm ci` reproduces it).
