| CMH-BUILD-17 | Element-clipped tutorial screenshots are DIMENSION-STABLE across renderers. Their clip height is derived from the element's laid-out height, which depends on FONT METRICS, not on the browser. The capture does not use the report's own font stack: `freezeMotion` pins it to `font-family: Arial, sans-serif !important`, and that pin is only as shareable as Arial is - Windows resolves real Arial, while the pinned Linux container ships no Arial at all and fontconfig substitutes Liberation Sans, which is metric-compatible with Arial in ADVANCE WIDTHS (so the width is identical to the pixel and no shot drifts horizontally) but not in VERTICAL metrics. Issue #698 measured `.cmh-checklist` under identical CSS (`font-size: 15px`, `line-height: 23.25px`) and an identical lockfile-pinned chromium: each row renders 23.391 CSS px tall on Linux versus 23.250 on Windows, so the element measures 230 CSS px instead of 228, which at `deviceScaleFactor: 2` is a 4 device px PNG delta with no content change. `tools/shot_clip.mjs` is the single source of that geometry (`CLIP_QUANTUM`, `DEVICE_SCALE`, `DIMENSION_DELTA_PX`, `MAX_WIDTH_DELTA`, `quantizeClipHeight()`, `clampedClipHeight()`, `heightDeltaAllowed()`), and every CONTENT-derived clip height in `capture_tutorial.mjs` - the element clip, the fixed-region clip, and the comment-search clip - is snapped onto that grid, so the drift collapses onto one value and the PNG dimensions stop depending on which renderer produced them (verified: the same checklist scene renders 2444x464 on a Windows host and in the pinned container). A clip bounded by the viewport or by a panel is quantized LAST and DOWNWARD (`clampedClipHeight`), so a clamped clip lands on the grid too; quantizing up and then clamping would leave an off-grid height, and an element that clamps on one renderer but not the other would differ by an arbitrary sub-quantum amount - the same bug moved rather than fixed. Only the height is quantized, because the layout width comes from the fixed viewport; full-viewport clips are a fixed 1320x900 box and are left alone. The guarantee holds while the per-shot renderer drift stays under one quantum (about 0.6% of a clip height for the measured font pair, so ~5.4 px at the 900 px viewport ceiling); a wider gap moves two quanta and fails loudly, which is the signal to raise the quantum rather than widen the budget. Because no pure function of a drifting measurement can be boundary-free, the `--check` HEIGHT comparison (`heightDeltaAllowed`) admits exactly one non-zero value - one whole quantum - and only BETWEEN TWO HEIGHTS THAT ARE BOTH ON THE GRID: an exact value rather than a band keeps a sub-quantum delta failing (that can only be real content added or removed at the bottom edge, which the overlap-cropped pixel diff cannot see), and the on-grid requirement keeps the allowance away from clips that are NOT quantized, so removing or appending exactly one quantum of visible rows on a fixed-viewport shot still fails. Width keeps its own strict budget. The comparison lives once in `tools/shot_compare.mjs` - dimension gate in Node, only the pixel diff in the browser - imported by both the tool and the heavy freshness spec (they previously carried byte-identical copies that could silently diverge), and `--print-paths` reports the geometry and budgets so the two cannot drift apart. | `tests/80-shot-clip.spec.js` - `quantizeClipHeight collapses any sub-quantum drift onto the grid (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `quantizeClipHeight never crops the element and is idempotent (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `a clamped clip lands on the grid and never exceeds its bound (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `the straddle allowance applies only between two on-grid heights (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `dimensionsMatch keeps width strict and rejects an unreadable PNG (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `capture_tutorial reports the shared clip geometry and budgets it renders with (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `every committed tutorial shot is on the clip grid or full-viewport (CMH-BUILD-17)`; `tests/54-tutorial-shots.spec.js` - `a grid-line straddle in the baseline does not fail --check, a smaller shift does (CMH-BUILD-17)`, `regenerates every garden shot into a nested out dir, and --check passes on fresh output (CMH-TUT-SHOTS-01)`; source: `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/shot_clip.mjs`, `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/shot_compare.mjs`, `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/capture_tutorial.mjs`; docs: `docs/testing-guidelines.md` |
| CMH-BUILD-18 | A failed screenshot drift gate leaves the pixels it saw behind as evidence. Because the tutorial PNGs are rendered ONLY in the pinned container (CMH-BUILD-16), a contributor without Docker cannot reproduce a drift failure locally, so the CI run has to carry the proof: `capture_tutorial.mjs --check` KEEPS its freshly rendered PNGs in `tmp/tutorial-shots-check/<pid>` on ANY unsuccessful run - a stale or missing shot, and equally an exception thrown mid-capture (a browser crash, a selector timeout), which previously fell through the cleanup and DELETED the shots already rendered - and deletes them only on a clean pass, and the required `playwright-heavy` job uploads that tree as the `tutorial-shots-drift` artifact instead of letting it die with the runner (unzipped, its root is the `<pid>/<scene>/` tree). For each FAILING shot the check also writes a `<scene>-<name>.diff.png` beside the fresh PNG, painting every pixel that differs by more than the gate's own channel tolerance in magenta over a faded copy of the committed shot. It renders on the MAXIMUM bounds of the pair and marks any pixel present in only one image, so a dimension change - a normal failing result - is marked rather than clipped away into a diff with no magenta at all, so a reviewer sees WHAT moved instead of eyeballing two near-identical screenshots. It is produced only on failure (so a green run pays no extra render), lands inside the tree the artifact already uploads (so no workflow change is needed), and is best-effort - a diff that cannot be rendered is skipped and never changes the pass/fail outcome. The upload is conditioned on the gate STEP's own outcome (`failure() && steps.shots.outcome == 'failure'`), not the job's, so a green run never pays for it and the shards that skip the once-only gate never upload an empty artifact; a gate that failed before the comparison (an unpinned digest, a docker error) warns rather than adding a second, misleading failure, and `overwrite: true` keeps "Re-run failed jobs" - which reuses the run id an artifact name is unique within - from dying on the existing artifact instead of recording the fresh evidence (one name is enough because only the single once-only shard ever uploads). The evidence is kept for 14 days: long enough to outlive a review round without paying the default 90 days of storage for a failure that is usually fixed the same day. The action is pinned by full commit SHA like every other third-party action, and `docs/testing-guidelines.md` names the artifact and the committed files to compare it against, so a rename cannot silently orphan the instructions. | `tests/test_shots_linux.py` - `DriftEvidenceRetentionTests` (`test_the_scratch_is_removed_only_on_a_clean_pass`, `test_the_clean_flag_is_set_only_after_the_comparison_passed`, `test_a_failure_says_where_the_evidence_is`), `MidCaptureCrashTests` (`test_a_crash_after_the_first_scene_keeps_the_rendered_pngs` drives the REAL check through the pinned renderer with the `CMH_SHOTS_FAIL_AFTER_SCENE` fault hook and asserts the already-rendered PNGs survive, `test_the_fault_hook_is_unset_in_a_normal_run`), `DiffImageTests` (`test_the_comparator_exports_a_diff_writer`, `test_the_check_writes_a_diff_only_for_a_failing_shot`, `test_the_diff_lands_inside_the_uploaded_scratch_tree`, `test_a_diff_failure_cannot_change_the_gate_outcome`); `tests/81-shot-diff-image.spec.js` - `a differing pair produces a diff image marking the changed pixels`, `an identical pair marks nothing`, `a missing input is reported rather than throwing`, `a dimension change is marked, not silently dropped`, `the diff marks exactly what the gate counts, at the tolerance boundary`, `the tolerance the diff marks with is the same one the gate counts with`; `tests/test_shots_linux.py` - `test_a_drift_failure_uploads_the_fresh_screenshots`, `test_the_evidence_upload_never_runs_on_a_green_job`, `test_the_artifact_action_is_pinned_by_commit_sha`, `test_the_guide_tells_a_contributor_where_the_artifact_is`; source: `.github/workflows/plugin-tests.yml` - the `playwright-heavy` drift-evidence upload, `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/capture_tutorial.mjs` - `checkScreenshots` keeps the scratch on failure; docs: `docs/testing-guidelines.md` |
| CMH-BUILD-28 | The drift gate's evidence artifact is ADOPTABLE, so a stale screenshot on `main` is fixable without Docker. The committed PNGs render ONLY in the digest-pinned container (CMH-BUILD-16) and a failing gate already uploads exactly what that container rendered (CMH-BUILD-18) - but nothing consumed it, so the documented fix was `npm run shots`, which needs a renderer. That is not hypothetical: issue #1275 was FILED rather than fixed for precisely this reason, while every open pull request inherited a red required check it did not cause. `tools/shots_linux.py --adopt <dir>` re-baselines the committed screenshots from an unzipped `tutorial-shots-drift` directory, and `--adopt-run <run-id>` fetches that artifact with `gh` first. The run id is bound to THIS checkout's repository: gh resolves it from `GH_REPO`, then `gh repo set-default` (recorded in the checkout's OWN git config, so running in `REPO_ROOT` SELECTS that override rather than neutralizing it), then the cwd's remotes BY NAME preference - never from where the script lives. Running in `REPO_ROOT` therefore settles none of it on its own, so `GH_REPO` is FORCED to the `host/owner/name` parsed from this checkout's `origin` remote, which overrides all three while staying derived from the worktree rather than hardcoded. The HOST is part of it because `GH_REPO` takes the documented `[HOST/]OWNER/REPO` form and gh falls back to an ambient `GH_HOST` when it is omitted, so an enterprise host in the environment could otherwise serve the same run id and artifact name from a different server. When `origin` cannot be read, `GH_REPO` is removed rather than left at an ambient value and gh falls back to resolving from the cwd. It is downloaded into a uniquely-named scratch dir under `tmp/`, removed on success but KEPT on a refused ADOPTION (with its path named), because that refusal tells the operator to inspect the artifact and it is the only unzipped copy - the same keep-the-evidence rule CMH-BUILD-18 follows. A failed DOWNLOAD is a separate phase that removes the directory instead: nothing was fetched, so keeping it would both misreport and accumulate empty directories on the commonest failures (a bad run id, no `gh`, an expired artifact). `--adopt-run` also REPORTS what produced the bytes (`gh run view --json headSha,headBranch,event,url`) and warns on two counts the operator cannot otherwise see at decision time: the run rendered a commit other than the checked-out one, and - more important - the run's EVENT is not `push`, because the drift artifact is uploaded by `pull_request` runs too and those pixels were rendered from that pull request's own source. Repo-binding cannot catch that second case, since such a run IS a run of this repository. Both are warnings rather than refusals (a maintainer fixing `main` from a worktree legitimately has a different HEAD), and the whole lookup is best-effort so no failure costs the operator the fix. The artifact tree is walked depth-agnostically and keyed by FILE NAME (it unzips as `<pid>/<scene>/`), suffix matching is case-INSENSITIVE so a `.PNG` is adopted-or-refused rather than silently skipped (a silently adopted SUBSET is the one outcome this tool must never produce), and the per-shot `*.diff.png` the check writes beside a failing render is excluded - it is a magenta-marked report of the failure, not a render. The whole plan is decided, and every source byte READ, before anything is written, and it REFUSES as a whole rather than partly applying: a path that is not a directory; a PNG whose name is not already a committed baseline, matched against the EXACT `os.listdir` names because `os.path.isfile` answers case-insensitively on Windows and would rewrite a tracked file under a new spelling (such a name is either a foreign artifact or a shot this repository renders but has never committed, and a NEW baseline has to come from the renderer); a file that is not a USABLE PNG, validated by walking the chunk stream with `zlib.crc32` and requiring a 13-byte `IHDR` first with non-zero dimensions, at least one `IDAT` whose compressed stream inflates to a NON-EMPTY result and reaches its zlib end-of-stream (`decompress` does not raise on a stream that merely stops, so a partial download would otherwise read as "inflates fine"), bounded by what the DECLARED dimensions could hold - one filter byte per row plus 8 bytes per pixel, the widest PNG format - so a decompression bomb is refused after a few dozen bytes rather than inflated in full, all streamed and discarded so no decompressed frame is ever held; and an empty terminal `IEND` with nothing trailing - not by testing the 8-byte signature; the gate DECODES these files, so a truncated download keeps its signature and would red the gate permanently with an undecodable baseline, and a signature test would have made that refusal message untrue; a non-regular entry such as a symlink, and equally a linked DIRECTORY, whose contents would otherwise be read from OUTSIDE the artifact - `os.walk(followlinks=False)` does not follow a POSIX directory symlink but DOES descend into an NTFS junction, reproduced with `mklink /J`, so every candidate must additionally `realpath` inside the root; a file larger than any tutorial screenshot could be (32 MB, ~60x headroom), so a hostile artifact cannot be read wholesale into memory; one name appearing twice under the root, folded for case so two spellings that address one baseline on Windows collide here instead of racing; and an empty directory, refused loudly because "nothing to adopt" and "you pointed me at the wrong place" must not both read as success. The WRITE phase is all-or-nothing too, not just the decision: each file is replaced through a sibling temp file and `os.replace` (whose descriptor is closed before reopening by name, or the cleanup unlink would fail on Windows and strand the temp file, and whose mode is copied from the baseline, or `mkstemp`'s 0600 would silently make the committed screenshots owner-only), so a failure can never truncate a baseline in place; and if ANY exception interrupts the loop - a Ctrl-C between two files as much as a disk-full error - every file already written is restored from the bytes the plan read, attempting them all and reporting each restore that itself failed rather than abandoning the rest. The plan carries BOTH sides' bytes for that reason, so neither the write nor the rollback re-reads a file that changed after the comparison. Adopting cannot be combined with `--check`, `--native`, `--print-image` or `--record-digest` (it installs pixels another run rendered, so pairing it with a mode that renders here would leave it ambiguous which pixels won), `--skip-without-renderer` (meaningless when nothing renders), takes no forwarded capture arguments (it runs no capture, so a typo'd flag would otherwise vanish and read as a clean adoption), and rejects an EMPTY `--adopt`/`--adopt-run` value instead of treating it as absent - a falsy empty string used to skip the adopt branch entirely and fall through to the container REGENERATE path. Adoption deliberately does NOT require the artifact to cover every committed shot, because a mid-capture crash legitimately uploads only the scenes rendered before the throw; the no-drift report therefore states the artifact's OWN coverage and says so explicitly, so it can never read as "every committed shot is fresh". It relaxes nothing: the pinned container's `shots:check` stays the sole authority on whether the screenshots are right, and adopting is a re-baseline from that same renderer's output, never a verdict. | CMH-BUILD-19 | The tutorial-screenshot drift gate is EXACT: no differing pixels are allowed, sized to the determinism ONE pinned renderer actually gives rather than to two renderers agreeing. It used to downsample 2x, quantize colors onto a 64-step ladder (snapping near-white to white) and tolerate a channel delta of 96 across up to 20% of the pixels, so a real visual regression could pass the required gate unseen - a budget sized before the renderer became a single digest-pinned container. Issue #710 measured what that renderer gives: two independent renders of all 19 committed shots are BYTE-IDENTICAL, in the container and on a host browser alike, including under four concurrent captures and a 6-worker stress run. So `tools/shot_compare.mjs` applies NO normalization (no downsample, no quantize, no near-white snap - `PNG_DOWNSAMPLE` and `PNG_QUANTIZE_STEP` are gone) and `MAX_DIFF_PIXELS` is 0. The volatile BUILD STAMPS that would otherwise repaint a shot on every release - the runtime version badge and the document's "Generated on" date (which falls back to `document.lastModified`, volatile per checkout) - are neutralized at CAPTURE time (`tools/shot_stamps.mjs` rewrites them to the fixed `v1.x` / `Jan 1, 2026` placeholders before each clip is measured and again before each shot is taken) instead of being bought off with a pixel allowance: an allowance applies to the WHOLE image, so a budget wide enough for a repainted badge is also wide enough to hide a small real regression anywhere, and because the same comparison drives the WRITE path, `npm run shots` would refuse to update a shot whose intended change fell inside it. The freeze is deliberately NARROW - only the elements the runtime stamps those two values into (`#cmVersion`, `.cm-version`, `.cm-footer-ver`, the Help heading and About paragraph; `#cmGenerated`, `.cm-footer-gen`) and only the value inside them - so layer copy that merely LOOKS like a stamp (a rendered comment) is never rewritten and the authored document (`#commentRoot`) is never touched, even when it names the same version or date. Each label is preserved and a value that is not a real rendered date (`unknown`, a malformed stamp) is left alone, so a vanished badge, a reworded label or a broken stamp still moves the shot and fails; only the date VALUE is deliberately un-gated by screenshots. The freeze is idempotent, so a shot cannot depend on how often it ran. The one deliberate slack is `PIXEL_CHANNEL_TOLERANCE` 2: nothing measured needs it, it is insurance for the single input the digest pin does NOT fix (the host CPU, since Chromium rasterizes in software and Skia dispatches on CPU features), it is invisible at 2 steps out of 255, and the smallest regression it still catches is a delta-3 wash where the retired budget waved through delta 96. The rule is a pure function (`withinPixelBudget`) in Node, so only the pixel COUNT is computed in the browser, and `compareImages` reports WHAT differed - a dimension mismatch, or the differing-pixel count and ratio against the budget - so a red `--check` run or determinism assertion names the magnitude instead of only failing, and a jitter budget can be re-sized from a measurement rather than a guess. `--print-paths` reports the budget and the placeholders so the capture tool, the `--check` gate and the specs that mirror it cannot drift apart; `tests/54-tutorial-shots.spec.js` imports the same comparator rather than copying it, so it can never be stricter or laxer than the gate (it shares the comparator, not the renderer - it captures with the runner's own browser and compares two runs in the same environment). | `tests/80-shot-clip.spec.js` - `the pixel diff is exact and rejects a deliberately altered shot (CMH-BUILD-19)`, `no differing pixel is allowed, whatever the shot size (CMH-BUILD-19)`, `the budget is exact, its tolerance is invisible, and the tool reports both (CMH-BUILD-19)`, `the capture freezes the volatile build stamps, and only in the review layer (CMH-BUILD-19)`; `tests/54-tutorial-shots.spec.js` - `garden capture is deterministic across two independent runs (CMH-TUT-SHOTS-01)`; source: `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/shot_compare.mjs`, `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/shot_stamps.mjs`, `plugins/commentable-html/dev/tools/capture_tutorial.mjs` - the `--print-paths` budget report and the freeze call sites; docs: `docs/testing-guidelines.md` |

Companion filenames are version-agnostic, so a version bump does not rename dist files. `dist/manifest.json` records SHA-256 and byte size per companion and is serialized with sorted keys for a deterministic, diff-stable payload. | `tests/test_build.py` - version single sourced, manifest hashes, `test_manifest_is_deterministically_key_sorted`, single declaration tests |

Each shipped `examples/report-*.html` is a pure build artifact assembled by `build.py` from its INDEPENDENT content source in `dev/examples/src/report-*.html`: `build.py` swaps in the current CSS/COMMENT UI/JS layer and re-stamps the `<meta>` version, and `--check` compares the shipped file to a fresh assembly, so a hand-edit or a stale/clobbered committed example - of its CONTENT as well as its layer - fails the build (closing the self-sourced hole the site pages had before #91; content edits must be made in `dev/examples/src/`). `build.py --check --check-fixtures` additionally runs the Playwright fixtures' `generate.mjs --check` (skipped only when node is absent), so the required `dist-in-sync` gate also owns fixture freshness (a version bump that leaves a fixture stale fails the fast gate, not only the slow `plugin-tests` job). | `tests/10-more.spec.js` - `committed sample fixtures are not stale (generate.mjs --check)`; `tests/test_examples.py` - example exists, validates, inlines images, exercises every feature, `test_examples_embed_current_version`, `test_build_check_catches_example_drift`, `test_build_check_flags_an_orphaned_example_with_no_source`; `tests/test_build.py` - `test_check_subprocess_passes`, `test_check_fixtures_passes_and_is_reported` |

| CMH-BUILD-11 | The vendored rich-libraries blob (the inline gzip+base64 mermaid/Chart.js payload) is reproducible across zlib implementations. `build.py` does NOT recompress the libraries at build time (gzip DEFLATE output differs between stock zlib and zlib-ng, which Python 3.14 ships, so a live recompress makes the dist blob depend on the builder's machine and breaks `dist-in-sync`); it reads a committed `assets/vendor/<lib>.gz` artifact and only base64-encodes it, which is deterministic everywhere. `build.py --regen-vendor-gz` regenerates those `.gz` artifacts when a vendored library changes (the only step that gzips), and `build.py --check` fails when a committed `.gz` is missing, corrupt, or does not DECOMPRESS to the current source (decompression is deterministic across zlib impls, so the guard never recompresses). | `tests/test_vendored_gzip.py` - `VendoredGzipReproTests.test_blob_reads_committed_gz_not_recompressed`, `test_drift_guard_detects_missing_and_stale_gz`, `test_regen_roundtrips_through_decompression` |
| CMH-BUILD-26 | The layer that SHIPS carries no developer commentary. `build.py` runs the source through `tools/build_parts/05-minify.py` after the version stamp and before every consumer, so `dist/commentable-html.js`, `dist/commentable-html.css`, the asset registry, both templates and every built example embed one identical stripped copy; `assets/js/**` and `assets/css/**` stay fully commented and remain the single source of truth. Measured on #1250's corpus the commentary was roughly 44% of a 1.2 MB runtime and rode along in every generated document and every offline export. The transform is deliberately NOT a general minifier - no identifier mangling, no statement joining, no semicolon insertion - it only DELETES comments and layout whitespace, and never a byte inside a string, template literal or regex literal. Five properties make it safe to run unattended: (1) ASI is preserved exactly - wherever the source had a LINE TERMINATOR (any of LF, CR, U+2028, U+2029, not LF alone) the output has one, and a block comment that CONTAINS one collapses to a newline rather than a space, because the spec treats such a comment as a line terminator; (2) whether a `/` opens a regex is DECIDED FROM PARSE CONTEXT, never guessed, because a wrong guess silently rewrites the regex (`if (ok) /\d+ \w+/.test(s)` shipping as `/\d+\w+/`) or swallows a comment opener and deletes the rest of the file: after `]`, an identifier, a number, a string, a template literal or a trailing `.` (a numeric literal may end in one, as in `1. / 2`) an expression has ENDED so `/` divides; after `)` it opens a regex only when that paren closed an `if`/`for`/`while`/`with` HEADER; after `}` only when that brace closed a BLOCK rather than an object literal or an arrow body, where a `function`/`class` body counts as a block exactly when the keyword stood in STATEMENT position (`function f(){}` may be followed by a regex, `const f = function(){} / 2` divides); and a regex keyword only opens regex context when it is a keyword rather than a property name (`x.return / 2` divides). A regex literal is then copied through verbatim, and the separator after it is never dropped (`/re/ instanceof X` must not close up into `/re/instanceof`, where the flags would swallow the operator); (3) an inter-token space is removed only when the two characters cannot fuse - identifier pairs, an identifier before a `\uXXXX` escape, `1 .toFixed()`, `+ +`, `/ /`, `/ *`, `= "`, and the markup delimiters `< !`, `< /` and `- >` all keep their separator, so the strip can never manufacture an HTML attribute or close the `<script>` element the layer is inlined in; (4) a source that leaves a comment, string, template literal or template SUBSTITUTION unterminated is refused, so a truncated file cannot be silently shipped as whatever part of it was still valid; (5) the result is checked twice - the strip re-reads its own output and compares literals and whitespace-free code (which catches an assembly that dropped or invented a byte, but shares a scanner with what it checks and so is NOT a defence against a misread - property 2 is), and `verify_js_syntax` parses the stripped bytes with an INDEPENDENT parser (`node --check`) whenever node is present. Legal-notice comments (`/*!`, `@license`, `@preserve`) are kept, which is how the vendored lz-string MIT notice - copyright and permission text in full - keeps travelling inside every document and offline export: unlike mermaid and Chart.js, whose notices the offline exporter emits beside the inlined library, lz-string is baked into the runtime, so that comment is the only notice accompanying the redistributed copy. CSS keeps every inter-token space (descendant combinator, `calc()`) and never ADDS one: a CSS comment is removed at tokenization and leaves no whitespace token, so `.a/**/.b` is the compound selector `.a.b` - but it does TERMINATE the token before it, so where the neighbours would fuse (`bl/**/ue`, `1px/**/2px`) the comment is kept as an empty `/**/`. | `tests/test_minify.py` - `JsCommentStripTests`, `JsSeparatorSafetyTests`, `AmbiguousSlashTests`, `UnterminatedSourceTests`, `LineTerminatorTests`, `LicenseCommentTests`, `RoundTripGuardTests`, `SyntaxOracleTests`, `CssCommentStripTests`, `ShippedLayerTests`; and the whole Playwright suite, which runs against the stripped built stage |
| CMH-BUILD-27 | A per-component byte budget gates the shipped payload. `tools/size-budget.json` names a ceiling for each generated component that documents embed verbatim (the runtime, the stylesheet, the asset registry and both templates); `build.py` measures them on every build AND every `--check`, prints each one against its ceiling, and REFUSES - before it writes anything - when one is exceeded, so the required `dist-in-sync` job fails a pull request that blows a budget and no oversize artifact is left in the tree for the next `git add` to sweep up. A budgeted component the build no longer produces is also a failure, so renaming an output cannot silently retire its ceiling; so is a generated `dist/` PAYLOAD component (a script, a stylesheet or a template, as opposed to metadata such as `manifest.json`) that no ceiling covers, so the payload cannot simply move into a new unbudgeted file; and a missing or malformed budget file is a build failure rather than a silent skip. Raising a ceiling is a deliberate, reviewed edit to that file plus a changelog line: #1250 measured the runtime growing 3.5x across versions with nothing to notice it, because no single commit looked expensive. Two limits are stated in the file so a reader does not over-trust it: it is a CEILING, not a ratchet (growth under the headroom is invisible, and a shrink does not tighten it automatically, because a true ratchet would make every unrelated feature PR edit it), and it budgets the shipped LAYER, which a document embeds verbatim, not the document - the vendored diagram payload and a document's own generated DOM are workstreams A and D of #1250 and have no ceiling here. | `tests/test_minify.py` - `SizeBudgetTests` (`test_the_committed_budget_covers_the_generated_components`, `test_the_built_stage_is_inside_its_budget`, `test_an_oversize_component_fails`, `test_a_component_inside_its_budget_passes`, `test_a_budgeted_component_the_build_no_longer_produces_fails`, `test_a_missing_or_malformed_budget_is_a_build_failure`, `test_the_budget_file_documents_why_it_exists`); `tests/test_build.py` - `BuildTests.test_main_check_ok_prints_version`, `BuildTests.test_main_writes_outputs_removes_stale_and_reports_sizes` |

| CMH-VAL-05 | NonShareable validation checks local companion refs, existing files, assets registry warning, version meta, missing-asset banner, watchdog, http(s) or protocol-relative remote URL rejection, non-`file` scheme rejection, local `file://` refs, and absolute-path warning. A `?query`/`#fragment` cache-buster on a companion ref (e.g. `commentable-html.js?v=1.7.0`) is stripped before the suffix detection and the on-disk existence check, matching what the browser fetches. `validate()` accepts an optional `base_dir` to resolve companion refs against the file's final location, or `None` to check structure only when placement is deferred. When a NonShareable document is explicitly requested, `new_document.py` defaults to absolute `file://` companion refs, while `--assets-relative`, `--copy-assets`, and `--assets-href` keep their explicit modes. `--assets-relative` REFUSES (exit 2, naming `--assets-href` and `--copy-assets`) when `--out` and the skill sit on different Windows drives or mounts, because no relative path exists across them - a broken relative ref, or a bare traceback, would both be worse answers. A `file://` companion ref's HOST is read the way the URL parser reads it, not as a literal: the parser percent-decodes a file host and maps it through domain-to-ASCII before the file-host state empties the exact string `localhost`, so `file://local%68ost/x` resolves to the same LOCAL path as `file://localhost/x` instead of a bogus UNC/SMB path whose on-disk existence check then reported a companion sitting right there as missing (the cased `file://LOCALHOST/x` always did, and is pinned as a control). The ref goes through the same input cleanup the network-URL predicate uses, so a BACKSLASH host terminator (`file://localhost\x`, which the parser ends at the `\` exactly as at a `/`) is local too. A TRAILING DOT stays outside that special case, so `file://localhost./x` keeps a real authority and is egress - the same call the network-URL predicate's `_PCT_LOCALHOST`, and the terminator its shared `file_network_arm` builds around it, make, and the two are pinned to agree about the `localhost` spelling. Only the PERCENT-ENCODING and CASE half of canonicalization is modelled: an IDNA/UTS-46 spelling that only maps onto `localhost` (`file://%EF%BD%8Cocalhost/x`) is read as a real authority on both sides, the accepted over-detection the network-URL predicate already records, and that predicate's drive-letter exclusion and its `..`/empty-segment over-detection are deliberately outside the parity claim. A `file:` companion ref that names no local path is reported as a FINDING, never as an uncaught exception and never as a wrong SCHEME. Two stages can throw on such a ref and both are guarded: `urlsplit` VALIDATES a bracketed authority, so `file://[foo]/x`, `file://[127.0.0.1]/x` and the unclosed `file://[::1/x` raise `ValueError` on EVERY platform before any host test runs, and `nturl2path.url2pathname` raises `OSError('Bad URL')` on an authority or path shape it cannot map (`file://[::1]/x` on Windows) - either used to kill `validate()` with a raw traceback and hand every fail-closed caller (`retrofit.py`, `content_replace.py`, `chart_block.py`, `finalize.py`) a traceback where a finding belongs. Resolving such a ref to `None` is not the fix either: that falls through to the non-file-scheme branch and blames the scheme, the one part of the ref that is right, so the resolver returns a distinct UNRESOLVABLE outcome and the finding stays cause-neutral (the ref does not resolve to a local file path). The HOST shapes that name no path - an IPv6 literal, a host:port, and its `|` spelling, which `nturl2path` reads as the same drive delimiter as `:` - are settled by the resolver ITSELF rather than by the platform's `url2pathname`, which raises on Windows, hands the string back unchanged on POSIX, and mangles a host:port into the bogus drive path `T:8080\x`; for those the verdict is identical on both platforms. An authority carried a slash deeper (`file:////host:8080/x`, which parses to a PATH under an empty authority) is screened the same way, since the resolver maps it the same way. A Windows DRIVE-LETTER prefix is exempt, so `file://C:/x`, `file://C|/x` and the separatorless `file://c:evil.example/x` the network-URL predicate also calls local still resolve and the guard widens nothing, but only the PREFIX is exempt: `file://c:evil:80/x` names no path, and an ENCODED colon (`file://C%3A/x`) is not a drive letter to the parser at all. | CMH-VAL-08 | The validator enforces the self-contained guarantee on the finished document: an `<img>`/`<script>`/`<iframe>` that loads over the network is an error (Chart.js CDN is an exempt opt-in in shareable mode), a fetching external `<link>` is a warning in shareable mode, non-fetching remote links such as canonical and alternate metadata are ignored, and a local-path `<img>` warns to inline it. WHICH scripts are read that way through `src` is decided by the script TYPE (issue #1144), because HTML decides it that way: "prepare the script element" classifies a `<script>` whose type is neither a JavaScript MIME type nor `module` nor `importmap` nor `speculationrules` as a DATA BLOCK and RETURNS before the fetch step, and for the two remaining KEYWORD types the `src` step fires an `error` event and returns, since external import maps and external speculation rule sets are not supported (a ruleset arrives inline or through the `Speculation-Rules` response header, never through `src`). It is the same KIND of reasoning `check_charts` and the offline active-data rules already apply - decide by TYPE - though `check_charts` reaches it through `script_external_load` / `script_code_runs`, the spec-exact predicate this row deliberately does not use, so on a residual spelling the two checks can disagree about the same element (this rule calls it a loader; `check_charts` does not, and may report that a canvas has no renderer). The predicate is `script_src_fetches`, and the RESIDUAL the earlier reading left is now closed (issue #1171). It used to be the type-only, deliberately over-inclusive `_is_executable_js`, chosen because THAT was the predicate PINNED to the exporter's `_offlineIsRunnableScriptType`, so the gate and the offline strip kept calling the same scripts loaders. The price was every shape whose type ESSENCE names JavaScript while a browser requests nothing: a MIME PARAMETER (`text/javascript; charset=utf-8`), `nomodule` on a classic script, a whitespace-only `type=" "`, and a non-JavaScript `language` fallback. Each was reported here as a network load AND had its whole element - body and all - deleted by the offline strip (CMH-OFFLINE-04 carried that cost on its side): a document refused over a request no browser makes, and an author's content removed behind the same verdict, which is the false-positive direction a gate that withholds the validated stamp cannot afford. The fix keeps the PAIRING rather than trading it away, because both sides moved in ONE change: the exporter grew `_offlineScriptSrcIsFetched`, a JS mirror of `script_src_fetches`, and `test_the_python_and_js_script_src_fetches_predicates_agree` pins the two over a shared corpus of ATTRIBUTE SETS - every namespace, the whitespace class, and every one of the shapes - evaluated in a real JS engine, comparing what the two shipping CALLERS compute rather than the predicates under matching assumptions. The question this arm asks is FETCH, not EXECUTION, and the difference is MEASURED rather than reasoned - which is the correction that separates this rule from a first attempt that read it through `script_code_runs` (CMH-VAL-27). Chromium issues the `src` request from its speculative PRELOAD SCANNER, which reads the tag soup ahead of the parser, so it differs from execution in two ways that a spec reading alone gets wrong. First, the legacy `event`+`for` pair does NOT stop the request: `<script type="text/javascript" for="x" event="y" src=...>` is REQUESTED and then never run, so skipping it here would have blessed a document that really does reach the network - the one direction a self-contained gate must never get wrong - and would have left a live reference in a zero-network export. Second, it is namespace-BLIND in BOTH directions: an SVG `<script src>` is requested even though SVG ignores `src` for loading, while an SVG `<script nomodule src>` is NOT requested even though `nomodule` is an HTMLScriptElement rule that an SVG script ignores for EXECUTION (an SVG `<script nomodule>` with an inline body does run). That blindness is why `script_src_fetches` takes no `ns` at all - there is no namespace to consult, by construction rather than by omission - and it is what lets this flat, namespace-less tokenizer answer the question exactly. The browser fact is not left as a claim: the `CMH-VAL-08: a browser requests exactly the script shapes the gate calls a load` spec drives every shape through a real engine, records which ones it actually requests, and compares that set to the shipped predicate's own verdicts, so an engine that ever changed its mind reds a test rather than silently invalidating this row. The namespace-blindness is MEASURED across the rules rather than extrapolated from one: the corpus carries the `language` fallback, the essence match and the whitespace-only `type` in the SVG and MathML namespaces too, so no rule is asserted for HTML and merely assumed elsewhere. `_is_executable_js` stays where over-inclusion is genuinely the safe direction, and that is recorded per caller rather than left implied: the offline inline-body EGRESS scan on both sides (a body it skips is a network import nobody looked at), and `_csp_predecessor_fetches`, whose question is "could anything before this policy fetch or execute" - over-inclusion there over-reports rather than blesses, and its input is a flat tag/attribute pair with no namespace. Only `src` is decided by type: the SVG `href` / `xlink:href` arm stays unconditional, since this tokenizer has no namespace to consult and an SVG `<script>` has no type-keyed data-block concept to read instead. The exporter moved with the gate rather than after it (CMH-OFFLINE-04): `_offlineStripScriptLoad` removes a FETCHING script outright as before, takes only the dead ATTRIBUTE off a data block instead of deleting the author's data with it, and leaves an ACTIVE-DATA block's `src` untouched for the active-data pass that judges the block by it, so the export keeps no network-looking reference and never turns a map the source browser IGNORED into a live one. CMH-VAL-25 inherits the verdict element for element, so the nested spelling of an inert data block is clean too. For descriptor mode `offline`, every network-loading script, fetching link, image, iframe, media source, form target, meta refresh (whatever its target), CSS `@import`, and CSS `url(...)` is an error with no Chart.js exemption, the restrictive offline CSP is required, and data URLs remain valid. SHAREABLE mode covers the same AUTOMATIC SUBRESOURCE set as offline, and the SCOPE of that guarantee is a recorded decision rather than an accident of where a check happened to sit (issue #1145). The rule the scope is drawn on: the guarantee covers every network reach a browser makes when a reader merely OPENS the file, with no user action. Only a network target, unlike offline: a relative refresh reaches no network, and shareable mode has no export strip to keep unconditional parity with, so offline keeps its own stricter "every refresh, whatever its target" rule and the two never double-report one element. Two things about an offline report DO change, and neither is a wording change: the moved findings now precede the offline-only ones instead of being interleaved with them (nothing consumes the order), and the universal `background` read ADDS offline findings for the table parts the old tag list missed, which is the point of making it universal and is asserted by that same test. The widening is a BREAKING change for authored documents, stated as such in the changelog: a file that passed before may now fail `--strict`, be refused the stamp, and be refused outright by the fail-closed tools that run the validator first (`retrofit` / `upgrade` leave the target unchanged on any validator error). That offline scope is decided by the DECLARED descriptor mode ALONE, never by the NonShareable classification (#988). It used to read `not nonshareable and mode == "offline"`, which keyed the GATE to a lineage the exporter's offline STRIPS never consult: `saveOffline` reaches `_buildOfflineHtml` from the NonShareable path too (`_buildStandaloneHtml` inlines the companion CSS/JS and removes the NONSHAREABLE BOOTSTRAP block first, and the descriptor is then stamped `offline`), so a document that DECLARES offline while still carrying a companion reference - which a mangled or missing CSS/JS region marker leaves behind, and a hand-authored file can carry outright - switched OFF every rule in this paragraph at once: the zero-network CSP requirement, the media/form/background egress checks, the inline-script navigation and import scans, the active-data (importmap/speculationrules) rules, and the event-handler and meta-refresh gates. That is fail-OPEN in SCOPE, though not in verdict: such a document was never certified clean, because `_check_layer_descriptor` rejects the NonShareable-plus-offline pair on its own and did so before this change. What was lost was the REPORT and the second layer - a live `on*` handler and a missing offline CSP were not named at all, and the egress that WAS named carried the shareable wording, so the list an author worked from was incomplete and the rest of it appeared only once the descriptor line had been corrected - and the scope of a fail-closed gate should not depend on a different check happening to be right. That principle is applied where the widening is free, not absolutely: a descriptor that is MISSING, unparseable, not an object, or carries a mode outside the allowed set still leaves the offline rules off and is caught by the descriptor rule alone, deliberately, because defaulting those to offline would add wrong `offline mode:` errors to an ordinary shareable document whose descriptor merely failed to parse - a worse report, for no verdict, since none of those documents validates clean either way. The two sides are made to agree the way CMH-OFFLINE-05 settled the meta-refresh direction - the GATE widens to match the strips, rather than the exporter refusing an offline export on the NonShareable path, which would remove the only way a companion-file document becomes a single offline file. The check no longer even RECEIVES the classification (`_check_self_contained(html, parser)`), so it cannot regress to consulting it. The widening rejects nothing legitimately: the descriptor error and the offline errors are now reported together, and a document that declares `nonshareable` keeps its own rules unchanged - its companion `<link>`/`<script src>` stay ordinary local references, and the shipped bootstrap's `onclick` dismiss button (`dist/NONSHAREABLE.html`, `tests/fixtures/nonshareable/kitchen-sink.html`) stays clean, since no offline export ever keeps it. `<a href>` navigation is exempt. The META REFRESH gate decides its target by APPLYING the HTML shared declarative refresh steps (`meta_refresh_target`), not by matching `url=` in the raw attribute text, because a text scan was wrong in BOTH directions. The keyword and its `=` are OPTIONAL - after the time and its `;`, `,` or whitespace separator, anything that is not `url` is taken as the URL itself, so `content="0;https://evil.example"` navigates while a `url=`-anchored pattern saw nothing at all, a bypass CHEAPER than the scheme-only spelling this row was widened for; each letter of `url` is consumed before the next is tested, exactly as the algorithm advances, so a near-miss (`0;urhttps://host`) resumes where the match gave up. In the other direction a value with NO time is not a refresh at all (`url=https://evil`), a QUOTED value is TRUNCATED at its closing quote (`url='./x;url=https://evil'` is an ordinary local path), only ASCII whitespace is skipped (`url<NBSP>=...` makes the whole tail a relative reference), and a later `url=` inside a relative target's query string is just text - all four used to be reported as network egress. The extracted target is then handed to the SHARED `is_network_url` - the same predicate, after the same `normalize_url_value` cleanup, that every other egress gate in this row reads - rather than to a pattern of the refresh rule's own. That cleanup is the URL parser's (ASCII tab and newline removed anywhere, leading AND trailing C0-or-space removed, every backslash mapped onto a slash), so the prefixes a browser resolves to a network host all count: scheme plus slashes, protocol-relative, SCHEME-ONLY (a `https:`/`http:` with NO slashes after the colon, which the special-authority states resolve to the same host), a BACKSLASH authority (`\\host`, `/\host`, which a special scheme's relative-slash state treats like `//host`, resolving to a `file://host` UNC fetch off the machine), and the EXPLICIT `file://host` spelling of that same fetch. SHARING the predicate is the rule here rather than an implementation detail, because the bespoke copy drifted in BOTH directions the moment the shared one moved on without it (issue #979): it read exactly two leading separators, so the four-or-more-separator `file:////host` the attribute gate counts (a REAL AUTHORITY to Chromium, and the separator arithmetic is empirical because Chromium DEVIATES from the spec here: measured in Chromium 149 that URL parses to host `host` and re-serializes as `file://host/...`, where a spec-conformant parser takes the WHATWG file-host state's EMPTY host and leaves `//host/...` as the path - which is why the count is NOT `two or more`; the two counted arms are the BASE-INDEPENDENT set, since a zero- or one-separator spelling reaches a host only when parsed ABSOLUTE and inherits the base's host (so is local) against the `file:` base a document actually has - issue #1229 SETTLED that, see the paragraph below) was reported as local, and so was every slash run of three or more, which the shared `/{2,}` arm counts deliberately: what `///host` resolves to depends on the BASE - from a document SERVED over http/https (the marketplace site publishes these reports that way) the special-authority states ignore the run and it is that host, while from a `file:` base the file-host state takes an EMPTY host and it is a local path - so counting it is the fail-CLOSED reading, which here costs only wording. In the other direction a Windows DRIVE LETTER - which the file-host state turns into a path, so it reaches no host at all - was named a beacon that does not exist. The exclusions are therefore the shared ones: `localhost`, a drive letter (`file://C:/x`, `file://c|/x`), an empty authority (three separators after `file:`, and `url=https:` / `url=https://`, which are parse failures a browser does not navigate on, so reporting one would make the gate reject a file with no egress at all), and a single leading slash or backslash, which is a path. Issue #1229 asked whether any surface makes that inherited host reachable, and the answer is recorded here rather than left tracked: it does not, and the reason the LEADING run of a zero- or one-separator `file:` value cannot open an authority is structural. `file:` IS a special scheme - its backslashes are mapped exactly as any other special scheme's, so `file:\\evil.example/x` really is counted - but it does not take the special-authority-(ignore-)slashes states that collapse the slash-less `https:host/x` onto a host in the arm right beside it. The scheme state routes `file:` to the FILE state, which resolves against the document's BASE and reads the leading run as PATH, and EVERY surface that consumes this predicate resolves against that base: an attribute, a refresh target, and an `iframe srcdoc`, which inherits its parent's. A CSS `url()` is deliberately NOT in that list - the CSS readers are assembled from `CSS_NETWORK_PREFIX`, which carries no `file:` arm at all, so they never reach this question (issue #1230 tracks that separate gap). The refresh case was CAPTURED rather than reasoned about - a real Chromium navigating out of a `file:///C:/dir/report.html` document went to `file:///C:/dir/evil.example/x`, the ordinary local sibling an author means by `file:notes.html`, never the SMB share - and from a UNC base the value takes that document's OWN host, which it cannot choose, exactly as the plain relative `evil.example/x` beside it does. Two neighbouring contexts were measured rather than assumed, so the answer does not rest on the one case. A `<base href>` onto a non-`file:` base DOES rebase them onto a host the value names, and that is closed one layer up and unconditionally - a `<base href>` is held to the stricter `offline_is_non_local_ref` in EVERY mode and the offline strip removes it (the gap issue #924 closed; the still-open wording left beside the offline refresh rule was stale and is corrected). A document whose AMBIENT base is not a `file:` one - a report SERVED over http/https - does resolve them to a host the value names, and that case rests on the ENGINE rather than on this arm: a `file:` load from an http(s) document is refused outright (`Not allowed to load local resource`), measured for the already-counted two-separator spelling equally, so counting the short runs would buy nothing there while costing the false positive of calling an authored `file:notes.html` a beacon - the class the `localhost` and drive-letter exclusions exist to prevent, and the one a gate that withholds the `commentable-html-validated` stamp cannot afford. Both are Chromium measurements, like the closed scheme set, and nothing is claimed for other engines. The four-or-more reading is itself a WINDOWS one and the arm is deliberately fail-CLOSED about it: the same engine build parses `file:////evil.example/x` to host `evil.example` on Windows but to an EMPTY-host local path on Linux (measured in the pinned CI container), and the gate counts it on both, because Windows is where the UNC fetch exists. The exemption is scoped to the LEADING run and no further: a zero- or one-separator value whose PATH canonicalizes onto the four-separator form is still counted by the `..` and empty-path-segment arms (`file:/..//x.js`, `file:a//b.png` are corpus rows), which remain the deliberate base-less over-detection recorded above. The measurement is re-run on every CI pass rather than left as a claim in this row, comparing a real engine to this predicate's own verdicts, so an engine that ever changed its mind reds a test instead of silently invalidating it. A non-empty HOST is required, and that host test is a one-character approximation of the URL parser's, so a MALFORMED authority (`https://:80`) is still reported, the fail-CLOSED direction and the right one for a gate whose miss is a beacon. The RESIDUAL is now the shared predicate's own rather than this rule's - what `NETWORK_URL_RE` misses (a percent- or entity-encoded separator, a scheme assembled only at runtime) this misses identically - and it is bounded by the rejection above: since the exporter removes every refresh unconditionally and the validator rejects every one, a miss here costs only the WORDING of a rejection that still happens, never the rejection itself. This is the widening CMH-OFFLINE-05 gave the scripted-navigation literal, for the same reason: a meta refresh is a TOP-LEVEL NAVIGATION, the one channel no meta-delivered policy can close (`navigate-to` was dropped from CSP Level 3 and `sandbox` is ignored in a meta-delivered policy), so while the pattern required `url=` and the slashes, the whole channel was open to a one-token spelling change and `--strict` certified such a file as offline-clean. None of it introduces gate/strip drift, and the two now agree in BOTH directions rather than the gate merely staying looser: offline mode rejects EVERY `meta[http-equiv=refresh]`, exactly as the export removes every one whatever its URL (CMH-OFFLINE-05 records why that direction was chosen over the exporter keeping a relative one), and this target parser decides only WHICH message the rejection carries. A `javascript:` or `data:` target is therefore still not reported as network egress - mainstream engines refuse both as refresh targets - but the meta itself is rejected like any other. The NEIGHBOURING CSS network-literal gates - `CSS_NETWORK_URL_RE` and `CSS_NETWORK_IMPORT_RE`, the `@import` scan - now read the same widened shape (#961), and so does `NETWORK_URL_RE`, the ATTRIBUTE predicate the `_link_loads` path and every media/form/background check feed, whose parser-faithful input cleanup and `file:` authority arm landed earlier with #923. All three CONSUME the run of slashes after a special scheme rather than requiring two, because the special-authority states ignore that run, so `url(https:host/x.png)`, `@import "https:host/t.css"` and `src="https:host/x.js"` are caught as the network loads a browser resolves them to; and all three require a non-empty HOST, so an authority terminated at once - `url(https://)`, `url(//)`, a bare `https:` - stays local rather than being reported as a beacon it cannot be (which also closed a small pre-existing drift, where the CSS gate reported `url(//)` and the strip left it alone). Those are FETCH channels the required offline CSP closes IN OFFLINE MODE (`default-src 'none'`, `img-src data:`, `font-src data:`, and a `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` carrying no host source), unlike a top-level navigation - and that qualifier is load-bearing rather than pedantic: SHAREABLE mode requires no CSP at all, so there the literal gate is the ONLY layer and any narrowness in it is reachable, not merely theoretical. Issue #1230 measured that: the CSS readers carried no `file:` authority arm while the ATTRIBUTE predicate beside them had one (#923), so a shareable document with `url(file://evil.example/beacon.png)` passed `--strict`, earned the `commentable-html-validated` stamp, and made an SMB request off a Windows reader's machine on open. Both sides now read ONE shared arm (`file_network_arm` in `tools/validate/checks/resources.py`, mirrored as `_offFileNetworkArm` in the exporter and pinned to it as TEXT for every `stop` its callers use), so the separator arithmetic, the `localhost` and Windows drive-letter exclusions, the non-empty-authority rule and the two canonicalization arms cannot answer differently in a stylesheet than in an attribute; `CSS_NETWORK_START` is what the `url(...)`, `@import`, `image-set()`, anchored-candidate and deck readers are all assembled from, so no reader can be widened - or left behind - alone. Which characters END a CSS value is part of that arm, and the memberships are load-bearing: ASCII tab does NOT end one, because it is among the three characters the URL parser removes from anywhere, and counting it fired the `localhost` exclusion on `url("file://localhost<TAB>evil.example/x")`, whose host a browser reads as `localhostevil.example`; a raw LF or CR DOES, for a CSS reason rather than a URL one (it makes a bad-string token whose declaration a browser drops); and an OPEN paren does not, because a quoted string may legally contain one. What a PATH may CONTAIN is a DIFFERENT set from what ends a value, and conflating them was a measured bypass: the two canonicalization scans read the path, so scanning to a terminator truncated the scan and hid the popping segment behind it - `url("file:///a(/..//evil.example/x.png")` canonicalizes onto the four-separator UNC form and Chromium 151 requested `file://evil.example/x.png` for it while every CSS reader called it local. The scans read `_PATH_CHAR` and are bounded by `_PATH_SCAN_MAX` instead, which is what keeps them LINEAR: unbounded they are quadratic, and since these readers run unanchored over authored content while the exporter runs its mirror to convergence in the reader's browser, a sheet of repeated `url(file:a` (17.2s at 156 KB, 69.3s at 312 KB) was a hung tab. The cap's residual is bounded and recorded - a canonicalization-only spelling whose path runs past it before the popping segment is not scanned - and costs nothing on the channel this exists for, since the two AUTHORITY arms are exact and uncapped. Each is mirrored in the exporter's own JavaScript (`_OFFLINE_NETWORK_URL_RE` and the two CSS strips in `assets/js/68-export-offline.js`), so the widening had to land on BOTH sides in one change - widening the Python copy alone would make the gate REJECT a file the exporter had just produced, the CMH-OFFLINE-04 drift failure mode, where gate and strip have to move together. The CSS pair is pinned to the exporter's strips by a parity test that evaluates the runtime's own `_offlineCssNoNetwork` in node over a shared corpus, the same way the attribute predicate is - and the corpus carries the `file:` spellings in both directions, including the LOCAL controls (`url(file:///C:/x.png)`, `url(file://localhost/x.png)`, `url(file://C:/x.png)`, `url(file://localhost)`) and the tab- and space-padded ones, because a widening that deletes an author's local reference is the failure mode this gate can least afford. That CSP reason is only as strong as the CSP check itself, so the check now ENFORCES the premise rather than leaving a reader to take it on trust (#968); two halves of it used to be missing. (a) EXCLUSIVITY was enforced only for the directives whose required token is `'none'`. For `script-src`/`style-src`/`img-src`/`font-src` the check merely asked whether the required token was PRESENT, so `script-src 'unsafe-inline' https://evil.example; img-src data: https://evil.example` passed - and combined with the slashes-required shape above, a document carrying `<script src="https:evil.example/payload.js">` was certified offline-clean while a real browser fetched and EXECUTED it. The rule is now stated PER DIRECTIVE rather than left implicit: a `'none'` directive must be EXACTLY `'none'`, and each of the four fetch directives must contain its required token AND carry nothing outside a per-directive ALLOWLIST of source expressions that cannot fetch (`OFFLINE_CSP_ALLOWED`: `'unsafe-inline'`, `'unsafe-eval'`, `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, `'unsafe-hashes'`, `'report-sample'`, `data:`, `blob:`). An allowlist rather than an exact match on the string the exporter emits, so a legitimate hand-authored policy is not rejected for no reason - and four shapes that LOOK inert are deliberately kept OUT of it, each for a stated reason: `'self'` (a `file://` document has an opaque origin, so what it matches is unspecified and has historically meant the containing directory - a fetch off the file), a HASH source (CSP3 matches a hash against an EXTERNAL script carrying `integrity`, so a hash in `script-src` is a network source), `'strict-dynamic'` (grants whatever an already-trusted script loads) and a NONCE (only meaningful for markup the author controls, and it propagates trust through `'strict-dynamic'`). Directive names and source expressions are both ASCII case-insensitive, so both are folded with `_ascii_lower` rather than `str.lower()` - a Unicode fold could map a non-ASCII look-alike onto a real token, and here that direction is fail-OPEN. A REPEATED directive is read the way a browser reads it, FIRST copy wins and every later one ignored, where the dict this was built from kept the LAST: a permissive first copy could be masked by a strict repeat written after it, and the browser enforces the permissive one. (b) PLACEMENT: the policy was read off the shared tag index, which records EVERY start tag, so a meta parked in an inert `<template>` - or written after the head is over, where the HTML pragma directives are not processed at all - satisfied the requirement while enforcing nothing (a `<noscript>` body was already excluded, since a scripting-enabled browser never creates the element inside it). The check now reads `_DocParser.csp_metas`, which records only a meta a browser really applies. Enforcement across several policies is CONJUNCTIVE - a resource must be allowed by every one - so ANY applied policy that meets the contract clears the check, and a failure reports the FIRST policy's shortfalls, the one an author wrote to be the document's policy. No gate/strip drift is introduced: the exporter emits exactly the required tokens and inserts them as `head.firstChild` (CMH-OFFLINE-05), so the policy it produces passes unchanged. Three more ways a policy could be read as enforcing something it does not are closed with it, each found by asking what a BROWSER does rather than what the string looks like. (c) The required set is not the whole policy, and an EXTRA directive may only TIGHTEN. CSP's more specific fetch directives OVERRIDE the ones this contract pins whenever they are present - `script-src-elem` decides a `<script src>` load rather than `script-src`, `style-src-elem` decides a stylesheet - and `worker-src`/`child-src`/`media-src`/`manifest-src`/`prefetch-src` are safe here only while they are ABSENT and fall back to `default-src 'none'`, so `script-src-elem https://evil.example` beside a compliant `script-src` re-opened the hole verbatim (and `worker-src` opens it with no attribute spelling at all, through `new Worker(...)` from the inline script the policy deliberately allows). The NAME set is therefore CLOSED rather than a list of dangerous names to enumerate, which is the only shape that stays fail-closed against the next directive CSP adds: a directive outside `OFFLINE_CSP_REQUIRED` is an error unless its source list is exactly `'none'` or empty, neither of which can widen anything. The directives that carry no SOURCE LIST at all are named in `OFFLINE_CSP_NON_FETCH` instead (`upgrade-insecure-requests`, `block-all-mixed-content`, `require-trusted-types-for`, `trusted-types`, `sandbox`), because running a sink group, a policy name or a sandbox flag through a source-list test asks a question their grammar does not have, and rejecting them would turn away a hand-authored file that layers on Trusted Types hardening. `report-uri`/`report-to` are deliberately NOT in that set, and the reason is stated exactly rather than overclaimed: a meta-delivered policy IGNORES them, so they enforce nothing and a document promising zero network has no use for a reporting endpoint - rejecting them keeps the emitted policy and the accepted one the same shape, and that same inertness (every effect a second policy could add is either conjunctive or ignored in a `<meta>`) is what makes the multi-policy short-circuit sound. It is also why `'report-sample'` is safe in the allowlist above: with no endpoint, a sample has nowhere to go. A required directive with an EMPTY source list is accepted for the same "matches nothing" reason `'none'` is, since reporting it as missing its token would reject a browser-equivalent policy. (d) The policy is TOKENIZED the way CSP tokenizes it, on ASCII whitespace only. Python's `str.split()` is Unicode-aware, so a NON-ASCII space - a NBSP - separated a directive name from its value here while a browser read the whole run as ONE unrecognized directive name and enforced nothing at all: one character per directive neutralized the entire policy while the gate reported it complete. Tokenizing the browser's way leaves the mangled name unmatched, so the required directive is simply MISSING and the document is rejected. (e) A policy meta that arrives LATE is reported rather than read. A meta-delivered policy is NOT retroactive - it governs only what the parser reaches after it - so a `<script>` that runs, a `<style>` that can `@import`, a FETCHING `<link>` or a `<noscript>` fallback written ABOVE it loads with no policy in force, which is exactly the channel the slashless spellings ride. Lateness is decided by CAPABILITY, not by tag name: the six predecessors that can do neither whatever their attributes are inert (`html`, `head`, `meta`, `title`, `base`, `template`), and a `<link>` is judged by whether its `rel` FETCHES and a `<script>` by whether it carries a load attribute or a type a browser RUNS - because a `rel=canonical` link loads nothing and a `type=application/json` block neither runs nor loads, so rejecting a policy written after one would be a false rejection carrying a message that claims something the element cannot do. (`meta` is inert here only because the one meta that DOES reach the network, a `http-equiv=refresh`, has its own offline gate rejecting every one of them; that gate is the single point of failure for this entry.) Three head-boundary details fall out of the same "what does a browser do" question and are settled in DIFFERENT directions, which is why this view is its own flag rather than the favicon check's `_head_ended`: non-whitespace CHARACTER DATA in the head pops the head and opens the body, so a meta written after it is a body child and its pragma never runs (and only ASCII whitespace counts, since a browser ends the head on a NBSP - `str.strip()` would have kept it open for exactly the character that closes it); an end tag named `body`, `html` or `br` is "anything else" in both the "in head" and "after head" modes and ends it the same way, while every OTHER end tag in those modes is IGNORED and must not (a `</div>` before the policy leaves it a head child); and `</head>` does NOT end it either, because the "after head" mode re-pushes the head element for a `base`/`link`/`meta`/`script`/`style`/`title`/`template` start tag, so a meta written there really is a head child and dropping it would report a document that HAS a policy as having none. The three obsolete elements the "in head" mode also holds (`basefont`, `bgsound`, `noframes`) are added to this view's head set rather than to `_HEAD_TAGS`, which deliberately mirrors `tools/authoring/_favicon.py`. What the OFFLINE CSS gate and the export strip gates still do not read is the CSS TOKENIZER's output: a CSS ESCAPE (`url(https\3a evil/x)`), a comment between the at-keyword and its URL, an embedded tab inside a quoted value, or a network reference carried by a bare string rather than a `url()`. (The BARE-STRING `image-set(...)` spelling is read by the SHAREABLE gate only - see residual (a) - which is why this pair is scoped to the offline side, where the strip is the thing it must stay in step with.) The exporter's strips do not read any of those either, so the two agree and the miss is shared rather than a drift; issue #1029 tracks giving both sides a CSS-token-aware reader. The one place they are NOT a fixed point is a reference written inside a CSS COMMENT: the gate reports it (raw text) and the strip deliberately leaves it, because consuming a `/*` would delete a comment's opener, leave its `*/`, and turn commented-out CSS into LIVE CSS - a fetch created by the strip itself, verified in a real Chromium. That is the same #1029 residual seen from the other side, and it is a loud `--strict` rejection rather than a silent beacon. Several shapes that WERE drift are closed here, because the gate reported them while the strip left them behind: an `@import` whose URL is followed by a media query, a `layer()`/`supports()` clause or nothing at all (the strip now consumes the at-rule's prelude to its `;`, block boundary or end of sheet, as a CSS parser does, stopping at the next `@` so a LOCAL `@import` after a network one survives), a QUOTED value carrying a `)` or the other quote character (the strip now reads a quoted string as a string), an unterminated `url(` token or an `@import` string that is never closed (both are consumed the way a browser consumes a bad-url token; the `url(` shape was verified FETCHING in a real Chromium), and `@import"https://host/x.css"` with NO whitespace after the at-keyword (a `"` cannot continue an ident, so that is a valid at-rule a browser fetches). The strip also runs to CONVERGENCE and replaces a removed at-rule with a space, since a deletion can otherwise splice two inert fragments into a live `@import`. Both sides also spell their whitespace out as the ASCII set rather than `\s`, since a JS `\s` takes U+00A0 and U+FEFF where Python's does not and neither is CSS whitespace, and both skip the padding the URL parser strips from inside a quoted value. The pair set this rule enforces is now PINNED to the other two implementations of the same contract rather than kept in step by hand (issue #1179, CMH-BUILD-22): `tests/test_egress_list_parity.py` reads `_MEDIA_LOAD_ATTRS` plus the core groups above out of this module, the deck gate's `_EGRESS_ATTRS` / `_EGRESS_ANY_ATTRS` out of `deck/deck_validate.py`, and the offline exporter's strip passes out of `assets/js/68-export-offline.js`, and fails when a widening lands on one side only - every intentional difference (the deck's outright ban on `iframe`/`object`/`embed` and on any external `<script>`, its untyped `<input src>` read, and the exporter's `feImage` selector spelling) is named in that test as data with a reason rather than silently excluded. It is the mechanical version of what a human or a review panel caught one spelling at a time in #992, #961 and #1165, and the first two divergences it found were real. The deck gate had no `feimage` rule at all, so a deck could still fetch through the SVG filter primitive this gate has reported since #992. And the deck treated the legacy `lowsrc` as a fetch on ANY element while this gate and the exporter carried no rule for it: that one was settled by MEASUREMENT rather than by a second unmeasured claim - in Chromium, with the `lowsrc` image FIRST in the document, a plain `src` and a legacy `background` are both requested and the `lowsrc` is not requested at all - so the deck's rule was retired to match this gate, and reviving it means moving all three lists together. The same reading reaches an SVG PRESENTATION ATTRIBUTE, whose value is a CSS declaration value rather than a URL (issue #1186): `<rect clip-path="url(https://host/x.svg#c)">` is neither a (tag, attribute) pair the element rules read nor part of a stylesheet the `style=` / `<style>` reads inspect, so a document carrying one validated STRICT-CLEAN, was given the `commentable-html-validated` stamp, and fetched the moment a recipient opened it - and in shareable mode there is no CSP behind the gate, so this reading is the only layer. The attributes are asked as the universal ATTRIBUTE question (`_find_attr_egress`) for the same reason `background` is, and judged by the shared `CSS_NETWORK_URL_RE` in BOTH modes, with the shareable-only `image-set(...)` reading beside it. That second reading is deliberately NARROWER than the `url()` one - `SVG_IMAGE_SET_PRESENTATION_ATTRS`, today `mask` and `cursor` - because only an attribute that takes an IMAGE fetches a bare remote string with no `url()` wrapper: `fill`, `stroke`, `clip-path`, `filter` and the markers take a paint server, a shape reference or a filter and request nothing (measured), so reading a candidate on them would REFUSE a document with no egress at all. The narrower list is held to the measurement in BOTH directions - every attribute the `url()` list enforces is answered by the image-set measurement as a fetch or as inert - because the first cut of it said "only `mask`" and left `cursor`, an image-taking attribute added in the same round, blessed and fetching (round-2 review panel, 4 of 8 ducks). Its shareable-only scope is the same split this row already records for `style=`, and the claim under it - that offline the zero-network CSP, not the strip, is what stops the fetch - is now PROVEN live rather than asserted. WHICH attributes are in scope is decided by MEASUREMENT rather than by the list of properties the specs say accept a `<url>`: in Chromium 149, with every request routed and aborted, the negative probes first in the document and the page settled to network-idle, `clip-path`, `mask`, `fill`, `stroke`, `marker-start`, `marker-mid`, `marker-end` and `cursor` are REQUESTED while `filter`, `mask-image`, `mask-border-source`, the `marker` shorthand and `color-profile` are not. The probe SHAPE decides the answer, so each attribute is probed the way the property is really used rather than all of them in one shape: `cursor` needs a fallback keyword (`url(...), auto`) to be a valid declaration at all, and measured INERT while it was probed without one, when a valid one really is fetched (round-1 review panel). `filter` is carried anyway - Chromium REMOVED external filter references, so its negative is an engine decision rather than a structural one, and a rule that fires only on a NETWORK reference costs an author with a local `url(#f)` nothing - while the other measured negatives are carried by nobody, on the `lowsrc` precedent (CMH-DECK-04). A LOCAL `url(#clip)`, which is how these attributes are almost always written, is untouched. The reading is the SHARED pattern, so it inherits that pattern's declared literal residual unchanged (a CSS-escaped scheme or function name, a reference written inside a comment): a presentation attribute is neither better nor worse covered than a `style=` attribute, and closing that residual is one change across all three CSS surfaces at once, not a per-attribute one. Scope is the ATTRIBUTE, not the property: an SMIL animation element that supplies the same property's value indirectly (`<set attributeName="mask" to="url(https://host/x.svg#m)">`, and the `to` / `from` / `by` / `values` of `<animate>`) is measured to fetch and is NOT read here - a different surface with its own `attributeName` indirection, tracked as its own issue rather than folded in, so
