| CMH-HL-07 | `markdown` (aliases `md`, `mdown`, `mkd`) is a supported highlighting language. Markdown carries no keywords, so `highlight_code.py` dispatches it to a dedicated line-oriented tokenizer that reuses the six shipped `cmh-code-*` classes: ATX headings, setext underlines (`=`, and a `--`-or-longer run under paragraph text) and bold and a fence info string are `kw`; emphasis, strikethrough and HTML comments are `com`; inline code spans (1 to 3 backticks), a fenced-code body whose info string names no known language, autolinks and link/reference destinations are `str`; link and image text, reference labels and footnote references are `fn`; ordered-list marker digits are `num`; and structural punctuation (fence delimiters, blockquote `>`, list bullets, task checkboxes, thematic breaks, table pipes and delimiter rows, link brackets, inline HTML tags) is `op`. A fenced body is tokenized in the language its INFO STRING names - the first word, aliases resolved, so ` ```py ` and ` ```python title="x.py" ` both select Python - and falls back to one opaque `str` run when the label is unknown (`kusto`, `text`) or absent. The body is buffered and tokenized as ONE unit when the fence closes, so a multi-line construct inside it (a C-style block comment, a Python triple-quoted string) reads exactly as it would in a standalone block of that language; the nested body therefore inherits that language's accepted author-time-versus-runtime tokenizer differences (operator-run grouping, the runtime's smaller keyword set) and nesting adds no new divergence. Markdown is the one language that can nest into itself, so a ` ```markdown ` body recurses through a DEPTH BOUND (`_MD_MAX_NESTING`) and past it stays opaque - a hostile document of thousands of ` ```markdown ` openers cannot exhaust the stack. An HTML comment carries across lines like a fence; an intraword underscore (`some_long_name`) never starts emphasis, a backslash-escaped marker stays literal, and an unterminated or space-padded marker (`**bold **`, CommonMark right-flanking) is left plain. Every scan that can fail is length-capped, so adversarial input (a line of 30k `[` or `<`) cannot blow up quadratically in the browser. Deliberate simplifications, both of which need full block parsing to do properly: a 4-space indented code block and YAML front matter are tokenized as prose. Like every other language the rendered text is the source character for character and every character is escaped exactly once. | `tests/test_highlight_markdown.py` - full unit suite (`MarkdownLanguageRegistrationTests`, `MarkdownBlockTokenTests`, `MarkdownInlineTokenTests`, `MarkdownFalsePositiveTests`, `MarkdownFidelityTests`, `MarkdownPerformanceTests`); `tests/test_highlight_golden.py` - `test_highlight_matches_preannotated_golden`, `test_golden_text_roundtrips_to_the_sample` (the `markdown` golden pair); source: `tools/blocks/highlight_code.py` - `_highlight_markdown()`, `_md_fence_language()` |

| CMH-STAMP-02 | `validate.py` and `finalize.py` write a `<meta name="commentable-html-validated">` timestamp AND a `<meta name="commentable-html-validated-hash">` content signature into the file ONLY on a STRICT-CLEAN FULL pass (no errors AND no BLOCKING warnings, and both the layer and chart halves ran - a `--charts-only`/`--layer-only` partial run never stamps), so the validated stamp means the document actually passed the whole strict validator. Stamping works when `validate.py` runs as a standalone CLI subprocess (it puts the sibling `authoring/` tools on `sys.path` via the shared bootstrap so `_stamp_validated_file`'s `import doc_stamp` resolves), not only in-process; `validate.py` is not read-only. A CRLF document remains uniformly CRLF when those missing meta tags are inserted. A stamp-write failure is a visible NOTE, never silent, and never blocks validation. `--no-stamp` keeps a pure/CI run read-only (no write); a doc with a BLOCKING warning is not stamped, while a doc whose only remaining warnings are ADVISORIES (CMH-VAL-18) IS stamped - an advisory names something the author cannot clear, so withholding the stamp would leave the runtime `not validated` banner up forever. The stamp WRITE is ATOMIC: both `validate.py` and the single write `finalize.py` makes stage the stamped bytes in the target's own directory and swap them in with `os.replace` (shared `_atomic_io.atomic_write`, CMH-PORT-04), so an interrupted or failing write leaves the ORIGINAL bytes untouched instead of truncating a document that just passed validation - the old `open(path, "w")` truncated first, and because stamping is best-effort the loss was reported as only a NOTE. | CMH-TOOL-08 | `tools/authoring/upgrade.py` upgrades a standalone document by replacing the CSS, COMMENT UI, and JS regions (preserving handled ids, embedded comments, content, and the root) and re-emitting the shell-baked mermaid loader bootstrap (see CMH-MMD-09), validates the result in a temp file, and leaves the target unchanged if validation fails or the validator crashes. It also restamps the `<head>` `<meta name="commentable-html-version">` to the template's runtime version (inserting it when a pre-version legacy document lacks it) so an upgraded file no longer self-reports the old version; the restamp is scoped to `<head>` so the marker-like JS export regex literal (`content="[^"]+"`) is never matched or rewritten. Post-upgrade validator warnings are surfaced (not discarded) and the upgrade still commits by default so a version-only upgrade is never blocked by a pre-existing content warning; the opt-in `--strict` flag treats those warnings as a failure, leaving the target unchanged and exiting non-zero. A region boundary is matched only on a COMPLETE marker line (the keyword phrase alone on its line, optionally wrapped by its comment delimiter and/or a `====` banner, with nothing else on the line), so an inline mention or a line-leading marker phrase carrying trailing authored text cannot corrupt a swap. The shipped upgrader, maintainer build tool, and runtime export slicers reject duplicate BEGIN or END markers for every layer region instead of silently slicing through authored content. It also preserves the input file's DOMINANT newline (detected from the raw bytes) through the transform, so a Windows-authored (CRLF) document is not silently normalized to LF on upgrade; newline-style differences alone do not make an up-to-date CRLF file stale, and output never doubles a retained carriage return. An unreadable or invalid-UTF-8 input exits 2 with a diagnostic instead of a traceback. The swap also PRESERVES THE DESTINATION'S FILE MODE: the validated staging file comes from `mkstemp` (POSIX `0600`) and `os.replace` carries the staged inode's mode to the target, so without the mode step an upgraded `0644` report would silently become owner-only. The shared `_atomic_io.preserve_mode` copies the destination's `0777` permission bits onto the staged file just before the replace (special setuid/setgid/sticky bits are never copied onto a freshly staged inode, and a destination that exists but cannot be statted is left alone so a guess can never WIDEN a private file); a `--out` to a path that does not exist yet has no mode to preserve, so it takes the SOURCE document's mode rather than a process default that could widen a private report. The destination is resolved with `realpath` first (as `atomic_write` does), so upgrading through a symlink rewrites the real document instead of replacing the link with a regular file and stranding it, and cleanup goes through `_atomic_io.quiet_remove` so a staged file that inherited a read-only mode cannot leak. | `tests/test_upgrade.py` - region swap, preservation, stale `--check`, validation-failure-leaves-target-unchanged, validator-crash-surfaced, marker-line tests, duplicate BEGIN/END tests, `test_version_meta_is_bumped_to_template_version`, `test_version_meta_is_inserted_when_missing`, `test_version_meta_noop_when_already_current`, `test_version_meta_bump_ignores_js_regex_literal`, `test_cli_surfaces_warnings_without_strict`, `test_cli_strict_aborts_on_warning_and_leaves_target_unchanged`, `test_cli_strict_commits_when_clean`, `test_cli_preserves_crlf_line_endings`, `test_cli_keeps_lf_when_lf_is_dominant_despite_a_stray_crlf`, `test_cli_check_reports_a_crlf_document_up_to_date`, `test_cli_invalid_utf8_returns_2_without_a_traceback`, `test_cli_preserves_the_target_file_mode`, `test_cli_preserves_an_executable_target_file_mode`, `test_cli_out_to_an_existing_file_preserves_that_file_mode`, `test_cli_out_to_a_new_file_takes_the_source_file_mode`, `test_cli_upgrades_through_a_symlink_instead_of_replacing_it`, `test_cli_leaves_no_temp_file_when_the_replace_itself_fails`; | CMH-TOOL-11 | `tools/authoring/generate_toc.py` creates or replaces `nav.cm-toc` under `#commentRoot`, injects missing `h2`/`h3` ids, de-dupes against existing ids, strips a redundant leading author section number from each entry and writes the entry's own number into it as a `cm-skip` `span.cm-toc-num` - the number the HEADING displays when the document numbers its own sections, else a hierarchical one computed from the heading depth - so the Contents list and the side menu show one number for the same heading rather than two that disagree (CMH-TOC-10), and preserves the dominant newline style. The nav is placed BELOW the document title and its reading-time strip: after the top-level title container inside `#commentRoot` (the `<h1>` itself or its wrapper, e.g. `header.cmh-lede`) and after a direct-child `div[data-cmh-doc-stats]` overview strip (CMH-STATS-01) that IMMEDIATELY follows that title, which is the only shape `doc_stats.py` produces - so a reader meets the title and the reading time before the contents list. The TITLE is what earns the move: a strip placed anywhere else never drags the nav down to it. A candidate anchor is discarded - and the nav keeps the top-of-`#commentRoot` placement - when it lands inside the `.cm-toc` being replaced (so the insert and the removal can never overlap; an anchor exactly AT the removal's start is adjacent, not overlapping, and is kept), when its element was not closed by its OWN end tag (an ancestor's closer, an implicit close, or end of input leaves the extent INSIDE the open element), or when it would land after the first section the nav lists (a slide deck or single-wrapper document whose title shares a container with its sections, or a document whose first section precedes its title). A nav that lists NO sections is held to the same rule rather than exempted from it, since with nothing to measure against the title container's extent is exactly as misleading. A document with no `<h1>` keeps the top-of-root placement too, an existing nav above the title is MOVED down rather than duplicated, and the rewrite is idempotent for every shape this row describes. A heading inside the `nav.cm-toc` the rewrite REPLACES is navigation chrome: it is never listed, never receives a generated id, and its own ids do not reserve a slug, so the rewrite stays lossless and idempotent instead of queueing an id insertion inside the span it deletes; any two rewrite spans that did overlap are refused rather than applied. The rule is scoped to the replaced span, so a `.cm-toc` the rewrite leaves in place (one closed by an ancestor's end tag or by end of input, or one wrapping or being `#commentRoot`) still has its headings listed rather than silently yielding an empty table of contents. In-place document rewrites: `authoring/mark_handled.py`, `mark_reviewed.py`, `generate_toc.py`, `doc_stats.py`, `normalize_typography.py`, `wrap_sections.py`, `fix_skip.py`, `inline_images.py` and `vendored_libs.py`, `notes/notes_apply.py`, `checklist/checklist_apply.py`, `blocks/highlight_document.py`, and `deck/deck_fix_fonts.py`. Caller-named `--out` targets, which can name a file that already holds the user's bytes: `authoring/content_extract.py`, `notes/notes_scaffold.py`, `checklist/checklist_scaffold.py`, `deck/pptx_to_fragment.py`, `deck/deck_scaffold.py`, and `authoring/new_document.py --force` (without `--force` it is an EXCLUSIVE create that refuses an existing file, so there is nothing to lose). The NonShareable companions `new_document --copy-assets` refreshes beside a document are copied the same way (`_atomic_io.stage_copy` + `commit_staged`), because a half-copied runtime or stylesheet breaks a document just as effectively; the whole SET is staged before any of it is swapped in, so a failure DURING staging cannot leave a document pairing a new runtime with an old stylesheet (the renames themselves are still separate - see the residuals below). A copy does NOT inherit its source's mode by default: a companion's source is the skill's own installed `dist/`, whose permissions say how the plugin was extracted rather than what the user wants beside their report, and a read-only one would land a companion that could never be refreshed again. SKILL.md points an agent straight at a real document, so the truncating `open(path, "w")` these used emptied the user's only copy BEFORE the replacement bytes existed: a full disk, an encoding error, a killed run or a Ctrl+C left half a document, or none. A failed or interrupted write now leaves the original byte for byte, leaks no staged file, and is reported rather than silently half-applied; a destination whose DIRECTORY cannot be written is reported in terms of the document and the directory rather than as a failure on a `.cmh-write-` path the user has never seen. A CLI writing to `--out` names its SOURCE document (or, for a scaffold or a converter, its input file when it is not stdin) as the mode fallback, so a transformed copy written to a path that does not exist yet keeps the source's visibility - capped by the mode a plain create would produce, so it is never wider than either the source or the umask allows. The writer lives at the `tools/` ROOT rather than in `authoring/`, because tools in five buckets plus the validator's stamp now depend on it and a shared guarantee must not be reachable only from inside one bucket; the three tools that hand-roll their own staging (`authoring/upgrade.py`, `authoring/retrofit.py`, `deck/deck_theme.py`) share the swap itself through `_atomic_io.commit_staged` and flush their staged bytes with `_atomic_io.fsync_file`, so the durability and the retry are not properties only `atomic_write` callers get - a rename is only as durable as the bytes it points at. A NEW tool cannot quietly reintroduce the truncating write: a static guard parses every shipped tool and FAILS CLOSED on any call that can empty a named file - `open`/`io.open`/`Path.open` with a truncating mode OR with a mode that is not a literal (the `"w" if force else "x"` spelling that hid one), `Path.write_text`/`write_bytes`, `shutil.copyfile`/`copy`/`copy2`/`move` (including when imported under a bare or renamed name), and `os.open` whose flags are not provably read-only - unless the call is marked (`# atomic-write: <reason>`) as a write to a file the tool staged itself and so has no bytes to lose. The guard's own detection surface is pinned by a test, both the spellings it must catch and the ones it must NOT (a `dict.copy()` is not a file write, and a guard that cries wolf gets silenced). Each behavioral case also proves the sabotaged run REACHED the shared writer for its target, so a tool that aborts earlier cannot pass the case vacuously. Replacing rather than rewriting inherits CMH-PORT-04's residuals (the document is a NEW inode carrying the original's mode, so ownership/ACLs and hard-link identity are not carried over; because it is the DIRECTORY's write permission that permits the swap, a document the user marked read-only can now be replaced where a truncating write would have failed, and a document in a directory the user cannot write can no longer be rewritten at all; and a hard kill in the window between the mode step and the swap can strand a `.cmh-write-` copy of the document carrying the destination's mode). | `tests/test_atomic_document_writes.py` - `AtomicDocumentWriteTests` (`test_an_interrupted_write_leaves_the_document_untouched`), `StagedWorkFileTests` (`test_a_keyboard_interrupt_mid_transaction_leaves_no_work_file`), `NoTruncatingWriteTests` (`test_no_shipped_tool_truncates_a_file_it_did_not_stage`, `test_the_guard_detects_every_truncating_spelling_it_claims_to`); `tests/test_atomic_io.py` - `ReplaceRetryTests`, `AtomicCopyTests`, `test_atomic_write_passes_the_fallback_through_to_a_new_destination`; `tests/test_tools_layout.py` - `test_tools_root_holds_only_the_bootstrap_and_buckets`; source: `tools/_atomic_io.py` |

Tools that legitimately rewrite their document IN PLACE are guarded on their OTHER inputs, since the in-place one is the same artifact: `authoring/upgrade.py` (`--template`, checked immediately before the write so the read-only `--check` and already-up-to-date runs are never refused for a write they do not make), `authoring/retrofit.py` (`--brand` and BOTH templates it reads - Shareable mode consults the NonShareable one for its theme variables), `deck/deck_theme.py` (`--theme`). It never over-refuses: an in-place transform may still write its `--out` over its own input (`normalize_typography --out <input>`), and `new_document` WITHOUT `--force` compares the RESOLVED target, so a run that `resolve_output_path` has already redirected to a suffixed sibling still succeeds. A NEW tool cannot skip the check: a static guard fails any shipped tool (walked recursively and keyed by its path under `tools/`, never by basename) that takes an `--out` and neither refuses an aliasing destination nor is listed as needing no check with the reason. The guard is deliberately strict about what counts: the refusal must be the whole test of an `if` INSIDE the tool's `main`, whose branch returns non-zero, raises, or exits - a call whose bool is ignored, an inverted or conditional test that lets an aliasing run fall through, and a call parked in an unrelated helper all read as UNGUARDED - and its detection surface is pinned by a test of what it must catch and what it must not. Residuals: `authoring/inline_images.py` is exempt because the images it reads are discovered from the document rather than named on the command line, and their bytes survive base64-encoded inside the document it writes; and `same_file`'s fallback does not detect a HARD LINK, which costs nothing here because the writer swaps in a NEW inode, so the other name keeps the original bytes either way. | `tests/test_out_aliases_input.py` - `test_a_destination_that_resolves_to_an_input_is_refused`, `test_a_destination_that_aliases_a_file_read_off_the_install_is_refused`, `test_a_read_only_mode_is_never_refused`, `test_a_distinct_destination_is_never_refused`, `test_a_distinct_out_still_produces_the_artifact`, `test_an_in_place_tool_may_still_write_its_out_over_its_own_input`, `test_new_document_without_force_still_writes_a_suffixed_sibling`, `test_copy_assets_companions_cannot_land_on_an_input`, `test_retrofit_copy_assets_companions_cannot_land_on_an_input`, `test_same_file_is_canonical_not_textual`, `test_same_file_follows_a_symlink_to_its_target`, `test_same_file_folds_case_where_the_filesystem_does`, `test_two_different_files_are_not_the_same_file`, `test_a_path_the_platform_cannot_represent_answers_no_rather_than_raising`, `test_an_input_that_is_not_a_file_is_never_an_alias`, `test_a_file_genuinely_named_dash_is_still_protected`, `test_the_message_names_both_paths_and_the_resolved_file`, `test_there_are_tools_with_an_out_option_to_check`, `test_every_tool_with_an_out_option_checks_it_or_is_listed_as_in_place`, `test_the_in_place_list_names_only_tools_that_exist_and_take_an_out`, `test_the_guard_detects_every_spelling_it_claims_to`; source: `tools/_atomic_io.py` |

## Claude Code compatibility

commentable-html output is a shareable HTML artifact that works with any agent, and the plugin is installable in Claude Code as well as the GitHub Copilot CLI. It ships a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` beside the Copilot `plugin.json` and is listed in the repo-root `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (a subset mirror of `.github/plugin/marketplace.json`). The auto-updater is dual-agent too (its own `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and Claude `hooks/hooks.json`), so both published plugins install in either agent.

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |

| CMH-HARNESS-01 | `dev/tools/skill_flow_harness.py` is a LOCAL-ONLY regression harness that drives the installed `copilot` executable non-interactively through the skill's create / retrofit / deck / export / validation-handoff routes (copying the shipped `pkg/skills/commentable-html` into `<ws>/.github/skills/` and extracting its `skill-resources.zip` so `copilot -C <ws> --add-dir <ws>` discovers the full shipped skill with file access SCOPED to the workspace, not `--allow-all-paths`) and then RE-VALIDATES each produced document READ-ONLY with the repo's own tools - `validate.py --strict --no-stamp`, `deck_validate.py --strict` for the deck, a self-contained (no companion asset) plus embedded-review-layer check for the shareable export, and on EVERY flow the AGENT-written `<meta name="commentable-html-validated">` stamp (the harness never writes it, so a skipped finalize/validate handoff is caught). Because a live model run is non-hermetic and consumes credits, only the harness PLUMBING is automatically tested; the end-to-end model invocation is an intentional manual coverage gap. | `tests/test_skill_flow_harness.py` - `CiGuardTests`, `ScratchTests`, `CommandTests`, `ContentCheckTests`, `SafePathTests`, `WorkspaceTests`, `CorpusTests`, `PathTests` |
| CMH-BUILD-20 | `finalize.py` reads the document ONCE, threads it through the pure phase transforms in memory, and writes ONCE. Each phase used to re-read and re-write the whole file, so a 1.4 - 2.5 MB document paid a read/write pair and an independent full-document parse per phase (measured on a real document: 6 reads and 2 - 3 writes before validation and stamping read it again) - and `content_replace.py` calls finalize on every write-back, so the agent edit loop paid that on each iteration. The phase ORDER and every transform are unchanged, so the output is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the phase-by-phase pipeline. The per-phase `_run_*` read/modify/write wrappers are DELETED rather than kept: nothing called them once the pipeline threaded the document in memory, and leaving them would have let a future caller silently reintroduce the per-phase I/O this removes. Equivalence is proven against a FILE-CYCLE reference that reads, applies one phase, and writes back once per phase - the shape finalize had before this change - rather than by driving the same transforms in memory, which would compare the new code against itself; a guard test asserts the fixture exercises every always-on phase CUMULATIVELY (in the state the pipeline hands it), so equivalence can never be proven on a no-op. Byte equivalence alone CANNOT pin the phase order - every always-on phase commutes with its neighbours on any fixture tried, so a shuffled pipeline still emits identical bytes - so the order is pinned directly by recording the actual call sequence, and the opt-in phases (`--toc`, `--fix-skip`, `--inline-images`) get their own byte-equivalence run. Mutation checks confirmed the harness goes red both when a phase is dropped and when two adjacent phases are swapped (the swap slipped past the equivalence test alone). The win is proven structurally by counting the file operations EXACTLY (ONE read and ONE write for a changed document, including a strict-clean CLI run, and ZERO writes when nothing changed). Validation and the validated provenance stamp run on the same in-memory document - `validate.validate()` takes an optional `html=` and `validate.stamp_validated_text()` is the in-memory half of `_stamp_validated_file` - because otherwise a clean run still paid a second and third read to validate and stamp, plus a second write, not by a wall clock (a timing assertion would be flaky and the testing guidelines forbid it). Also fixes a quadratic scan in the KQL tokenizer: the per-identifier call test sliced the ENTIRE remaining query (`src[m.end():]`) on every token, and is now a bounded `[ \t]*\(` lookahead - `[ \t]`, not `\s`, so a newline before the paren is still not a call and the golden output is unchanged. | `tests/test_finalize_pipeline.py` - `PipelineEquivalenceTests` (`test_finalize_output_matches_the_phase_by_phase_pipeline`, `test_a_second_finalize_is_a_no_op`, `test_the_toc_phase_still_runs_when_requested`, `test_the_result_validates`), `PipelineEquivalenceTests.test_the_fixture_actually_exercises_every_phase`, `test_the_phases_run_in_the_documented_order`, `test_the_optional_phases_are_threaded_equivalently_too`, `IoAmplificationTests` (`test_the_pipeline_writes_the_document_once`, `test_the_pipeline_reads_the_document_once`, `test_a_strict_clean_run_still_writes_only_once`, `test_the_document_is_actually_stamped_when_clean`, `test_an_unchanged_document_is_not_rewritten`, `test_the_toc_run_does_not_add_a_read_write_pair`); the KQL golden output is pinned unchanged by `tests/test_kql_highlight.py` and `tests/test_highlight_parity.py`; source: `tools/authoring/finalize.py` - the `_apply_*` transforms and `finalize()`; `tools/kusto/kql_highlight.py` - `_CALL_AHEAD_RE` |
| CMH-BUILD-29 | `dev/examples/` holds SOURCES only - it never carries a built report, deck or prompt. `build.py` reads its content sources from `dev/examples/src/` and writes the built documents to `--examples-dir`; the canonical invocation points that at the shipped `../examples`, which is also the tree the site copies its demos from (`scripts/build_site_data_parts/00-imports-constants.py` - `EXAMPLES_REL`). The trap is that omitting the flags is enough: `--examples-dir` DEFAULTS to `<out-dir>/examples` and `--out-dir` defaults to the `dev` directory itself, so a bare `python tools/build.py` targets `dev/examples` and quietly fills the SOURCE directory with 12.6 MB of its own output beside the sources it reads. That is what happened in #1258, and it then sat tracked, unreferenced and unnoticed until #1293 - so the rule detects the output rather than assuming nobody will ever run the tool without its flags. The reason this earns a rule rather than a one-off deletion is that such a copy keeps the state it was BUILT in and nothing ever refreshes it: each of the two chart examples there still inlined a 205,031-byte `Chart.js v4.4.0` bundle and reached Chart.js through no CDN loader at all, long after `CMH-SIZE-09` removed exactly that from the shipped files, so a reader grepping for how an example loads Chart.js found the WRONG answer in a bigger, more prominent file - and `CMH-SIZE-09` had to carve them out of its own claim. The rule is scoped to the shapes a build can emit there, so it catches build output without policing unrelated files - and it asks the BUILD which shapes those are rather than hand-copying its patterns. `tools/build_parts/30-examples.py` enumerates them in `_OUTPUT_NAME_RES`, the guard matches against those compiled regexes directly (never a concatenation of their `.pattern` strings, which would renumber a backreference and could raise at import time), and a covering test asserts that EVERY `*_NAME_RE` the build module declares is enrolled in that tuple. That last assertion is what makes the guarantee real rather than rhetorical: going by how `prompt-*.md` arrived, a fourth output shape means a THIRD regex, not a widened existing one, so without it the guard would simply never see the new shape and would stay green while the build littered. The match is case-INSENSITIVE, deliberately wider than the build's own case-sensitive matching, because a build writes lower case but an offender must not escape on case; and it does not filter to files, because a DIRECTORY named `report-x.html` is just as wrong and skipping it left a trivially evadable hole. It is paired with a companion assertion that `src/` and `images/` (the garden example's source images, per `dev/README.md`) still exist - otherwise emptying the directory would satisfy it. This is DISJOINT from `build.py`'s own `_orphan_examples` check, which flags a built report in the OUTPUT directory whose `dev/examples/src/` source has vanished: every one of the 12.6 MB of copies had a same-named source, which is exactly why that check never fired on them in the eight months they sat there. One rule is about a built file with no source, the other about built files in the SOURCE directory; do not consolidate them. | `tests/test_examples.py` - `DevExamplesHasNoBuiltCopiesTests`, `DevExamplesHasNoBuiltCopiesTests.test_dev_examples_holds_no_built_documents`, `DevExamplesHasNoBuiltCopiesTests.test_the_sources_the_build_actually_reads_are_still_there`, `DevExamplesHasNoBuiltCopiesTests.test_the_guard_consults_every_output_shape_the_build_declares` (the pin: every `*_NAME_RE` the build declares must be enrolled in `_OUTPUT_NAME_RES`, so a fourth output shape cannot quietly gain a way to litter here), `DevExamplesHasNoBuiltCopiesTests.test_the_guard_accepts_every_name_the_build_can_emit`; source: `tools/build_parts/30-examples.py` - `build_examples`, `build_prompt_examples`, `_OUTPUT_NAME_RES` |
## Deck integration (frontend-slides)

The commentable-html skill incorporates the third-party frontend-slides design system (MIT, Zara Zhang) as NATIVE CMH deck theme presets: curated preset profiles under `dev/skill/tools/deck/themes/` recolour the deck stage, components, and reusable recipe classes with system-font, contrast-safe tokens, so a themed deck needs no per-deck CSS and no per-deck hand-translation. A curated, pristine subset of the upstream skill is still vendored under `dev/skill/vendor/frontend-slides/` (enforced pristine by a required CI gate) as design provenance and the maintainer refresh source, and to supply the inlined `viewport-base.css` and the PPTX extractor. The author-time deck tools live under `dev/skill/tools/deck/`, and the runtime deck profile lives in the layer (activated only by `data-cmh-mode="deck"`, so non-deck documents are unaffected). See `references/deck-contract.md` for the runtime interface contract.

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CMH-DECK-01 | The skill detects a presentation/deck request ("slide deck", "presentation", "pitch deck", "convert this ppt") and CONFIRMS with the user before building a real deck rather than silently producing a flat document; if the user declines it falls back to a normal flat document. This is an agent-behavior convention in `SKILL.md` ("Deck capability"), so its coverage is `manual`. | `manual` - documented in `SKILL.md`; agent-behavior convention, not automatable |
| CMH-DECK-02 | `deck/deck_scaffold.py` produces a valid, create-only, commentable-native fixed-stage deck: `#commentRoot` carries `data-cmh-mode="deck"` and a `commentable-html-kind` of `slides`, the body holds `.deck-viewport > .deck-stage` with `viewport-base.css` inlined, every slide is a `<section class="slide">` with a unique stable `data-slide-id` and ONLY the first is `.active` - an input fragment that already marks a LATER slide active is NORMALIZED (the first LIVE slide gains the class, every later slide has `active` and `visible` removed) rather than carried through, because two active slides, or an active one that is not the first, is a deck that opens on the wrong slide and the deck contract now refuses it (CMH-DECK-04). "FIRST" is the first slide a BROWSER renders, taken from the gate's own parse (`deck_validate.first_live_slide_offset`) so the scaffold and the gate it must satisfy hold ONE reading: the tag WALK above already keeps a `<section>` inside a comment or a raw-text body out of the rewrite, but a `<template>` SUBTREE is tokenized all the same while a browser renders it nowhere, so a templated slide would otherwise consume the first-slide position, put `.active` on markup nothing shows, and leave every real slide without it - turning a fragment that scaffolded cleanly into a hard refusal. That parse also decides which slides are STRIPPED, not only which one is marked: a `<section class="slide active">` an author DISPLAYS as sample text is not a slide, so rewriting it to satisfy a rule that does not apply to it would edit the document's own content. Where the two readings disagree about which slides exist at all, the choice DEGRADES to the slides the rewrite can reach, rather than marking nothing active and emitting a deck the gate refuses, the deck body has no inline editor / remote fonts / host script, ids are deterministic, and it refuses to overwrite an existing output without `--force`. Before writing it runs BOTH the base validator AND the deck contract (`deck_validate.deck_checks`) and fails closed (writing nothing) on any contract violation; its deck-mode injection targets the real content root (never the template decoy) idempotently. The ids ALREADY TAKEN in an input fragment are read through the shared raw start-tag reading (`_browser_attrs.raw_attrs_pairs`), so an authored `data-slide-id` on a slide `<section>`'s OWN start tag is seen in any of HTML's three quoting forms and is compared BROWSER-DECODED exactly as `deck_validate` compares it, rather than through a double-quote-only search that left it free to be minted again; a DUPLICATED `data-slide-id` reads its FIRST occurrence on both sides, as HTML5 and `deck_validate` do, and is written back once. Only a SLIDE section's id is reserved, so an unrelated `<section>` cannot push a slide onto the collision branch and make its id depend on a non-slide. That reading is also what decides which attributes SURVIVE and what they SAY, since the rewrite re-serializes the whole start tag from it: on a PARTIAL install, where the shared reading is unavailable, the degraded stand-in in `tools/_browser_attrs.py` answers the WHOLE attribute list, folds a NUL to U+FFFD as a browser does in an attribute name and value alike, and decodes a value by the browser's ATTRIBUTE rule from its own pinned copy rather than through the host's `html.unescape`, so a partial install writes the deck a full one writes. A class-only stand-in there deleted every non-class attribute; the host's decode resolved a named reference that is only a PREFIX of the value or is followed by `=` (an authored `title="x&ampy"` became `x&y`) and DELETED the code points it considers invalid (`&#1;`, `&#x7f;`, `&#xfffe;`); and an unfolded NUL was written back literally. All three are silent, and all three pass the deck contract with a ZERO exit, so the deck is written carrying a value the rendered DOM never has. The `data-slide-id` is the one attribute whose SHAPE is gated, but that gate is only as good as the decode feeding it: because the host's decode DELETES a character a browser keeps, an authored `data-slide-id="slide-aaaaaaaa&#1;"` - which a browser reads as the shape-INVALID `slide-aaaaaaaa\u0001`, and which must therefore fail closed - decoded to the perfectly valid `slide-aaaaaaaa`, passed the contract and was written, silently RENAMING the authored id that create-only exists to keep stable. The browser rule keeps the character, so the shape gate now sees what a browser sees on both readings. That re-serialization is ROUND-TRIP FAITHFUL for a VALUELESS attribute too: it is written back as `name=""`, not as a bare name. The bare name dropped the `/` HTML uses to terminate an attribute name, so two ADJACENT valueless attributes whose second name legally begins with `=` (HTML5's unexpected-equals-sign-before-attribute-name state) FUSED into one attribute WITH a value on the way through - `<section class="slide" data-a/=onload>` came back as `data-a =onload`, which re-parses as `data-a="onload"`, a value the input document never had (#1191). An absent value IS the empty string to a browser, so the quoted empty value is the same attribute and cannot be terminated by the next name's `=`. That rule now lives in ONE shared writer (`_browser_attrs.serialize_start_tag`, CMH-VAL-21) which all four start-tag re-serializers in the skill route through, because three siblings kept their own copy and carried the identical bug for a release (#1195). The fused NAME could be an `on*` one (`onclick/=alert(1)` fused into `onclick="alert(1)"`), but no deck the scaffold EMITS could carry a handler minted that way: on a slide `<section>` `deck_checks` rejects an attribute whose name starts with `on` - valued or valueless alike - and the scaffold runs it on the final HTML before it writes `--out`, so that shape failed closed on both sides of this fix. It is a correctness bug either way, not a vulnerability: a document's own author is trusted (`CMH-SEC-01`). The same round trip holds for a CR, which took BOTH sides of the shared pair to make unambiguous. The READ (`_browser_attrs.raw_attrs_pairs`) now applies HTML's INPUT-STREAM PREPROCESSING first, the browser's own first step: every CR and CRLF becomes a single LF BEFORE tokenization, so no value a browser holds carries a CR unless a character reference put one there. The WRITE (`serialize_start_tag`, through the new `_browser_attrs.escape_attr_value`) escapes a CR back as `&#13;`. `html.escape(quote=True)` alone escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` but NOT CR, so the literal CR it wrote was not the character the input named - an authored `title="a&#13;b"` came back as a `title` a browser reads as `a\nb`, silently changing an authored value (#1196). Neither half works alone: the two spellings of a CR are INDISTINGUISHABLE once decoded (both are `"\r"`), so escaping without the read-side fold would turn a LITERAL CR - which a browser reads as LF, and which only a reader that preserved the document's line endings with `newline=""` can present - into a CR the input never meant, the exact inverse of the bug. Making the distinction at the READ, as a browser makes it, is what lets the escape be unconditional for every re-serializer. The fold goes into the SHARED reading (`validate/checks/parsing.raw_attrs_pairs`) so the rule is stated once and any future caller of it inherits it - a no-op for the validator, which already folds the WHOLE document (`validate._browser_newlines`) before it parses, and which is exactly what the tools were NOT doing - and is repeated in the `_browser_attrs` wrapper so the degraded partial-install split gets it too; for a `newline=""` reader it is deliberately NOT a no-op, and a CRLF inside a rewritten value comes back as a lone LF, which is the value a browser holds either way. `authoring/upgrade.py` carries BOTH halves itself (`preprocess_input_stream` then `escape_attr_value`) because it rewrites ONE value's own span rather than rebuilding the tag, so neither shared rule reaches it; and `retrofit._root_tag`, which INJECTS a new content root rather than re-serializing one, now builds it through the shared writer as well - it kept its own `html.escape`, so a `--label` carrying a CR reached a browser as two different values depending on which of retrofit's two root branches ran. LF and TAB are deliberately NOT escaped: preprocessing leaves them alone and a quoted value keeps them verbatim. The escape is also TOTAL: it folds to U+FFFD the two characters a document can never HOLD - a NUL (the attribute-value tokenizer folds it) and a LONE SURROGATE (it cannot be encoded as UTF-8 at all, so it would otherwise raise at the file write, far from the value that caused it). That fold is repeated on the write side rather than left to the read, because it lives in `raw_attrs_pairs` and not in `unescape_attr_value`, which a span-rewriter decodes through alone. It is pinned as a SPELLING on the escape's own output, because a round-trip assertion cannot see it: the read folds NUL too, so a literal NUL written into the tag reads back as U+FFFD whether or not the write side folded. The fold makes the escape deliberately LOSSY (an authored U+FFFD and a NUL produce identical output, as they do in a browser), so it is not a change detector. Only `None` is accepted as a non-string, because a valueless attribute decodes to the empty string; anything else raises `TypeError` rather than serializing as empty, since the earlier `value or ""` turned a falsy `0` into `""` - the same silent-rewrite class. The slide is also LOCATED by that same shared reading, not only read with it: `_section_tags` WALKS the fragment's tags left to right and consumes each one's whole extent, taking every boundary and every tag NAME from the shared browser readings (`checks/parsing.scan_start_tag` / `end_tag_close`, reached through `_browser_attrs`), rather than from a quote-aware `<section ...>` regex whose quoted run opened at ANY quote. That regex disagreed with the tokenizer it then handed the attributes to, in BOTH directions: `<section class="slide" a"b>` is a real slide with an attribute NAMED `a"b` (HTML opens a value only after an `=` and takes a stray quote into the name), yet as the first of three slides it was SKIPPED - no id, and `.active` on slide two, which then failed closed on the contract; and `<section class=slide foo" bar="x>` reaches EOF inside a quoted value, so HTML5's eof-in-tag error DISCARDS the tag and a browser builds no such element, yet it matched and was re-serialized into a live, contract-passing slide (#1197). Three shapes are refused, leaving the markup exactly as authored so a slide without an id fails the deck closed rather than shipping: a tag that never finishes (the walk STOPS there, since a browser discards it and every character after the opening quote - so a later `<section>` inside that runaway value is not a slide either), a `<section` whose name is not `section` under HTML's own ASCII fold and tag-name terminator, and one the shared tokenizer did not fully consume (`raw_attrs_pairs_consumed`), which would re-serialize with every attribute past that point silently dropped. The NAME is decided by the shared fold rather than matched by a `<section` pattern because Python's `re.IGNORECASE` folds UNICODE: `<section\b` plus `re.I` promoted BOTH the custom element `<section-foo>` and the custom element `<\u017fection>` into a real `<section>`, and since the authored `</\u017fection>` stayed behind as an unknown end tag the phantom slide never closed and swallowed the real one, with a zero exit and both gates passing. Walking every tag is also what keeps a `<section>` or `</section>` spelled inside ANOTHER tag's quoted attribute value out of the slide list, since that tag's own extent is consumed whole. The walk skips an HTML COMMENT and a raw-text `<script>` / `<style>` / `<textarea>` body WHOLE, through the same shared readings (`comment_close`, `raw_text_elements`), because their content is prose a reader SEES: a commented-out slide is therefore not scaffolded, and - the reason this is a correctness matter and not a nicety - a commented-out or scripted tag carrying an unterminated quoted value (`<!-- <a href="x -->`) no longer runs a start-tag scan through the LIVE markup after it, which consumed the real slide that followed and made it VANISH. That loss was silent whenever the lost slide already carried a `data-slide-id` - which every slide `pptx_to_fragment` emits does - because the deck contract then had nothing to object to. Every other NON-ELEMENT region a `<` can open is skipped the same way: a markup declaration (`<!DOCTYPE ...>`) and a BOGUS COMMENT (`<?...`, a `<!` that is not a comment, a `</` with no tag name), each of which a browser ends at its first `>`, so a `<section class="slide">` written inside one is a decoy that would otherwise be minted an id and handed `.active`. `title` is deliberately left out of the walk's raw-text set, and `<![CDATA[` is read as the bogus comment it is in the HTML namespace rather than as character data: both are namespace-dependent (nothing is raw text and only CDATA is character data inside `<svg>` / `<math>`), the walk keeps no namespace stack, and both choices err toward FINDING a decoy rather than toward LOSING a real slide, which is the safe direction. The END tag is ended by the shared reading too - the first `>` outside a quoted value - so the ordinary `</section >` and `</section foo="a>b">` close a slide instead of leaving every later slide unscaffolded and failing a benign deck. The FIRST `</section>` closes a section, as the non-greedy regex this replaces did, which is a deliberate divergence from a browser (which NESTS sections) and is what keeps a slide's body - and so the id minted from it - the same text the old scan hashed. The partial-install stand-ins for all three boundary readings are pinned COPIES of them, like the value decode and the NUL fold and for the same reason: the scaffold RE-SERIALIZES the start tag it locates and SPLICES at the boundaries it finds, so a degraded boundary is written into the deck rather than merely read. Active-content and egress checks are HTML-parser based (not regex), so they cannot be bypassed by a solidus attribute separator (`<svg/onload=>`), an entity-encoded scheme (`&#106;avascript:`), an unquoted attribute (`<img src=//evil>`), or an SVG `<image>`/`<use>` `href`. That candidate list feeds the dangerous-scheme and `../` checks too, so both narrowed with it: a scheme or a `../` buried in parenthesised or unclosed-paren DESCRIPTOR text is no longer reported, because HTML puts no candidate boundary there and a browser measurably acts on none of it, while a genuine comma-separated candidate carrying one is still rejected. The import degrades rather than crashing: a broken or partial install warns through `_toolpath.warn_missing_tool` and falls back to the strictly over-inclusive union reading, so the gate still fails CLOSED on egress. The "is this remote" question is the SHARED one too: the egress attributes ask `checks/resources.py`'s `is_network_url` and the CSS reads ask that module's `url()` / `@import` patterns, the same readings the strict validator and the offline strip use, instead of the gate's own `^(?:https?:)?//`. That regex required the two slashes; the URL parser's special-authority states CONSUME the slash run after a special scheme, so `https:host/x.png`, `https:/host/x.png` and `https:\host/x.png` resolve to the same host as `https://host/x.png` and were MISSED loads - and outside descriptor mode `offline` the base validator's media rules do not run, so for a deck this gate is the only checker `source[srcset]` gets (#1129; the other two surfaces were widened for exactly these spellings in #961, CMH-OFFLINE-04). The deck-only `image-set()` reader, which the deck gate needed FIRST and which now lives in the has no shared CSS reading (`checks/resources.py`'s `css_image_set_args` / `css_network_image_set`, asked by the strict validator's shareable CSS gate too since #1166 - so the deck holds the shared PREDICATE by identity rather than a copy, and keeps a local COPY of the same quote- and paren-aware scanner for the broken-install path, deliberately duplicated because a regex-shaped fallback truncated at the `;` inside a quoted `data:` candidate and dropped every candidate after it, failing OPEN in the one path whose point is to fail closed; a corpus test pins the copy to the shared scanner so the seam cannot drift), counterpart, is BUILT from the shared prefix and host-character fragments rather than a hand copy, and it scans EVERY candidate in the list, read with a quote- and paren-aware scanner rather than a regex: a regex that stopped at the first `)` stopped at the one closing a nested `url(...)` / `type(...)` or a literal `)` inside a quoted candidate, so `image-set(url("a.png") 1x, "//evil/x.png" 2x)` hid the candidate a 2x-DPR browser fetches. That scanner keeps the quote-faithful reading for a CLOSED list, so a legal `<` inside a candidate (`image-set("a<b.png" 1x, "//evil/x.png" 2x)`) cannot hide the candidate after it; a list that never CLOSES is re-read with markup as a hard boundary even inside a quote, because the open quote is then almost certainly the one ending the `style` attribute rather than a CSS string, and reading on would swallow the rest of the slide - reporting an allowed `<a href>` further down as a remote CSS reference. An unquoted `;`, `{` or `}` ends the scan either way, and a `data:` candidate's own `;` separator cannot truncate the list before a later remote candidate. Both CSS reads also run over a copy of the body with the parser-removed controls normalized away, which the URL parser does in TWO different ways: it removes ASCII tab from ANYWHERE, but every other C0 control only from the LEADING run of a reference. So `url("//<TAB>host/x.png")` and `url("<VT>//host/x.png")` really load `//host/x.png` - which the shared host-character class (tab-excluding) and CSS's own whitespace class cannot see - while the mid-token `url("/<SOH>/host/x.png")` stays LOCAL and is deliberately not reported, since normalizing it away would reject a reference that loads nothing. LF and CR are kept in both readings (a newline in a CSS string is a bad-string token and the declaration is dropped, so nothing loads). This deck-local normalization is a COMPENSATION, not a shared fix: the strict validator and the offline strip still read those spellings with the shared patterns alone. Two boundaries are DECLARED rather than implied: the CSS reads are a whole-body TEXT search, not a parse of style contexts, so a slide that merely DISPLAYS remote CSS text is reported (the fail-closed direction, and the gate's behavior before this change); and an EMPTY authority (`url(//)`, `https://`) is not reported, because no browser fetches from one and reporting it would delete an author's value over a reference that loads nothing - the shared predicate's own documented rule, which the deck gate now inherits along with its documented fail-closed `file:` readings. This import degrades the same way (warn, then a strictly over-inclusive local reading that requires no non-empty authority), and the degraded CSS reading is selected per CALL so a test can reach it. It tolerates a local-relative image, a `data:` image URI, an external hyperlink (`<a href>` is not egress), and a local `<link href>`; it does not false-positive on the plain-text token "edit-toggle" in prose. The content region is anchored on the full HTML-comment markers and uses the LAST end marker, so slide text containing the bare marker text cannot truncate validation. The four STRUCTURAL checks - the `.deck-viewport` wrapper, the exactly-one `.deck-stage`, the `<section class="slide">` list with its `data-slide-id`s, and the stripped-editor guard - decide class membership through the SHARED class reading (`class_tokens`, CMH-VAL-21 clause 11) over PARSED elements, not through a raw-text regex that matched a class by SUBSTRING and only in the DOUBLE-QUOTED form. That regex was wrong against a browser in both directions (#1159): `class="my-deck-stage"` satisfied the one-stage check for an element a browser never matches `.deck-stage` on, `my-slide` was read as a slide (and then reported as missing its id) and `not-edit-toggle` as the upstream editor; while `<section class='slide'>`, `<div class=deck-stage>` and `class="deck-viewport cm-skip"` - the same classes to a browser - were not seen at all, so a hand-authored deck failed for having no slides and every per-slide check then silently inspected nothing. Three boundaries of that reading are DECLARED rather than implied. (1) The structural scan reads the body BOTH ways, like the active-content scan beside it, and unions the findings: `<noscript>` is raw TEXT to a scripting-enabled browser and live markup to a scripting-disabled one, so a second `.deck-stage`, a duplicate slide id or an un-stripped editor parked in one is real to the reader who is on that side (and the raw-text regexes saw them). (2) A `<template>` SUBTREE carries no structure: its content is a fragment a browser renders nowhere, and the runtime finds the stage and the viewport with `#commentRoot.querySelector(".deck-stage")` / `.deck-viewport`, which reaches neither a template fragment nor a shadow root a declarative template attaches - so a deck whose only stage or slides sit in a template has none. Only the SUBTREE is skipped: a `<template>` ELEMENT stays in the document tree, so a `<template class="deck-stage">` really is what that query returns (and then holds no slides), and its own classes are counted. The EDITOR guard stays inclusive of templates and fails CLOSED, because an `<edit-toggle>` parked in one is still upstream editor chrome a generated deck should not carry. (3) NAMESPACE is deliberately not filtered: an undeclared-namespace type selector and a class selector both match in ANY namespace, so `querySelector(".deck-stage")` really does find an SVG-namespace element carrying the class, and this scan reads the document the way that query does. The slide reading is the one place the scan is deliberately NOT that query: it collects every `<section class="slide">` in the BODY, while the runtime asks `stage.querySelectorAll(".slide")` - so a section outside the stage is still checked for its id, and a `<div class="slide">` inside it is not. That is the pre-existing (body-wide, `<section>`-only) scope the regexes had, kept because narrowing it would silently drop id checks a deck relies on. A valueless `data-slide-id` decodes to the empty string exactly as an empty one does, and neither names a slide, so both read as MISSING - which is also what keeps an empty id out of the duplicate-id line. Asking ELEMENTS rather than the body text also means a structural class a reader merely SEES - in slide prose, or inside a `<script>` body, which is text to a browser - is not deck structure, and each slide's `data-slide-id` is read from the browser-decoded attribute dict rather than from a double-quote-only match. It also runs the base validator. Its egress index is PINNED to the strict layer gate's `_MEDIA_LOAD_ATTRS` and to the offline export strips by `tests/test_egress_list_parity.py` (CMH-BUILD-22, issue #1179), because outside descriptor mode `offline` this gate is the only checker a deck's egress gets, so a pair the other two carry and this one does not is a live hole rather than a stylistic difference. Two divergences were live when that pin was added. `feimage` was missing here, so a deck could fetch through `<feImage href="https://...">` - an SVG filter primitive the strict gate and the export strip have both covered since #992 - and it is now in the index (the key is lowercase because `HTMLParser` lowercases a tag name, while the export selector must spell it `feImage` to match in both namespaces; both readings stay namespace-blind for the reason CMH-OFFLINE-04 records). The legacy `lowsrc` went the other way: this gate treated it as a fetch on ANY element, on a comment asserting it still loads, while the strict gate had no rule for it and the export strips none. It does not load, and the warrant is stated exactly because a retirement is only as good as its evidence: HTML's own spec lists `lowsrc` as a NON-CONFORMING legacy feature with no step in the embedded-content loading algorithm (the IDL attribute merely reflects a URL); it is not documented as a supported feature by MDN and has no browser-compat entry at all, so nothing records support for it - which is different from something recording its absence; and it is MEASURED not to fetch in the engine CI runs, with the `lowsrc` image FIRST in the document (so a parse-time fetch would be requested before either control's) and the page then settled to network-idle (so a DEFERRED fetch is caught too), where a plain `src` and a legacy `background` are both requested and the `lowsrc` is not requested at all. IE fetched it historically; no evergreen engine does. So the rule and its stale comment were RETIRED, and `lowsrc` left `_URL_ATTRS` with them, since that membership also reported an authored `lowsrc="../x.png"` as a parent-directory reference no browser acts on. That is the evidentiary bar a future retirement is expected to clear too - a measurement with positive controls, a spec/compat reading, and a revival path that moves every surface - rather than an assertion that some engine no longer does something. The two deck lists are themselves pinned to each other by that test, because `_scan` filters on `_URL_ATTRS` BEFORE it consults `_EGRESS_ATTRS`: an egress entry whose attribute is not also a URL attribute is a rule this gate declares and never applies, so a widening that lands in only one of the two lists now fails with its own message instead of reading as covered. The "remote media/resource" list above is the SHAPE of the rule rather than an exhaustive index - the index itself is `_EGRESS_ATTRS` / `_EGRESS_ANY_ATTRS`, which also carry `input` `src` and, since #1179, `feimage` - and CMH-BUILD-22 is what keeps that index in step with the other two surfaces. A network `url(...)` written in an SVG PRESENTATION ATTRIBUTE (issue #1186) needs no rule of its own here: the deck's remote-CSS reading runs over the whole deck BODY, so it sees the reference wherever it is written, an attribute value included - which is why the deck keeps one CSS reading rather than gaining a fourth copy of the strict gate's attribute list. A FIFTH structural check gates WHICH slide opens the deck: exactly one slide must carry the `active` class and it must be the FIRST, and no slide other than the first may carry `visible`. `deck_scaffold` promises the first is `.active` (CMH-DECK-02) and runs this gate on the final HTML before it writes `--out`, but the gate could not SEE the promise - it read only the presence, format and uniqueness of `data-slide-id` - so a deck with `.active` on slide two, on several slides, or on none at all passed with a zero exit and simply opened on the wrong slide. That is what made the scaffold's silently-skipped-slide bug (#1197) only ACCIDENTALLY fail closed: it was caught because the skipped slide had no `data-slide-id`, and a fragment whose slides already carry ids - which is every fragment `pptx_to_fragment` emits - would have been written as a corrupt deck with every gate green. `visible` rides along because `viewport-base.css` shows a slide on `.slide.active, .slide.visible` and the runtime toggles the two in lockstep, so a later slide left `visible` paints stacked over the slide the deck opens on - the same failure with the same green gates. Membership is the SHARED class reading like the four checks beside it, so any quoting form and any character-reference spelling counts and a substring such as `inactive` does not. Unlike those four, this one is asked the way the RUNTIME asks it, and both divergences are DECLARED. (1) It reads the slides inside the FIRST `.deck-stage` - the set `root.querySelector(".deck-stage")` then `stage.querySelectorAll(".slide")` returns, which matches ANY tag, so a `<div class="slide">` beside the section the deck opens on IS counted here even though the `<section>`-only id checks never see it - not the body-wide list those id checks keep. That body-wide scope is order-INDEPENDENT, so it never answered wrongly for them; this is the first ORDER-dependent check, and body-wide it was wrong in BOTH directions: a stray `<section class="slide">` before the stage made a correct deck fail, and a stray ACTIVE one outside the stage made a deck with no active slide inside it pass. (2) Its POSITIONAL half is asked of the scripting-ENABLED reading only, not unioned across both passes: a stage, a duplicate id or an un-stripped editor parked in a `<noscript>` is real to a scripting-disabled reader, but WHICH slide is FIRST is not that kind of question - the layer only runs with scripting enabled, and a `<noscript>`-parked slide shifts every index without changing what any reader sees - so unioning it reported a correct deck as broken while numbering a slide the author's document does not have. The ORDER-INDEPENDENT half IS unioned: "at most one slide is shown at once" is real to that reader too, because the CSS paints every `.active` / `.visible` slide whether or not the layer ever runs - and that count is taken over EVERY `.slide` in the body rather than over the stage's list, since `.slide.active, .slide.visible` is a GLOBAL rule, so a second active slide parked OUTSIDE the stage paints beside the one the deck opens on even though the runtime never enumerates it. | CMH-DECK-THEME-01 | A native deck theme preset is a named JSON profile under `tools/deck/themes/<name>.theme.json` of allowlisted deck CSS custom properties (system-font stacks + colors, optional local `data:` fonts). `deck/_deck_theme.py` loads it fail-closed - rejecting an unknown token, an unsafe value (reusing the shared `_brand_profile` value validators), a non-color value for a color token, and, at load time, a preset whose own declared `contrastPairs` fall below AA - and `render()` emits a single `<style id="cmh-deck-theme" class="cm-skip">` block scoped to `.deck-viewport/.deck-stage/.slide`. `deck_scaffold.py --theme <name>` injects the block into the content region (so the deck-contract and contrast checks cover it) and the deck still passes `deck_validate.py`; the shipped `terminal` preset (dark/technical, system monospace) is adapted from frontend-slides. | `tests/test_deck_theme.py` - `test_terminal_preset_ships_and_lists`, `test_render_emits_cm_skip_scoped_block_with_tokens`, `test_unknown_token_rejected`, `test_non_color_value_for_color_token_rejected`, `test_unsafe_value_rejected`, `test_preset_level_contrast_self_check_fails_closed`, `test_terminal_preset_pairs_pass_self_check`, `test_scaffold_theme_terminal_is_valid_and_themed`, `test_scaffold_unknown_theme_fails_closed`; `tests/70-deck-theme.spec.js` - `CMH-DECK-THEME-01: the terminal theme recolours the stage, slides, code, and tables` |
| CMH-DECK-THEME-02 | `deck/deck_theme.py apply` re-themes an existing deck in place, idempotently and comment-safely: it swaps ONLY the `cmh-deck-theme` block (inserting one after `cmh-deck-stage` if absent) and never touches slide markup, `data-slide-id` values, or the embedded-comments / handled-ids blocks. Because the block is `cm-skip` it carries no comment-offset text, so re-theming a commented deck to a different-length preset never shifts a stored anchor - a restored highlight keeps its original text on its original slide. The validation temp preserves raw newlines, so Windows cannot double CRLF before the validator reads it. The write is atomic and fails closed (source untouched) on a non-deck, an unknown preset, or a deck that does not validate; it refuses a repo example/source deck without `--force`, and `--list` prints the presets. It uses the same shared mode handling as the other in-place rewriters (`_atomic_io.preserve_mode` / `quiet_remove`), so re-theming a `0644` deck in place keeps it world-readable instead of narrowing it to the staging file's `0600`, a `--out` to a new path takes the source deck's mode, and a symlinked destination is resolved before the replace. | `tests/test_deck_theme_apply.py` - `test_apply_is_comment_safe_and_idempotent`, `test_retheme_to_different_length_preserves_slides_and_comment_blocks`, `test_non_deck_fails_closed`, `test_unknown_preset_fails_closed`, `test_out_writes_target_and_leaves_source_unchanged`, `test_refuses_repo_example_without_force`, `test_list_presets`, `test_apply_preserves_the_deck_file_mode`, `test_apply_out_to_a_new_file_takes_the_source_deck_mode`, `test_apply_through_a_symlink_rewrites_the_real_deck`, `test_apply_leaves_no_staging_file_when_the_write_fails`; `tests/70-deck-theme.spec.js` - `CMH-DECK-THEME-02: re-theming a commented deck keeps every anchor on its original text and slide` |

The tool pins the capture clock, random seed, viewport, locale, timezone, motion preferences, browser font rendering flags, CSS animation state, and capture fonts, then writes each screenshot to disk raw and full-resolution (crisp, true-color, with no downsampling or color quantization) and judges freshness by applying that determinism normalization (downsample plus color-quantize) to BOTH the committed and the freshly-captured image only at compare time, with a bounded pixel-diff tolerance, so the committed tutorial images stay crisp while repeated captures stay in sync across browser environments even when Chromium text rasterization jitters by a few pixels. Reading the static committed PNG bytes (never a fresh capture, so the metrics are deterministic across platforms), it fails the build if any shot is color-quantized/faded (fewer than 2% off-grid pixels, the signature of the old downsample+quantize normalization), smooth-blurred (variance-of-Laplacian sharpness below a floor, skipped for sub-3px strips), under-resolved (either side below a 64px minimum-dimension floor; an exact-resolution regression such as a 1x recapture is additionally pinned by `capture_tutorial.mjs --check`), left with excess blank vertical margin (contiguous blank top+bottom rows above a fraction, judged only for shots at least 400px tall so a short element strip's inherent padding is exempt; horizontal blank is not gated because full-width badge/checklist strips legitimately have narrow content), or washed with a load-flash yellow color-cast (fraction of strong-yellow pixels above a threshold that a legitimate small yellow highlight stays under). `npm run shots:quality` runs it standalone, `npm run shots:quality --report` prints the per-shot metrics for calibration, and `npm test` runs the covering spec, so a low-quality shot can never reach the published tutorial again. | `tests/55-shot-quality.spec.js` - `the committed tutorial screenshots pass the quality gate (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)`, `the quality gate rejects a degraded (downsampled + color-quantized) screenshot (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)`, `the quality gate rejects a smooth-blurred (non-quantized) screenshot (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)`, `the quality gate rejects an under-resolved screenshot (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)`, `the quality gate rejects a shot with excess blank vertical margin (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)`, `the quality gate rejects a yellow-cast (load-flash) screenshot (CMH-TUT-QUALITY-01)` |

## Coverage gaps

The following features are documented but lack full automated behavior coverage, or have a known mismatch between spec and documentation:

**Remaining manual or design-only gaps:**
- CMH-HARNESS-01: the harness PLUMBING (CI guard, scratch-under-tmp, prompt corpus, copilot command construction, validator wiring) is automated in `tests/test_skill_flow_harness.py`, but the END-TO-END live model invocation (`copilot -p` actually driving each skill flow) is non-hermetic, consumes AI credits, and is non-deterministic, so it is a deliberate manual, local-only check - never a CI gate.
- CMH-DECK-01: deck-intent detection and the "confirm before building a real deck" gate are an agent-behavior convention in `SKILL.md` ("Deck capability"), not an automated test.
- CMH-DECK-03b: the "prefer the Anthropic `pptx` skill when installed, fall back to the local extractor" preference is prompt-level wording in `SKILL.md`; only the deterministic escaping and the local fallback (CMH-DECK-03a) are automated.
- CMH-CONTENT-05: ADO resource links in authored content are a manual authoring convention with no validator or E2E enforcement.
- CMH-CONTENT-06: prose cross-reference links are only partially covered by TOC anchor tests.
- CMH-KQL-01: a framed KQL figure (`figure.cmh-kql`) is now hard-enforced to carry a Run in Azure Data Explorer link (CMH-KQL-07, a validator error). Bare, unframed `<pre>` KQL blocks are now also enforced (CMH-KQL-08): they must be marked `data-cmh-kql-no-cluster` when there is genuinely no cluster to run them on, so a missing cluster is a deliberate choice, not an accidental omission.
- CMH-CHART-05: chart recipe semantics, dark chart palette choices, and data hygiene rules are documentation and review conventions, not automated tests.
- CMH-WIDGET-18: widget drag suppresses text selection inside draggable cards by design; drag behavior is covered, but the selection-suppression decision itself is a manual UX contract.
- CMH-NET-01 / CMH-MMDLOAD-01: CDN opt-in and local vendoring choices are manual. CMH-MMDLOAD-01 now has E2E coverage for the default CDN path; manual guidance for vendor/self-host advice remains.

**Documentation/implementation mismatches (spec is correct; docs or tooling do not reflect it):**
- CMH-COPY-06: `references/limitations.md` implies all copy paths have the `prompt` fallback; only Copy all does. The per-block no-prompt rule now has E2E coverage, but the docs still need alignment outside this tests-only pass.
- CMH-SEC-01: the "callers must sanitize untrusted host HTML before wrapping" rule is stated in the spec and is now documented in `SKILL.md` (the "Trust boundary (MUST)" note) and `new_document.py --help`; it still has no automated enforcement in the validator or tooling.
## Packaging and first-run extraction

The plugin ships a compact `skills/commentable-html/` (only `SKILL.md`, `LICENSE`, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, and a single `skill-resources.zip`) so the CLI installer writes very few files. This matters on Windows, where Defender briefly locks each file as it is written and the installer aborts the whole install on the first transient lock (the `Access is denied. (os error 5)` failure) - a large file count almost never gets through. The bulky runtime (`tools/`, `references/`, `dist/`, `vendor/`) is assembled by `build.py` into `skill-resources.zip`, and a SessionStart hook unpacks it on first run per version, retrying the same transient lock the installer does not. The large tutorial (`docs/`) and worked examples (`examples/`) are NOT shipped; they live at the plugin top level and online. The editable + built skill STAGE tree lives at `dev/skill/`.

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |

| CMH-SIZE-01 | A document carries the vendored rich-libraries payload (`cmhVendoredRichLibs`, the mermaid + Chart.js descriptor the OFFLINE export resolves; it was a gzip+base64 bundle until CMH-SIZE-08 made it byte-free) only when its CONTENT can actually use it, and never in the document head. It used to be stamped unconditionally into the head: measured on the shipped examples it is 1,363 KB - 55 to 61 percent of a 2.3 MB file - and it landed on line 7, so a prose-and-code review document paid for a renderer it could never call AND any tool reading the head of the file hit a megabyte-long line immediately. `finalize` now runs a last phase that drops the payload from a document whose content uses no mermaid and no chart, restores it when the content GAINS one (the decision is re-evaluated on every finalize, not made once at creation, so a stripped document that later grows a diagram is not left with a broken offline export), and moves an existing head-placed payload to just before `</body>`. Detection is done with a real HTML parser in ONE pass, not a regex, and that is not a style choice: review found three false NEGATIVES and one case of DATA LOSS in the regex version, all on documents that strict-validated cleanly. `<canvas class=cmh-chart>` was missed (CSS does not require quotes); `<canvas title="A > B" class="cmh-chart">` was missed (a `[^>]*` scan stops at the `>` inside the quoted attribute and never reaches the class); a literal `</main>` inside an HTML COMMENT truncated the scan region and hid everything after it; and worst, a document DOCUMENTING this feature that shows the payload element as a commented-out example had that authored content DELETED, because the regex matched inside the comment. The parser is quote-aware, comment-aware, and treats `<script>` as raw text - the same reading the browser gives, which is what the runtime selectors are evaluated against - and one pass answers classification, payload location, and placement in about 20 ms on a 2.5 MB document. The scan region is `#commentRoot`, matching the runtime exactly rather than the narrower CONTENT-marker span, so rich content inside the root but outside the markers cannot be missed. A second review round found three more defects in the parser version, each now a red-first test: an authored (not commented) `<script id="cmhVendoredRichLibs">` used as an EXAMPLE inside the content was deleted on the second pass, so payload identification is now restricted to scripts OUTSIDE the content root; misnested markup a browser REPAIRS (`<p><figure class="chart"></p>...<canvas>`) classified UNUSED and got stripped, so a chart figure and a canvas CO-OCCURRING in the root now count regardless of nesting, and an unclosed root is recovered at end of input the way a browser closes it rather than reported unclassifiable; and restoring the payload located the end of body by substring search, which could pick a `</body>` inside an HTML comment and bury the 1.3 MB payload there invisibly - the body end is now recorded by the parser. Every payload copy is removed in one pass, so a stale second bundle cannot survive; when copies differ the one kept is the RICHEST rather than simply the last, because a stale refresh can leave a COMPLETE copy followed by a right-sized one and discarding the complete one would be permanent whenever no template is reachable to restore from. Two further invariants make it safe. Detection is scoped to the CONTENT region, because the built review layer's own JavaScript carries `pre.mermaid, div.mermaid, figure.chart canvas, canvas.cmh-chart` as a literal selector string - a whole-document scan matches EVERY document and silently turns the feature into a no-op. And a document whose CONTENT region cannot be located is classified `UNKNOWN` and left ENTIRELY alone: fail-safe means "do not strip", never "insert", so a minimal or foreign document is never grown by 1.3 MB. Measured end to end: a prose report goes from 2,301 KB to 938 KB (-59%) and its longest line from 1,396,078 characters to 631; a chart report keeps the payload but no longer in the head. The carry decision is now PER LIBRARY rather than all-or-nothing: the payload is one object holding mermaid (~1,265 KB base64) and Chart.js (~92 KB base64), so a chart-only document paid for a renderer it could never call. `apply()` reconciles the payload against what the content uses - dropping a half the document cannot call and COMPLETING a half when the content gains that library, which the earlier code could not do because it returned early for any already-placed payload without ever reading its contents. Four properties keep the trim safe. (1) An UNCLASSIFIABLE document is returned untouched by the FIRST branch, before any key-set logic: it has neither usage flag set, so a needed-set computed for it would be EMPTY and would strip a payload whose runtime still wants it (the runtime falls back to `<body>` when there is no content root) - fail-safe means leave it alone in the TRIM direction as well as the insert direction. (2) A library counts as carried only when its MIT NOTICE and a usable SOURCE are both present and non-blank - the source being either its BYTES or a complete URL+integrity descriptor (`_lib_source`, since CMH-SIZE-08; a URL with no hash is unverifiable and so counts as no source at all) - and a payload carrying one without the other is a MISMATCH that gets reconciled whenever a source pair is reachable, so orphan bytes are dropped rather than silently shipped. A library carrying BOTH forms at once is a mismatch too, since only one can ever be used and the unused one would keep a right-sized document paying for the megabyte it shed. The LIMIT is deliberate: when the content needs a library that neither the document nor a reachable template can supply, reconciliation returns nothing and the document is left byte-identical - orphans included - so the export fails loudly instead of the tool handing back a half-written payload that looks healthy. (3) The nesting-tolerant chart repair is gated on the CHART verdict alone - gating it on the combined verdict would let a diagram satisfy the flag, skip the repair, and drop the chart half of a document whose misnested markup a browser repairs into a real chart. (4) Placement and CONTENT are independent: a payload that cannot be parsed is left byte-for-byte intact but is still moved out of the head, the inner text span comes from the PARSER (so a `>` inside a quoted attribute and a padded `</script   >` are read as a browser reads them), and rewriting plus relocating are ONE splice against ONE scan's offsets. The serialize-and-escape rule has a single definition (`skill/tools/authoring/_vendored_payload.py`) that the build and the shipped authoring tool both import, and it signals with `ValueError` so an authoring run degrades instead of aborting an agent's write-back. | `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `NeedsDetectionTests` (including
