| CMH-SIZE-02 | A generated document stores a checklist item's identity ONCE. A survey of 15 generated documents (#1250) found their bodies compress 18.7x because a tree of ~1700 rows repeats the same attribute values on every row, and two were byte-identical on all 1725 items of one document: `data-cmh-item="X"` and an authored `data-<ns>-id="X"` - about 168 KB of provably duplicated data in one file, plus the same duplication again between `data-cmh-parent` and `data-<ns>-parent`. `dom_slim.slim` (a `finalize` phase, on by default, `--no-slim` opts out) drops the `data-cmh-*` copy and stamps the SOURCE attribute name once on the container as `data-cmh-item-attr` / `data-cmh-parent-attr`; the runtime, the validator and `checklist_apply.py` all DERIVE the id from the attribute the container names, preferring the item's own `data-cmh-item` while it is still there. The authored attribute survives, because a document's own CSS and tooling reference it. Six independent conditions must ALL hold, each one a defect a review round found by counterexample. (1) The identity must provably be the same one: every item carries the alias with a byte-identical value, an item WITHOUT `data-cmh-parent` must not carry the parent alias either, no NON-item inside the container may carry the alias, and a `data-cmh-*` attribute is never eligible. (2) Those absence tests read PRESENCE, not truthiness, because the runtime selects on `[alias]` and an EMPTY value satisfies that just as well - and so does the check for whether the container ALREADY names an alias, where reading `data-cmh-item-attr=""` as "absent" stripped every row of its id while the container rewrite was refused (the name was already on it), leaving a document with no identity at all and nothing to derive it from. (3) Ownership is ancestor-or-SELF and by attribute PRESENCE, matching the runtime's `closest("[data-cmh-checklist]") === container` exactly: an empty `data-cmh-checklist=""` is still a BOUNDARY (reading it as "not a checklist" made a nested container invisible and its rows were stripped as the outer list's), and a nested container is never an ITEM of the list around it (recording one made a ghost row that shifted every positional key after it - that one was wrong in `checklist_apply.py` and the validator, not in the trimmer). (4) Ownership must be PROVABLE on a tag-nesting tree: this reader nests by tag while a browser REPAIRS, so a container a browser closes implicitly - a `<p data-cmh-checklist>` holding block children, already closed when the browser reaches them - is refused outright, as is any `<p>` on the path between an item and its container; ordinary structural nesting a browser preserves (`tbody`/`tr` under a `table`, `ul`/`li` under a `div`) is how every real checklist is built and is not refused. (5) The rewrite is ALL-OR-NOTHING per checklist: every row's start tag and the container's are proved rewritable BEFORE anything is mutated, so the pointer can never be committed against rows that keep their ids, nor rows stripped against a container that never gets the pointer. (6) The document's OWN embedded runtime must be able to read the pointer, proved by the alias name appearing in an EXECUTABLE script (no `type`, or a JavaScript one) OUTSIDE the content root - the scoping rule CMH-SIZE-01 adopted for the same reason. That leaves a NONSHAREABLE document untouched, since its runtime is a sibling `commentable-html.js` this tool can neither see nor version and a stale companion would read the trimmed rows as unidentified and fall back to POSITIONAL keys, silently orphaning stored checklist state; it also refuses an older embedded runtime, an inert `text/plain` island that merely mentions the attribute, and an authored example inside the content root - a document DOCUMENTING this feature being exactly the shape CMH-SIZE-01 records as having been destroyed once by an unscoped scan. The alias NAME is constrained to `^data-[a-z0-9-]+$`, so a hand-written or hostile value can never reach `querySelectorAll` as a selector injection or throw; that pattern is spelled IDENTICALLY in all four implementations and pinned by a test, because it was not - the writer was stricter than the three readers, so the shared-pattern claim was untrue and a future edit to one spelling would have drifted in silence. | `tests/test_dom_slim.py` - `IdentityDedupeTests` (the dedupe, the parent link, and eleven refusals, each run BESIDE an ordinary control checklist that must still be trimmed so a refusal can never pass merely because the transform stopped running), `RuntimeGateTests` (a document with no readable runtime, an inert script, an authored example inside the content root, and a pin that the SHIPPED runtime does satisfy the gate), `MeasuredWinTests` (a corpus-shaped document really does get smaller and keeps every item and parent link), `FinalizePhaseTests` (the phase runs by default and the opt-out flag skips it), `RuntimeParityTests` (the runtime reads the same two container attributes and all four implementations spell the alias pattern identically); `tests/98-dom-slim.spec.js` - `CMH-SIZE-02: a trimmed checklist derives the same identity, states and storage as the authored one`, `CMH-SIZE-02: the derived parent link still aggregates, propagates and bakes into an export`; source: `tools/authoring/dom_slim.py`, `assets/js/36-checklist.js`, `tools/validate/checks/checklist.py`, `tools/checklist/checklist_apply.py` |
| CMH-SIZE-03 | The trim changes what a document STORES, never what it DOES, and TWO further transforms were tried and deliberately REMOVED rather than shipped. A document generated by an earlier version opens, comments, exports and reopens byte-for-byte as it always did, because the runtime prefers the authored `data-cmh-item` / `data-cmh-parent` and only falls back to the container-named attribute; a trimmed document resolves the identical item keys, so comment threads, handled-comment ids, reviewed-section state and checklist storage carry over with zero data loss, a rendered-DOM snapshot of a trimmed document matches its untrimmed twin, and keyboard cycling and the announced state are unchanged. The transform is scoped to the `#commentRoot` content region and fails SAFE: an unlocatable content root, a start tag the shared tokenizer does not fully consume, one carrying a CR (which the tokenizer folds to LF the way a browser does, so writing the pairs back would change the document's line endings), and anything inside FOREIGN content (where attribute names are case-sensitive - `viewBox` would come back as `viewbox` and break the rendering) are all left exactly as they were. Re-running is a no-op, including on every shipped example. The REMOVED transforms are recorded because each is easy to re-add by reflex and each was measured at ZERO effect on every document this repository ships - seven example reports, the 2.3 MB showcase deck and the kitchen-sink fixture - while changing something a reader can observe. A CLASS HOIST (moving a token every child shares onto its container and extending each `.token` selector-list entry with `[data-cmh-cls~="token"] > *`) could not be made sound by a static tool: a rule can live in a `<link>` stylesheet or behind an `@import` it never sees, a generic `[class]` selector stops matching either way, a CSS-escaped `.\74 ok` evades a token scan, and a child-combinator selector matches children added later - and worse, it WEAKENED an enforcement layer, because `cmhval/contrast.py` refuses any selector carrying a combinator, so the rewritten entry became invisible to the WCAG contrast checker while the `.token` entry left behind matched nothing, silently dropping list items and table cells from contrast coverage. Doing it correctly needs an ALLOW-list of name-from-content roles, on which it fires nowhere in the surveyed corpus - so it buys nothing in exchange for a silent, user-observable accessibility regression whenever the list is wrong. `title` is not trimmed either: it is redundant only while the whole text is on SCREEN, and under CSS truncation it is the only way to read the rest. A body is refused outright when it sits inside another table or a `<template>`, when a row is implicitly closed, or when anything but whitespace and comments sits between its tail rows (a browser foster-parents such text out of the table, so hydration would silently drop it). | CMH-SIZE-04 | The `class` attribute is left exactly as the author wrote it: nothing hoists, renames, requotes, or rewrites it. #1250 measured `class` as the largest repeated attribute in one sampled document (42135 occurrences over 139 distinct values, 799 KB); CMH-SIZE-03 records the hoist that was written for it and then removed (issue #1261); this row records the answer to what that left open - whether ANY sound reduction exists (issue #1267) - as a decision rather than a plan, together with the measurement that reached it. `dev/tools/class_cost.py` (maintainer-only, nothing ships) reports for any document the bytes its class attributes really occupy, the distinct values and tokens they spell, the CEILING of each candidate reduction, and the constructs that defeat a static class rewrite. The ceilings are deliberately of three different kinds, and the row's argument depends on the difference: `rename` and `normalize` are OVER-estimates that assume the transform is free, always applies, and is sound; `quote_elision` is EXACT; and `hoist` is neither, because what a hoist can reach depends on the tree shape - it is an OBSERVATION on the parsed tree, so the shape-free bound on ANY class reduction is instead the delete-every-class-attribute figure, which exceeds all of them. Measured over every REAL generated document this repository ships (all SEVEN: six reports plus the 2.3 MB showcase deck): class attributes are well under half a percent of the file (0.17 to 0.35 percent, 2.2 KB to 8.2 KB); the observed hoist never exceeds 1.2 KB (0.05 percent) and is 0 on four of the seven; the rename ceiling never exceeds 4.3 KB (0.18 percent); the whitespace-and-repeated-token ceiling is 0 bytes on all seven; and DELETING every class attribute outright - strictly more than any reduction could ever remove - saves only 2.2 KB to 8.2 KB raw and about 1 KB GZIPPED at most, because a small set of values repeated many times is precisely what DEFLATE already collapses. A sound reduction does therefore EXIST, and the honest form of the decision is that it is not worth doing rather than that none is possible: rewriting `class="solo"` as `class=solo` is a syntax-only change that provably leaves the class VALUE untouched, so no selector, checker, or runtime read can observe it. It is worth at most 0.6 KB (0.03 percent) on any shipped document (the maximum is on `deck-showcase.html`), and its ceiling is 2 bytes per single-token class attribute, so even on the 42135-attribute shape behind the 799 KB figure it could not exceed about 82 KB raw of a 3191 KB body - and gzip collapses that redundancy too, exactly as the delete-everything measurement above shows. The other purely syntactic candidates were checked and measure ZERO on all seven: no document uses a character reference inside a class value, a duplicate `class` attribute, an uppercase spelling, spacing around the `=`, or an already-unquoted or single-quoted class attribute. Every reduction that touches the VALUE fails on soundness instead, independently of size and for a document of ANY shape, including the 1725-row one: every generated document carries the review layer, and the layer ALONE makes a static rewrite unprovable. Its CSS and its runtime select on the class attribute STRING (`[class*="cmh-code-"]`, `[class*="cmh-kql-"]` and `[class*="reveal"]` in `assets/css/90-deck.css`, and `pre code[class*="language-"]` in `assets/js/26-highlight.js`, which substring-matches the AUTHORS own tokens at RUNTIME, long after any generator has finished), so what they match turns on substrings no rewrite preserves; and the layer reads, writes, or matches class strings more than 450 times in every shipped document. A rename restricted to tokens no statically-visible hazard names does not escape this: proving a token is untouched by a dynamically built string is the same unprovable problem, and CMH-SEC-01 makes it strictly impossible, since a document author runs arbitrary inline script by design and so can name any token in any spelling the scan cannot see. Those are properties of the LAYER, not of the content, which is why measuring more documents cannot change the answer. The decision is therefore WILL NOT DO for any value-changing reduction, and NOT WORTH DOING for the sound syntactic one; and because no transform ships, the WCAG contrast checker sees the identical element set, elements the review layer adds at runtime are untouched, and rules in linked or imported stylesheets, generic attribute selectors, and CSS-escaped spellings cannot be mis-resolved, there being nothing to resolve. The corpus tests are the TRIPWIRE that keeps the decision honest: they go red if a shipped document ever spends more than 2 percent of its bytes on class attributes, if deleting every class attribute would ever save more than 8 KB gzipped, or if a document ever stops carrying the LOAD-BEARING hazards the argument names (an `attribute_selector` and a `scripted_class`) - | CMH-SIZE-06 | Every machinery block is explicitly delimited and announced, so a machine reader can skip it cheaply and deterministically rather than heuristically. One `BEGIN/END: commentable-html - MACHINERY` pair fences the whole trailer; its opening comment states in words that everything below it is NON-CONTENT MACHINERY and not authored prose, and names what it holds. `NON-CONTENT` rather than `GENERATED` deliberately: a per-document chart bootstrap has to run after the layer runtime, so it lives in the fence too, and labelling it `generated` would have been simply false. Inside the fence each block carries its own start and end markers plus a leading one-line note (`commentable-html machinery (non-content; generated layer or per-document bootstrap) - skip to the END marker below.`), so a reader that entered mid-file can still tell where it is - and the covering test requires the note to LEAD its block (no other fenced block may sit between a note and the block it announces), because a single note at the top of the fence would otherwise satisfy a naive `is the note somewhere earlier` assertion for all five. The fence is the last thing in the body: nothing but `</body></html>` follows it, which is also where a relocated vendored payload lands (`vendored_libs` inserts just inside the fence rather than after it, so a finalized document does not dangle its largest block outside the fence that announces it). The markers use the SAME line-anchored comment shape the validator and the runtime already agree on, so the fence is located by the shipped matcher rather than by a substring search - which matters because a quoted marker inside authored content (the deck showcase quotes the runtime's own region-strip source) would otherwise be mistaken for a boundary. The fence's own prose deliberately does NOT spell its END marker literally, so a substring search for the marker cannot match the sentence that describes it. `MACHINERY` and `FIRST PAINT` are not members of the five swappable region names, so nothing about region counting, ordering, or the layer descriptor changes. | `tests/test_document_layout.py` - `MachineryFenceTests` (exactly one matched BEGIN/END pair per document, whose lead comment says it is non-content machinery; every fenced block is preceded by a note that LEADS it, checked through the shared `_assert_skip_notes_lead_blocks` helper that the retrofit trailer is held to as well; nothing but the closing tags follows the fence) |

| CMH-SIZE-08 | A generated document NAMES the vendored rich libraries instead of embedding them, and the Offline export downloads and verifies them at export time. `cmhVendoredRichLibs` used to carry mermaid and Chart.js as a 1,392,096-byte (1,359 KiB) gzip+base64 payload, and measurement showed the VIEWER never read a byte of it: `assets/template.shell.html` imports mermaid from the CDN, an authored Chart.js arrives as its own CDN `<script>` with an SRI hash, and the only consumer of the payload in the whole runtime is `68-export-offline.js` - so every reader downloaded over a megabyte to pre-stage an export most of them never run. Subsetting mermaid by diagram type was measured and REJECTED: its ESM build is code-split into a 657 KB always-loaded core plus lazy per-diagram chunks, so core + flowchart is still 243 KB and needs a bundler and per-document variants; dropping the bytes is simpler and strictly better. The payload is now a byte-free DESCRIPTOR of 2,629 bytes - `mermaidUrl` / `mermaidIntegrity` and `chartjsUrl` / `chartjsIntegrity`, where the `sha384-` hash is computed at build time from the very bytes in `assets/vendor/`, so verification compares against this repository and not against the CDN - with `mermaidLicense` / `chartjsLicense` still EMBEDDED, so MIT compliance never depends on the network. Resolution is PER LIBRARY and the needs gate comes first: a library the content cannot call is never downloaded, never decoded, and cannot fail an export, so neither an unrelated URL going bad nor an unrelated corrupt legacy half can take a working export down. `_offlineResolveVendoredLib` prefers embedded BYTES when a document has them, so every document generated before this change keeps exporting exactly as it did with no network at all; otherwise it fetches the pinned UMD build (deliberately not the ESM entry the viewer imports: the exporter drives `window.mermaid` as a classic global, and a UMD file is self-contained where the ESM entry would still lazy-fetch its per-diagram chunks), verifies it with SubtleCrypto against the recorded hash, and inlines it exactly where it used to inline the inflated bytes. The download sends NO referrer, so it never discloses which document is being exported. When a document needs both libraries the two downloads are STARTED together and awaited in a fixed order, so they overlap and share ONE time budget: charging each its own doubles the worst case a stalled CDN can cost, while running them in sequence under a shared one would let a slow but working first download starve the second and refuse an export that was going to succeed, and the fixed await order keeps the error a reader sees deterministic for a given document. Failure is LOUD and produces NO download, with a message naming the library and the actual problem: a blocked or failed request, bytes that do not match the recorded hash, a malformed hash (never a reason to skip the check), a recorded URL that is not https, a REDIRECT that lands on a non-https address (Chromium refuses that downgrade at the network layer before the response comes back, and `response.url` is re-checked after the fetch as the backstop for any engine that does not, so the https-only refusal is a property of the transport the bytes actually travelled over and not merely of the recorded string), a payload that is present but is not an OBJECT (a broken infrastructure block, which must refuse rather than resolve every library to nothing and hand the export to the document's own copies), a page that is not a SECURE CONTEXT - where the browser withholds SubtleCrypto, so the message names the fix (open the file locally, or serve it over https) rather than the missing API - and a connection that is accepted and then never answers, which an `AbortController` bounds on a deliberately generous budget (mermaid's UMD build is ~3.5 MB, and killing a slow but working download would be a worse failure than the hang it prevents). A HALF descriptor - a URL with no hash, or a hash with no URL - is refused too, and that distinction is load-bearing: neither half present means the payload legitimately does not carry the library (it was right-sized out, or this is a re-export) and the ordinary missing-bundle path applies, but exactly one half present is a BROKEN descriptor, and reading it as absence would hand the export to the document's own unverified copy - the silent substitution `CMH-OFFLINE-07` exists to prevent. The authoring side accepts a descriptor only on the terms the RUNTIME will: an https URL and an exactly-`sha384-<base64>` hash. Without that parity a hand-edited `http:` URL or a truncated hash would leave `payload_matches` reporting the document settled, so `finalize` would leave it alone while the export kept refusing it - and the refusal's own advice, to re-run finalize, could never fix it. Treating an invalid descriptor as NO source instead routes it through `reconcile`, which replaces it from the canonical template. Because the recorded URL's version and the hashed bytes must describe the SAME release or every export of that library fails permanently, both libraries are held to a byte-level provenance guard against the installed npm tarball (`CMH-BUILD-25` for mermaid; the Chart.js half is new here, and closes a gap that only became load-bearing when the version string became a live URL). The trade is deliberate and recorded: this ONE export needs a connection; the file it produces is unchanged - still self-contained under the same zero-network CSP - and `tools/build.py --vendor-bytes` restores the old embedded form for an author who must export with no network at all (never used by the committed build, so it is refused alongside `--check` and does not enforce the size budget). Measured on the shipped examples: `report-metrics.html` 2,217,964 -> 831,745 bytes (-62%), the four diagram-carrying examples each down 57 to 62 percent, and the whole example corpus down 47 percent (12,035,861 -> 6,406,508 bytes). | `tests/test_vendored_libs.py` - `ByteFreeDescriptorTests` (a URL+integrity pair counts as carrying the library, a URL without a hash and a descriptor without its notice do not, a legacy byte payload is still honoured, reconciliation keeps a descriptor descriptor-shaped rather than re-inflating it, and the BUILD emits no library bytes), `MixedFormPayloadTests` (a payload carrying both forms for one library is a mismatch; the duplicate-payload merge replaces a library's whole form instead of leaving the two side by side; and a descriptor the runtime would refuse - a non-https URL, a non-`sha384` or malformed hash - counts as no source at all, while the shape the build emits still counts); | CMH-SIZE-09 | No shipped example INLINES a copy of Chart.js or mermaid; a document that draws charts reaches Chart.js through a version-pinned, SRI-guarded CDN loader. The rule names those two libraries rather than claiming to catch any embedded library, because that is what the covering test can actually detect: it looks for a script body over 50 KB carrying a Chart.js or mermaid vendor banner, exempting only the build-stamped `cmhVendoredRichLibs` payload (which the `--vendor-bytes` escape hatch legitimately fills with megabytes of library, and which `CMH-SIZE-08` and `CMH-BUILD-25` already govern), and every document legitimately carries one large script already - the review layer itself, which has no such banner. `report-community-garden` and `report-taxi` pin `chart.js@4.5.1/dist/chart.umd.min.js`, which is DELIBERATELY not the `chart.js@4.4.0/dist/chart.umd.js` that `tools/blocks/chart_block.py` emits and that `report-metrics` and `report-triage` still use: 4.5.1 minified is the byte-identical copy in `assets/vendor/`, so the loader's `integrity` is that file's own SHA-384 and the version the viewer loads is the version an Offline export inlines. That single-sourcing is the reason for the divergence, and it is what lets the covering test check the hash by VALUE - without which a Chart.js bump would move `assets/vendor/`, the payload descriptor and the `CMH-SIZE-08` provenance guard while leaving these loaders behind, SRI would block the script, and the `typeof Chart === "undefined"` guard would swallow it into silently blank charts. `report-community-garden` and `report-taxi` each inlined a complete `Chart.js v4.4.0` bundle (205,031 bytes) as authored content, which made them the two largest shipped documents. That was correct when a self-contained file had to ship its own renderer and is not any more: the viewer loads the pinned CDN copy, and since `CMH-SIZE-08` Export Offline downloads the vendored build, verifies it against a build-recorded SHA-384, and inlines it. An authored copy is therefore pure weight that no provenance guard covers - `CMH-BUILD-25` pins mermaid and `CMH-SIZE-08` pins Chart.js to the npm tarball, but neither reaches a body pasted into a document - and it was stale at 4.4.0 while the payload pinned 4.5.1. **It also inverted the export's own guarantee**, which is the part worth remembering: the exporter hoists author code BELOW the library it inlines so a constructing script cannot run before its dependency, and that hoist placed the authored copy AFTER the verified one, so the UNVERIFIED 4.4.0 deterministically won `window.Chart` while the downloaded, hash-checked 4.5.1 sat inert. Measured on a real export, not inferred: 4 canvases drawn, 0 errors, 0 network requests, `window.Chart.version === "4.4.0"`. Nothing was broken by it, which is why this is recorded as a property of the shipped examples rather than as a runtime defect - the behaviour remains reachable in principle for any document that carries its own copy of a library the export also inlines, and `CMH-OFFLINE-07`'s payload-wins rule governs only copies the exporter itself marked, never an authored body it is not allowed to touch (`CMH-SEC-01`). No SHIPPED example exercises that shape once these two are fixed. The claim is deliberately scoped to the shipped set rather than to the repository, and the covering test therefore scans `plugins/commentable-html/examples`, which is what ships, and says so rather than overclaiming. That scoping originally mattered because `dev/examples/*.html` (as distinct from its `src/` sources) were tracked ORPHANED build copies, last written by #1258 and referenced by nothing, which still carried the 205 KB body long after this row removed it from the shipped files. #1293 deleted them and `CMH-BUILD-29` now forbids their return, so that particular blind spot is closed; the scoping stays because it is the honest description of what the test measures, not because the orphans are still there. The TRADE is explicit and is the reason this is a spec row rather than a silent edit: those two documents were self-contained FOR CHARTS and now are not, matching the other two chart examples. Opened with no network at all the charts are blank - measured: the layer still loads, all four canvases and their captions are present, 13,170 characters of prose are readable, the comment layer works, and there are ZERO page errors, because the init is guarded with `typeof Chart === "undefined"` exactly as `CMH-CHART-03` requires. A reader who needs charts without a network uses Export Offline, which is what it is for. The paired rule is that removing a library must not leave the charts dead: an example that constructs a Chart must still carry a loader pinned to a FULL `x.y.z` version (a floating jsDelivr specifier such as `@4` or `@4.5` follows upstream releases, which is precisely what an integrity hash cannot survive) with Subresource Integrity and `crossorigin`, the last because SRI cannot be enforced on a cross-origin script without it. The covering test matches those attributes INDEPENDENTLY, since HTML attribute order is free and an ordered pattern would fail a correct tag that writes them in another order, and it checks ORDER and SYNCHRONY too: the loader tag must precede the first `new Chart(` in a script body and must carry no `defer`, `async` or `type="module"`, because the parse-time init is guarded with `typeof Chart === "undefined"` and would otherwise no-op into a permanently blank canvas with no error. Exactness matters because the capture can be pointed at an arbitrary example: answering some other document's request with these bytes fails that document's `integrity` check, and the `typeof Chart === "undefined"` guard turns that into a silently blank canvas in a committed screenshot rather than the honest catch-all abort. | CMH-COLD-09 | The cold tier's LOAD-TIME cost is MEASURED, by a repeatable harness rather than an argument. `tools/cold_tier_perf.mjs` stages a corpus of real layer documents (including the 3.2 MiB tree-heavy shape the #1250 survey found largest), compresses a copy of each with the SHIPPED `cold_tier.py`, opens both from `file://` in a freshly launched Chromium (COLD) and again after a reload (WARM), and reports first paint (the browser's own paint-timing entry, recording WHICH of `first-contentful-paint` / `first-paint` produced each sample so a run cannot silently average two different metrics), time to interactive (the exact instant the layer sets `window.__commentableHtmlReady`, captured by an accessor installed before the document runs, not by polling), the longest main-thread task and the total long-task time, and the count of BLANK loads whose first paint landed at or after `domInteractive` - the reader saw NOTHING until the parser finished. Four methodology rules carry the result, each of them a mistake this harness made first. (1) ORDER IS COUNTERBALANCED and every delta is the median of per-iteration PAIRED differences: measuring OFF then ON every time hands ON a warmed machine, the direction that would flatter the tier. (2) PAINT IS OBSERVED, not read at `load` - on a compressed document `load` regularly fires BEFORE the first paint, so a single read at `load` scored exactly the worst documents as "not measured". (3) SIGNIFICANCE, NOT A THRESHOLD. The compressed paint distribution is BIMODAL, so a median over it is a coin flip and a zero-tolerance rule is below the measurement's own noise floor: pairing a document's OFF samples against a rotation of THEMSELVES - a null control, the same file with no tier - produced p75 deltas of +12 to +132 ms, so a `p75 > 0` rule failed a document compared with itself and could never return PASS. Paint is therefore judged by one-sided SIGN TESTS at alpha 0.05, over the paired timing deltas and over the McNemar-style discordant blank loads; a nominally slower but non-significant result is reported as INCONCLUSIVE rather than counted as a regression. (4) A document that was not really measured FAILS and short-circuits: a tier that DECLINED to compress (both files identical, every delta a flattering zero), a hydration that did not restore every row (`CMH-COLD-06` makes that non-blocking, so it would read as a large improvement), or a load that never reported both numbers. The recorded run - 10 iterations per document, Windows/Chromium 149, reference machine, committed as `tools/cold-tier-perf-baseline.json` so every figure here has a checkable source - says: TIME TO INTERACTIVE is inside the 150 ms budget on every document (+5.1 ms cold / +3.3 warm on 0.03 MB, +62.9 / -30.7 on 0.7 MB) and is far BETTER than the plain document on the largest one (-1006 ms cold, -1799 ms warm), so #1263's interactivity criterion is MET. FIRST PAINT is NOT met COLD at the shipped thresholds: the blank-until-parsed rate rises from 0/10 to 5/10 on the 0.7 MB document (sign test p=0.031) and 0/10 to 7/10 on the 3.2 MiB one (p=0.008). Warm paint is equal or better on both, and the smallest document is INCONCLUSIVE in both states: its paired timing deltas are a coin flip (4 of 8 paired loads slower cold, p=0.64; 5 of 9 warm, p=0.50) and its blank counts, while nominally higher with the tier on (5/10 to 7/10 cold, 4/10 to 6/10 warm), rest on 3 discordant loads against 1 (p=0.31) and 2 against 0 (p=0.25). Inside a 2.2 MB layer document a 0.03 MB body reaches `domInteractive` and first paint within tens of milliseconds either way - the median margin moves from -32 ms to +17 ms - so a load falls either side of that line for reasons the tier does not control. The harness reports that as inconclusive rather than scoring it in either direction. The cause is structural: hydration is synchronous and parser-blocking by construction (`CMH-COLD-04`), and a compressed document's skeleton is so small that the parser reaches that script almost immediately, so a load either wins the race to paint the skeleton first or waits for hydration AND the layout of every restored row. Both of #1263's remediation levers were then MEASURED rather than argued away, and they did not answer the same way. The decoder was NOT SHOWN to be the lever, and the harness deliberately does not claim more than it measured: it does not isolate decode time from the insertion and layout that share the same task, so nothing here bounds what a faster decoder alone would buy. What it does show is that the tier does not add main-thread work overall - TOTAL long-task time FALLS with it on (8230 ms against 9156 ms on the largest document cold) - while the work concentrates into a single parser-blocking window that grows by 748 ms (3452 ms against 2704 ms). The deferral is therefore a SCHEDULING outcome (no paint opportunity before that window) rather than an amount of work, which is why the lever that did move it was the row threshold rather than raw speed; isolating decode cost is left to #1273 if the retune ever needs it. Raising the row thresholds IS the lever: at `--keep-rows 1000` the largest document's blank rate falls to 2/8 and stops being significant (p=0.25) and its paired cold paint delta is -64 ms, so it PASSES the paint bound, for 209,524 bytes of the compression win (3,295,594 against 3,086,070, from 5,546,695 uncompressed) - while forcing `min_rows` above 1000 makes the tier DECLINE the 0.7 MB document outright, which is "only engage where it pays" working as intended. Choosing a shipped default from one sweep point would be over-fitting, and it is a shipped-source change, so the retune is tracked as #1273 and the tier stays OPT-IN and default OFF (`CMH-COLD-08`) meanwhile; #1263's paint criterion is RENEGOTIATED with these numbers rather than ticked. The numbers are a reference-machine baseline, not a CI threshold - a timing assertion on a shared runner would be a flake rather than a gate - so the tests pin the harness's METHOD and its verdict logic, and the baseline artifact records the run. | `tests/86-cold-tier-perf.spec.js` - `measures paint and time-to-interactive on a real compressed document (CMH-COLD-09)`, `observes the main-thread blocking window in a real browser (CMH-COLD-09)`, `sources every timing from the pre-load probe, not from a read at load (CMH-COLD-09)`, `records an empty sample instead of losing the run when a load times out (CMH-COLD-09)`, `the corpus carries the largest surveyed shape and stages real layer documents (CMH-COLD-09)`, `the verdict enforces the paint and interactivity bounds #1263 set (CMH-COLD-09)`, `a nominally slower but insignificant result is inconclusive, not a regression (CMH-COLD-09)`, `an unmeasured document fails instead of scoring a flattering zero (CMH-COLD-09)`, `deltas are paired per iteration and the run is counterbalanced (CMH-COLD-09)`, `a mistyped numeric option is refused rather than silently disabling a bound (CMH-COLD-09)`, `the summary reports the median, the spread and the blank-until-parsed loads (CMH-COLD-09)`, `the recorded baseline is a real harness result and backs the figures the spec quotes (CMH-COLD-09)`; source: `tools/cold_tier_perf.mjs`, `tools/cold-tier-perf-baseline.json` |
| CMH-COLD-10 | The tier's row thresholds are chosen by MEASUREMENT, at a sample size that can actually reject, and the shipped defaults are `keep_rows` 2000 / `min_rows` 4000. `CMH-COLD-09` measured the previously shipped 20/40 pair as costing COLD FIRST PAINT, and re-measuring it at 30 paired iterations makes the size of that regression plain: on the largest document it painted nothing until the parser had finished on 19 of 30 cold loads against 0 of 30 with the tier off, and its median cold first paint went 332 ms to 4952 ms; the mid-size document went blank on 22 of 30 (median 292 ms to 1462 ms) and on 8 of 30 WARM loads. That is why #1263's paint criterion could not be ticked. The remedy #1263 named - raise the thresholds so the tier only engages where it pays - is measured in TWO STAGES, because the one-stage version gets the answer WRONG. Stage 1 SCREENS six pairs (20/40, 100/200, 250/500, 500/1000, 1000/2000, 2000/4000) over the whole corpus at 10 iterations; stage 2 CONFIRMS the candidate, the runner-up and the shipped baseline on a FRESH sample at 30. An exact sign test cannot reject below 5 DISCORDANT pairs - a property of that count, not of the iteration count - so at 10 iterations a pair can clear the gate purely by producing few of them: 1000/2000 cleared the screen (3 of 10, p=0.125) and FAILED the confirmation (10 of 30, p=0.00098). Reading the screen as a result would have shipped a pair that still regresses. The GATE is the paired blank-until-parsed sign test against the PLAIN document, cold AND warm, on every MEASURED document; paint time and time-to-interactive are recorded beside it as corroboration, not as extra pass conditions, and the blank RATE rather than a median is the reader-honest statistic because the paint distribution is BIMODAL - a load either paints in a few hundred ms or not until parse end. At 2000/4000 the largest document goes blank on 1 of 30 cold loads against 0 of 30, paint time shows no detectable change (+4 ms here, -88 ms on the same pair's screen run, so the two runs bracket zero), warm is identical on both, and time to interactive stays far BETTER than plain (-1517 ms cold, -1849 ms warm). Both stages, with the counts each p-value is computed from, are committed at `dev/tools/cold-tier-threshold-sweep.json` so a reader recomputes rather than trusts them. FOUR LIMITS are recorded rather than papered over, because a non-rejection is not a proof of equivalence. (1) The residual is BOUNDED, not zero: 1 of 30 puts a one-sided 95 percent Clopper-Pearson bound of 14.9 percent on the blank rate, and this design has 17.5 percent power against a true 10 percent rate - so the decision is a judgement made on a large measured improvement with the residual bounded above, not a demonstration of parity. (2) The measurement is EXTRAPOLATED at the gate: the corpus bodies are 200, 900 and 11500 rows, both smaller documents DECLINE at the chosen pair, so the entire result rests on the 11500-row body while `min_rows` gates at 4000 - the paint behavior of a document just over the threshold is unobserved, and `keep_rows`/`min_rows` were held at a fixed 1:2 ratio so nothing isolates `min_rows`. (3) A document the tier DECLINES measured nothing (both variants are the same bytes) and is excluded rather than counted as a pass; those byte-identical comparisons are also this measurement's false-positive floor, and it is not small - they reach blankP 0.0625 and ttiP 0.0107 with zero true effect. (4) Points were run sequentially, so the BETWEEN-point comparison is uncontrolled for machine drift; the confirmation re-measured the candidates on a fresh sample, which is what the ranking rests on. This sweep therefore diverges from `cold_tier_perf.mjs`'s own verdict in three enumerated ways (declined documents excluded rather than failed; its paired FMP sign test not used as a gate, since its smallest p anywhere in the screen is 0.1719 and gating on it would pass the very defaults being replaced; its TTI budget not re-imposed, since every confirmed point is far better than plain), all three recorded in the artifact. The trade is stated in bytes: the corpus win falls from 3,047,017 to 2,036,590, of which 586,392 is the two mid-size documents dropping out of the tier ENTIRELY and 424,035 is the largest document's shorter tail (it keeps 82.8 percent of its saving; 3,510,105 bytes instead of 3,086,070, against 5,546,695 uncompressed). Say plainly what that means for reach: at the chosen pair the tier engages on ONE of the three measured documents, so the whole 2,036,590 is that one 11500-row body; the eligible set narrows from a single `<tbody>` over 40 rows to one over 4000; and the roughly 1700-row generated shape `CMH-SIZE-02` records from the #1250 survey no longer engages at all. That narrowing is the measured PRICE of the paint bound, not an incidental benefit. Nothing a reader sees changes: the tier is opt-in and default OFF (`CMH-COLD-08`), and a recorded scan of every document this repository ships (all seven examples plus the upgrade corpus) shows it engages at NEITHER the old nor the new defaults, so this moves what `finalize.py --cold-tier` does when it is asked for, not what any shipped document does today. | `tests/test_cold_tier.py` - `ThresholdChoiceTests` (the shipped defaults are the pair the measurement chose; the screen and confirmation grids and the corpus are pinned exactly; every recorded p-value in BOTH stages is recomputed from its own counts; the gate is described identically everywhere; all three divergences from the harness are enumerated; the power floor, the null control, the drift and the coverage limit are recorded; the residual is a recomputed Clopper-Pearson bound rather than prose; the confirmation is powered to reject and does reject the baseline; the screen alone would have chosen a pair the confirmation rejects; a declined document is unmeasured rather than passing; and the shipped-document scan is re-run against the real files), `DerivedFixtureTests`, `ShippedThresholdPipelineTests`, `SpecFixtureTests` (the browser fixture is a body the shipped defaults would really compress), `EligibilityTests`, `SkeletonTests` (fixture sizes derive from the shipped thresholds, so retuning them can never silently turn an eligibility test into a no-op); source: `tools/authoring/cold_tier.py`, `dev/tools/cold-tier-threshold-sweep.json` |
## Doc-surface coverage (feature visibility)

Every user-facing feature must be discoverable from at least one documentation SURFACE, and every new
feature must declare where it is surfaced (or opt out) in the same pull request. The reader-facing
surfaces are:

- `tutorial` - the guided walkthrough in `docs/TUTORIAL.md` (the site tutorial page is generated from it).
- `site` - the marketplace pages under `site/pages/commentable-html` (a highlights page, not exhaustive).
- `help` - the in-runtime Help/About panel (`dev/assets/js/75-help.js`).

There is also a fourth SHOWCASE surface, tracked as its own required dimension:

- `deck` - the showcase presentation (`examples/deck-showcase.html`, built from
  `dev/examples/src/deck-showcase.html`), which runs the real runtime and demonstrates features as live
  interactive slides (or, where a live demo is impractical, a screenshot or an explicit on-slide
  mention). Because the deck has its own requirement - every user-facing feature should be demonstrated
  on a slide - it is a SEPARATE column in the registry, not one of the reader-doc surfaces above.

Governance rule (enforced): when a pull request adds a NEW feature-id row to this spec, it must also add
a row for that id to the "Doc-surface registry" table below with BOTH:

- a `Doc surface` value: one or more surfaces (a comma-separated subset of `tutorial`, `site`, `help`)
  OR `opt-out: <reason>` for a change that is not user-facing (internal hardening, build/authoring
  tooling, a robustness invariant, a security guard, an agent-facing export format, etc.), and
- a `Deck` value: `deck` when the feature is demonstrated on a showcase-deck slide (live demo,
  screenshot, or an explicit mention), OR `opt-out: <reason>` when it genuinely does not warrant a
  slide (a non-user-facing change, an in-runtime-panel-only detail, an internal robustness invariant).

`scripts/check_doc_surfaces.py` fails a PR whose newly added feature ids lack a registry entry, fails a
registry row that is missing either column or carries a malformed value, and fails if a registry row
names an id that no longer exists. Prefer a real surface and a real deck slide; use `opt-out` only when
the behavior is genuinely not something a reader needs documented or a viewer needs shown.

## Renamed feature ids (the ledger)

One feature id owns exactly ONE row (`CMH-BUILD-21` enforces it). When issue #904 found ids that
owned two rows each, the row touching the least reader-facing surface was given a free id. A reader
who follows an older `CHANGELOG.md` entry citing the OLD id lands on the row that KEPT it, which
now describes a different behavior, and released changelog history is never edited - so the mapping
lives here instead. This is a bullet list, not a table, deliberately: a table row starting with a
feature id would itself read as a second spec row for that id.

- `CMH-BUILD-13` -> `CMH-BUILD-21` for the `scripts/check_spec_test_refs.py` spec-to-test gate.
  `CMH-BUILD-13` kept the duration-based Playwright shard-balancing behavior, which AGENTS.md,
  `docs/testing-guidelines.md`, and the `tests/00-projects.spec.js` titles all mean by that id.
- `CMH-CONTENT-01` -> `CMH-CONTENT-IO-01`, `CMH-CONTENT-02` -> `CMH-CONTENT-IO-02`,
  `CMH-CONTENT-03` -> `CMH-CONTENT-IO-03`, and `CMH-CONTENT-04` -> `CMH-CONTENT-IO-04` for the
  `tools/authoring/` content round-trip tools (content extract/replace, edit locality, and the
  embedded-comment export). `CMH-CONTENT-01..04` kept the visual content-styling behaviors (section
  cards, tables, badges, the authored TOC), which own that number space up to `CMH-CONTENT-19`. A
  changelog entry citing `CMH-CONTENT-01..04` for the agent review loop means the `-IO-` ids.
- `CMH-DECK-21` -> `CMH-DECK-43` for the deck table-cell hover highlight. `CMH-DECK-21` kept the
  deck chrome project link and Overview/count pill styling, which claimed the id first. A changelog
  entry citing `CMH-DECK-21` for hover smoothness means `CMH-DECK-43`.
